Least privilege means every user and service gets only the permissions its job needs, nothing more. Identity and access management (IAM) is the system that grants those permissions. Data residency is a rule about the physical region where data is stored and processed. Encryption at rest protects stored data, and encryption in transit protects data moving across a network. Audit logging records who did what and when, so you can prove it later. Compliance is the set of outside rules you must show you follow.

Worked example: a health-records app with an invoicing service. Step 1: classify the data. Patient records are regulated and must stay in one region. Invoices are less sensitive. Step 2: set the location rule for the regulated store and refuse resources created elsewhere. Step 3: give the invoicing service read access to invoice data only, not to patient records. Step 4: turn on audit logs for every read of patient records and keep them for the period the regulation requires. Step 5: test the rule by trying an out-of-region create and an out-of-scope read, and confirming both are blocked and logged.

Common mistake: granting a team a broad project-wide owner role 'to unblock them' and planning to narrow it later. It rarely gets narrowed.

Consequence in a running system: if the invoicing service's credentials leak, an over-broad role exposes every patient record, and missing audit logs mean you cannot show regulators what was accessed. Security and compliance are part of the design, and they are judged by the Security, Privacy, and Compliance pillar of the Well-Architected Framework.

questions.prompt: A small lender stores loan application files in a bucket that must stay in the EU, and a reporting service needs to compute monthly approval rates. The design so far: Step 1, classify the loan files as regulated personal data. Step 2, set a location rule so the bucket stays in an EU region and resources created elsewhere are refused. Step 3, give the reporting service read access to an aggregated summary dataset only, not to the raw loan files. Step 4 is missing. Which action completes the design at that point?
choices: Turn on audit logging for reads of the raw loan files and keep those logs for the period the regulation requires.
Enable encryption in transit between the bucket and the reporting service, and skip logging because the data is encrypted.
Grant the reporting service the project owner role so its queries never fail, and review it later.
Move the loan files to the cheapest US region, since the reporting service is in the US.
questions.why: Audit logging of reads on the regulated store, kept for the required period, is the step that lets you later prove who accessed the data, and the other choices either widen access, break the residency rule, or replace logging with encryption, which does not provide that proof.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines least privilege?
choices: Each user and service is granted only the permissions its job requires, and no more.
Every user and service has the same role within a project so that no one is blocked.
Only administrators are allowed to create resources, and all other staff are read-only everywhere.
Permissions are reviewed once a year and removed only after an incident.
questions.why: Least privilege means each identity gets only the permissions its job needs, which is exactly the second statement, while the others describe broad access, infrequent review, or a different rule about who may create resources.

questions.prompt: A retail analytics service account holds a role that can read and write to four storage buckets, but its job only needs to read one of them. Its key is accidentally published online. What is the main exposure?
choices: Only the one bucket the service actually reads from, because that is the only one it uses.
Only the audit logs, because the attacker cannot change data without them being recorded.
Nothing, because a published key is useless without the matching service name.
All four buckets, because the leaked credentials carry the broad role rather than the single permission the job needs.
questions.why: A leaked credential exposes whatever its role allows, so an over-broad role on the service account means all four buckets are reachable, not just the one the job uses.

questions.prompt: A healthcare startup must keep its patient scheduling records physically stored and processed in Canada. Which design choice most directly enforces this data residency rule?
choices: Restrict resource creation so the scheduling store can only be placed in a Canadian region, and refuse resources created elsewhere.
Rely on a yearly policy document that asks engineers to choose Canadian regions manually.
Store the records in any region and turn on audit logs so you can see where they went.
Encrypt the records at rest with a strong key and assume the location does not matter.
questions.why: Data residency is about the physical region where data is stored and processed, so enforcing a location rule that only allows Canadian regions is the direct control, whereas encryption, manual policy, or logging do not fix where the data physically sits.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why access rules, data location and audit logging should be decided at design time rather than after launch, and name one limit or tradeoff of locking these down early.
lessons.modelAnswer: Decisions about who can access data, where it lives and what gets logged are cheap to make on paper and expensive to change once real users and services depend on them. If we add them after launch, we tend to inherit broad permissions that teams have grown used to, data already sitting in the wrong region, and gaps in logs we cannot reconstruct. Setting them early also gives us something to test against. The tradeoff is that strict rules early can slow delivery and block experiments, and we may guess wrong about future needs. So I would keep the rules few and specific, review them when requirements change, and accept some friction in exchange for being able to prove compliance later.
rubricPoints: Explains early decisions are cheaper and more complete than retrofitting protections after launch
Connects least privilege and data residency to a concrete design choice
Names a real tradeoff, such as slower delivery or the risk of wrong early assumptions
Mentions audit logging as evidence for compliance reviews

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style regulated-data scenario, choosing access, location and logging decisions together, adds the most to this objective.

lessons.plain: Observability means building a system so you can work out what is happening inside it from the signals it reports, without guessing or logging in to poke around. Designing for it from the start means deciding, before anything is built, which signals the system will emit and who will read them. Think of a car dashboard: speed, fuel, and warning lights tell the driver what is going on before the engine fails. Teams that skip this learn about problems from angry customers. Teams that plan it can see trouble forming and often fix it before users notice. In a cloud design, this is a decision made on the drawing board, not an add-on after launch.
lessons.guessPrompt: A checkout service is slow for some customers but not others, and nobody can tell why from outside the system. Before launch, what is the first piece of information you would have wanted the team to record, and why would that help?
lessons.teach: Observability is the ability to understand a running system's internal state from the outputs it produces. Those outputs are usually three kinds of signal. A metric is a number sampled over time, such as request count, error rate, or latency at the 95th percentile (the time that 95 percent of requests finish under). A log is a timestamped record of a discrete event, such as an error with its message. A trace follows one request as it passes through several services, recording how long each step took. An alert is a rule that notifies a person when a metric crosses a threshold for a set period. Designing for observability means choosing these signals so they can answer questions you have not yet thought of, and tagging them with context such as service name, version, and region so you can slice the data. This decision mainly serves the Operational Excellence pillar of the Well-Architected Framework, and it supports Reliability. Worked example: an order API. Step 1: a latency metric per endpoint shows the 95th percentile jumping from 200 ms to 2 s at 09:00. Step 2: logs from that minute show database connection timeouts. Step 3: a trace of one slow request shows 1.8 s spent waiting on the inventory service. Step 4: an alert configured for 'p95 above 1 s for 5 minutes' paged the on-call engineer within minutes. Common mistake: collecting enormous volumes of logs with no defined question, or relying only on averages, which hide the slow tail that customers actually feel. Consequence in a running system: without the alert and the per-endpoint breakdown, the team hears about the slowdown from support tickets, and the rollback decision waits on guesswork while customers are affected.

questions.prompt: A ride-booking company's fare-quote service has an error rate (the share of requests that fail) of 0.2% before a deploy and 4% after it, in one region only. Step 1: an error-rate metric labelled by region and version shows the jump is confined to eu-west and version 2.4.1. Step 2: logs from eu-west show 'currency service returned 503' messages. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: an alert set to 'error rate above 1% for 5 minutes' paged the on-call engineer at 14:16. Which choice correctly fills the missing Step 3?
choices: Step 3: the team raises the alert threshold to 5% so the page stops until the next business day.
Step 3: the team archives all logs older than seven days to reduce storage cost.
Step 3: a trace of one failed request, where a trace records the timed steps of one request, shows the time goes to the outbound currency-service call, placing the failure at that dependency.
Step 3: the team restarts all fare-quote instances so the errors clear before anyone checks the cause.
questions.why: A trace of the failing request is the step that connects the logged dependency error to the specific call where time and failure sit, whereas the other choices hide the signal, silence the alert, or discard data without answering the question.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team's label-printing endpoint averages 1 second per request, but a few staff report waits of 10 seconds. Which measurement best exposes the slow requests that staff actually feel?
choices: The average latency across all endpoints, since it summarises every request.
The total count of requests per hour, since more traffic causes slowdowns.
The number of log lines written per day, since verbose logs reveal slow requests.
The 95th percentile latency per endpoint, meaning the time within which 95 percent of requests finish.
questions.why: Averages hide the slow tail, while a per-endpoint 95th percentile shows the time that most requests stay under and exposes the slow requests people feel.

questions.prompt: A team logs every warehouse scan with its full payload, roughly 4 TB a month, but nobody has written down what question the logs should answer. What is the main problem?
choices: Metrics should be dropped entirely, because logs make them unnecessary.
Records older than a day stop being useful, so the monthly total is wasted and retention should be cut to one day to save money on storage.
Logs cannot carry a service name, so they can never be searched.
Too much volume without a defined question makes answers hard to find and raises cost, so the questions should be decided first.
questions.why: Observability design starts from the questions you need answered, and collecting large volumes with no defined question makes the signal hard to use and expensive to keep.

questions.prompt: A regional bank's payment service must let on-call staff know quickly when response times degrade. Which design decision best fits this requirement, and which Well-Architected Framework pillar does it mainly serve?
choices: An alert on a sustained percentile latency threshold, which serves the Operational Excellence pillar by notifying a person within minutes.
Encrypting every log line so unauthorised staff cannot read timings, which serves the security pillar.
Adding a second region so requests never slow down, which serves the performance pillar.
Switching to fewer, larger log files so each day stores less, which serves the cost pillar.
questions.why: A sustained threshold alert turns a latency metric into a timely notification for a person, which is what the Operational Excellence pillar is about, while the other choices address different goals or do not notify anyone.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we choose observability signals during the design rather than after launch. Name one limit or trade-off of collecting too much or too little telemetry.
lessons.modelAnswer: We decide observability during design because the questions we will need answered in an incident depend on how the system is split into services and where its risky steps are. If we add signals after launch, the first slowdown or outage happens with no data to explain it. The main trade-off is volume against cost and noise. Collecting every log at full detail is expensive to store and search, and it buries the useful lines. Collecting too little means we cannot reconstruct what happened. A sound design picks a small set of metrics tied to user experience, such as latency and error rate for each important operation, adds traces for the request paths that cross services, and keeps detailed logs for a limited time. We then set alerts on the metrics that matter to users, so people are told about problems before customers report them.
rubricPoints: Defines observability as understanding internal state from metrics, logs, and traces
Explains why signals chosen at design time answer incident questions that appear later
Names a real trade-off between telemetry volume, cost, and signal-to-noise
Connects the decision to the Operational Excellence pillar, with Reliability as support

suggested.rationale: A planned metric alarm builder would let the learner choose which signals to watch and set thresholds, which is the practical side of this design decision.

lessons.plain: When a team designs a system in the cloud, every choice helps some goals and hurts others. Keeping extra copies of data protects it but costs more, and a cheap option may be slower. The Well-Architected Framework is a shared checklist of six areas that good designs are judged against: running the system well, keeping it safe, keeping it working when parts fail, spending money sensibly, being fast enough for users, and using resources responsibly. Applying it means naming which of these a decision serves and which it strains, so the choice can be defended to a business owner in their own terms. Think of it as a building inspector's list applied to a blueprint before construction starts.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop owner says the new online checkout must never go down, but the budget is tight. Before any teaching, what two or three areas of a design would you expect to pull against each other, and why?
lessons.teach:
The six pillars are the lenses of Google Cloud's Well-Architected Framework. They are operational excellence (how you run, monitor and change a system safely), security, privacy and compliance (protecting data and meeting legal rules), reliability (the system keeps doing its job when parts fail and recovers when they do), cost optimization (getting useful value for the money spent), performance optimization (meeting speed and capacity targets for users), and sustainability (using compute and energy no more than needed). A pillar is not a score to maximise. It is a question to ask of each decision.

Why it works: almost every design decision moves one pillar and pushes another. Adding a second zone (an isolated data center inside one region) raises reliability and also raises cost and operational work. Caching raises performance but can serve slightly stale answers. Naming both sides is what makes a decision reviewable.

Worked example: a retailer wants checkout to stay up during sales. Step 1: the requirement is business-level, namely no outage at peak times. Step 2: the candidate decision is to run the checkout service in two zones behind a load balancer (a component that spreads traffic across servers and skips unhealthy ones). Step 3: reliability improves, because one zone failing no longer stops checkout. Step 4: cost rises, because idle capacity sits in both zones. Step 5: operational excellence improves only if health checks and alerts are added to the same design. Step 6: the trade-off is recorded: standby capacity is paid for to avoid a zone outage.

Common mistake: treating the framework as a checklist to tick once, instead of a set of trade-offs to name. The consequence is a design that looks secure and cheap on paper but fails when the first zone goes down, because nobody asked what reliability required.

The framework is a vocabulary for defending decisions, and a design is only as sound as the trade-offs it openly records.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency publishes live bus arrival times. Riders complain the app is slow at the morning rush, so the team considers a cache (a stored copy of recent answers, so repeat requests skip the slower prediction service). Step 1: The requirement is that riders see arrival times within two seconds during the rush. Step 2: The decision is to keep each stop's predictions in a cache that refreshes every 15 seconds. Step 3: Performance improves, because most requests are answered from the stored copy and never reach the prediction service. Step 4: Privacy is unaffected, because the data is public timetable information. Step 5: [missing: the reliability consequence of the cache] Step 6: Record the trade-off: a rider may see an arrival time up to 15 seconds old.
choices: Sustainability falls, because the extra cache servers use energy that outweighs the computing they save for every request.
Security improves automatically, because a cache acts as a barrier that blocks attackers from reaching the prediction service.
Reliability improves: if the prediction service fails, the cache can keep serving the last stored answers.
Operational excellence is unaffected, so the cache needs no monitoring or alerts at all.
questions.why: A cache that holds the last good answers lets riders still get something when the prediction service fails, which is a reliability gain, while the other choices misstate which pillar the decision moves or ignore the need for monitoring.

questions.prompt: A university library moves its catalogue database into a single zone (one isolated data center inside a region) to lower its monthly bill, and accepts that an outage there will stop searches. Which pillar does this decision mainly trade away, and which pillar does it mainly gain?
choices: It gains sustainability and gives up privacy and compliance.
It gains operational excellence and gives up cost optimization.
It gains security and gives up performance.
It gains cost optimization and gives up reliability.
questions.why: Running in one zone lowers spend, which serves cost optimization, but the system can no longer keep working when that zone fails, so reliability is traded away.

questions.prompt: A logistics company keeps all its shipment-tracking services in one zone to save money. A manager says the design is sound because the cheaper bill was the only thing the team needed to check. What is the most accurate criticism of that reasoning?
choices: The design may look sound on paper, but the team never recorded the reliability trade-off it accepted, so the failure of one zone was never weighed.
The manager should have chosen the most expensive option, since performance always outranks cost in a well-architected design.
The manager is right, because a framework is a checklist and cost is the only item that must be ticked.
The manager is wrong only about security, which the single zone already fully covers.
questions.why: The framework is a set of trade-offs to name, and treating cost as the only question means the reliability cost of one zone was never recorded or weighed.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit must delete donor records seven years after the last gift, because a legal rule requires it. The team adds an automated deletion job. Which pillar does this decision mainly serve?
choices: Sustainability, because less stored data always means less energy use.
Performance optimization, because deleting old rows makes queries faster.
Privacy and compliance, because it protects donor data and meets a legal deletion rule.
Reliability, because the job keeps the database from failing when it grows.
questions.why: The deletion job protects personal data and satisfies a legal requirement, which is exactly what the privacy and compliance pillar covers.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes storing every customer event in two regions for reliability, without discussing it with anyone. In your own words, explain how you would apply the six pillars to this proposal, naming the pillar it serves, the pillar it strains, and one limit of the framework itself.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking what the reliability requirement actually is: how much downtime or data loss the business can accept. Two regions does serve reliability, because a regional outage would not lose the events. But it strains cost, since storage and cross-region traffic are paid for twice. It also strains security and privacy, because customer data now lives in a second location that may fall under different rules. It adds operational work too, since replication lag and failover need monitoring and a tested runbook. So I would not approve it as stated. I would ask for the recovery target, compare a second-region copy against a cheaper backup, and record the trade-off. One limit is that the framework does not set the weights between pillars. The business does, so the pillars help us ask better questions rather than produce a verdict.
rubricPoints: Names the pillar the decision serves and the pillar it strains.
Ties the choice back to a business requirement such as acceptable downtime or data loss.
Notes that the framework does not weigh the pillars against each other; the business sets priorities.
Records the trade-off rather than declaring the design simply good or bad.

suggested.rationale: The design exercise on the vehicle-position ingest path requires choosing between options and naming their trade-offs, which is the pillar reasoning this objective trains.

lessons.plain: High availability means a system keeps working when one of its parts breaks. Failover is the moment work moves from the broken part to a healthy standby. Think of a restaurant with two kitchens: if one kitchen floods, orders go to the other, and customers may barely notice. The architect's job is to find every part whose failure would stop the whole service, then add a second copy in a place that is unlikely to fail at the same time. Businesses care because downtime costs money and trust. This decision serves the reliability pillar of the Well-Architected Framework, one of its six pillars, and it usually trades some extra cost for that protection.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your online store runs on one server in one building. If that server loses power, what happens to customers, and what single change would most reduce that risk?
lessons.teach:
Start with the terms. A single point of failure is any component whose failure alone stops the service. Redundancy means running more than one copy of a component so that losing one leaves another running. Availability is the share of time a service is usable, often written as a percentage such as 99.9 percent. A zone is an isolated area inside a region with its own power and cooling, so one zone can fail while others keep running. A region is a larger geographic area made of several zones. A health check is a periodic probe that asks each copy whether it is responding correctly. Failover is the shift of traffic from an unhealthy copy to a healthy one, automatically or by hand.

Why it works: failures in separate zones are largely independent, so two copies in two zones are very unlikely to fail together. Two copies in one zone share the same power and network, so they fail together.

Worked example: a regional ride-tracking API runs three instances spread across zones A, B and C, behind a load balancer. The balancer health-checks each instance every 10 seconds and removes any instance after three failed checks. Step 1: normal load is 900 requests per second, so each instance handles about 300. Step 2: zone A loses power. Step 3: within about 30 seconds, zone A's instances fail their checks and the balancer stops sending them traffic. Step 4: zones B and C now carry 900 requests per second, about 450 each. Step 5: if each instance can only handle 350, the survivors stay up but any spike drops requests.

Common mistake: placing two copies in one zone and calling the design highly available. A single zone outage takes both copies down together.

Consequence in a running system: a design that is redundant on paper but sized only for normal load fails under the very event it was built for, because failover moves the whole load onto the survivors and can overload them.

questions.prompt: A billing service at a company called Larkspur Books runs six instances, two in each of zones X, Y and Z, behind a load balancer that health-checks each instance every 15 seconds. Normal load is 1,000 requests per second, so each instance handles about 167. Step 1: zone X loses power and its two instances fail their health checks. Step 2: the load balancer stops sending traffic to those two instances. Step 3 is the one to complete: what happens to the traffic that the two failed instances were handling? Step 4: each surviving instance can handle 220 requests per second. Which option correctly completes step 3?
choices: Each survivor receives about 200 requests per second because the balancer caps traffic at the average of the six original instances.
The surviving instances keep their old share, so each still gets about 167 requests per second and nothing is overloaded.
The four surviving instances now share the full 1,000 requests per second, so each receives about 250, which is above their 220 capacity.
The two failed instances' traffic is split between only two survivors, so each of those receives about 500 requests per second.
questions.why: Failover moves the whole load onto the remaining instances, so 1,000 divided across four survivors is 250 each, which exceeds their 220 capacity.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is the job of a health check in a highly available design?
choices: It copies data from one zone to another so that both zones hold the same records.
It moves all traffic for a whole region to a second region after an outage.
It periodically asks each copy whether it is responding correctly, so that unhealthy copies can be spotted and taken out of service.
It sets the availability percentage that the service promises to its customers.
questions.why: A health check is a periodic probe that asks each copy whether it is responding correctly, which is how an unhealthy copy gets identified for failover.

questions.prompt: The Pinecrest Forms team runs three copies of its intake form service, all placed in zone Q of one region. Which statement about this design is correct?
choices: Because all three copies share one zone's power and network, a single zone outage would take all three down together, so the design is not highly available.
Adding a fourth copy in the same zone would make the design highly available.
The balancer will reach copies in other regions automatically, so no zone outage can stop the service.
Three copies give three independent chances to survive, so the design is highly available.
questions.why: Copies in the same zone share power and network and fail together, so spreading them across zones is what provides real high availability.

questions.prompt: A team runs four copies of a quote service spread across three zones in one region, each sized to handle its share of 800 requests per second at normal load. One zone fails. Which outcome is most likely?
choices: Each survivor takes no more load than before, because traffic is split so evenly that nothing changes.
The failed zone's copies keep serving traffic because health checks ignore zone-wide outages.
Failover cannot happen because the load balancer has no route to the surviving copies.
Failover works and the survivors stay up, but they now carry more than their sizing covers, so traffic spikes can drop requests.
questions.why: Failover moves the failed zone's load onto the survivors, and a design sized only for normal load can overload them during a spike.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make a service highly available across zones, and name one limit or trade-off of the approach you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would remove single points of failure by running copies of each tier in at least two zones, placed behind a load balancer that health-checks them and stops sending traffic to any copy that fails. Each zone must be sized to carry the full peak load on its own, because when one zone drops, the survivors absorb everything; otherwise failover only moves the outage. The main trade-off is cost, since duplicated capacity sits partly idle during normal operation. Multi-zone also does not protect against a whole region failing, so that needs a second region, which adds complexity and data replication lag. Data is the harder part: a stateless web tier fails over easily, but a database with one primary needs a standby and a clear rule for promoting it without losing committed writes. I would confirm the availability target first, since it sets how much redundancy is worth paying for.
rubricPoints: Defines a single point of failure and redundancy in plain terms
Explains that copies in separate zones fail independently while copies in one zone do not
Notes that each zone or copy must be sized for the full load so failover does not overload survivors
States a real trade-off such as cost, or that zone redundancy does not cover a whole-region failure
Recognises that stateful data, such as a primary database, needs a different failover approach than stateless services

suggested.rationale: The planned disaster-recovery planner would let the learner model zone and region failures and check whether failover capacity holds, which is the core reasoning of this objective.

lessons.plain: Designing for flexibility means building a system so its parts can be made bigger or smaller, moved, swapped, or rebuilt quickly, without a long purchase cycle or a rebuild from scratch. In an office data centre, adding capacity meant ordering hardware weeks ahead and living with it for years. In the cloud you can rent more capacity in minutes, return it when demand drops, and replace a component by creating a new one from a saved recipe. The skill is choosing designs where that freedom is actually usable, such as a system that grows and shrinks on its own rather than one fixed machine that someone must hand-tune.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop's website gets ten times its normal traffic every Friday evening and is quiet the rest of the week. Would you rather buy enough servers for the Friday peak and leave them mostly idle the rest of the week, or design the system so its capacity follows demand? Why?
lessons.teach:
Flexibility of cloud resources means the ability to change how much capacity you run, where it runs, and which parts you use, quickly and without a large upfront commitment. Three terms matter here. Elasticity is capacity that rises and falls with demand, ideally on its own. Ephemeral means a resource is expected to be disposable: you can destroy it and create a replacement without losing the service. Decoupling means components talk through a clear interface or a queue rather than depending on each other's internal state, so one part can be swapped or scaled without touching the others.

Why it works: cloud capacity is metered and can be rented by the minute, so the cost of guessing the wrong size drops sharply. A design that assumes fixed machines wastes that. A design that keeps servers stateless, stores session data in a shared service, and lets a managed group add or remove instances based on a measured signal can follow demand.

Worked example: a ride-booking API runs on a group of identical instances behind a load balancer. Step 1: the average CPU across the group is measured every minute. Step 2: when it stays above 70 percent for five minutes, the group adds two instances. Step 3: each new instance starts from the same saved image and registers with the load balancer. Step 4: when CPU stays below 30 percent for ten minutes, the group removes instances, but only after letting their in-flight requests finish.

Common mistake: storing user session data on an instance's local disk. When autoscaling removes that instance, the data vanishes and users are logged out mid-booking. Moving state into a shared store is what makes the group flexible.

Consequence in a running system: removing a busy instance during a traffic dip causes failed requests, so connections must be drained before capacity is taken away.

This choice serves the reliability and performance efficiency pillars of the Well-Architected Framework.

questions.prompt: A school enrollment platform creates enrollment confirmation PDFs. The design works like this. Step 1: each web request places a job in a managed queue, which is a service that holds pending work until a consumer picks it up. Step 2: a pool of identical workers pulls jobs from the queue, and the pool adds workers when the queue holds more than 200 jobs for three minutes. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: when the queue stays empty for fifteen minutes, the pool removes a third of its workers. Which statement completes step 3 so that removing workers never loses a confirmation?
choices: Each worker writes the finished PDF to a shared storage service rather than its own local disk, because the pool may remove that worker at any time.
Each worker writes PDFs to the same local disk path so that file names never collide.
Each worker keeps the finished PDF on its own local disk and copies it to storage on a nightly schedule.
Each worker holds finished PDFs in memory so that students can download them faster.
questions.why: Because the pool can remove any worker at any time, the output must live in a shared service, which keeps it available after the worker is gone.

questions.prompt: In the sense used for cloud flexibility, what does decoupling mean?
choices: Components run on separate physical machines in separate data centres.
Components exchange work through a clear interface or a queue instead of depending on each other's internal state.
Every service shares one database so that all of them stay in step.
A component is never allowed to change after it has been deployed.
questions.why: Decoupling means parts communicate through a defined interface or queue, so one can be swapped or scaled without touching the others.

questions.prompt: A retailer's checkout service runs on eight fixed servers sized for the holiday peak, so they sit mostly idle the rest of the year. Which change best applies the flexibility idea?
choices: Buy four more fixed servers so the holiday peak has extra headroom.
Replace the fixed servers with a group that adds and removes instances based on measured load, and keep session data in a shared store.
Keep the eight servers but power them down outside business hours.
Move the checkout database onto one larger server to handle the peak.
questions.why: A measured-load group with stateless instances follows demand and pays only for capacity in use, which is the core of flexible cloud design.

questions.prompt: A media app's autoscaled group saves uploaded photos on each instance's local disk. After a scale-in, users report missing photos. Which fix addresses the actual cause?
choices: Attach a larger disk to each instance so more photos fit.
Turn off autoscaling and hold the instance count at its highest value.
Store uploads in a shared object store and keep the instances stateless.
Raise the scale-in threshold so instances are removed less often.
questions.why: The photos are lost because they live on disposable instances, so moving them to a shared store makes the group safe to shrink.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who says 'the cloud is flexible, so we don't need to plan capacity' what flexibility actually buys us, and name one limit or trade-off of designing for it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Flexibility means we can add or remove capacity and replace parts quickly, so we pay for what we use and can absorb demand spikes without buying hardware in advance. But it does not remove planning. Scaling only works if the application is stateless, meaning session data lives in a shared store, and if new instances become healthy fast enough to take traffic when it matters. Scaling also has limits: quotas, the cost of running extra instances at peak, and a scale-up that arrives too late for a sudden spike. So we still set minimum and maximum sizes, test the scaling rule under load, and drain connections before scale-in. The trade-off is flexibility against design complexity and the discipline needed to keep state out of individual machines.
rubricPoints: Flexibility means changing capacity and components quickly, paying for use rather than buying in advance
Scaling only works if the application is stateless, with session data in a shared store
Flexibility has limits such as quotas, cost at peak, and slow scale-up during sudden spikes
Scale-in needs connection draining and minimum and maximum sizes to stay safe

suggested.rationale: The autoscale engine would let the learner watch scaling rules respond to load, which is the most direct way to feel what resource flexibility means.

lessons.plain: Designing for scalability means planning a system so it can handle more work as the business grows, without being rebuilt. Think of a shop: a small counter works on a quiet day, but on a busy day you either make the counter faster or open more counters. Architects start from the growth the business expects, such as double the customers in a year or a holiday spike, and choose designs where adding capacity is routine rather than a crisis. The real question is not whether it runs today, but what breaks first when demand rises.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web app runs fine on one server handling 200 requests per second, and the business expects 1,000 per second within a year. Would you rather buy one much bigger server or run several average servers behind a traffic splitter, and why?
lessons.teach:
Scalability is a system's ability to handle more load by adding resources, without a redesign. A growth requirement is the concrete demand you must plan for, such as a multiple of current traffic, a number of users, or a seasonal peak. There are two ways to add capacity. Vertical scaling means making one machine bigger, with more CPU and memory. Horizontal scaling means adding more machines and spreading the work across them. Vertical scaling has a ceiling and often needs downtime to resize. Horizontal scaling can keep growing if the work can be split. Horizontal scaling works best when each instance is stateless, meaning it keeps no per-user data in its own memory, so any instance can answer any request. A load balancer, a component that spreads incoming requests across instances, makes this possible. An autoscaling policy adds or removes instances automatically based on a signal such as CPU use or request rate.

Worked example: current peak is 500 requests per second. The business expects a holiday peak three times that, so 1,500 per second. One instance handles 200 per second at a comfortable 70 percent load target, so its usable capacity is 140 per second. Step 1: divide 1,500 by 140, giving about 10.7. Step 2: round up to 11 instances. Step 3: set the autoscaler minimum near that figure and the maximum somewhat above it, for surprises.

Common mistake: sizing for today's average instead of the peak, or keeping session data on one server so new instances cannot take over its users. In a running system, the consequence is that requests queue, latency climbs, and timeouts appear even though the new servers' CPU looks fine. The bottleneck often moves to a shared database or a single component, so scaling the web tier alone does not help.

Scalability is judged by whether the growth path fits the forecast, and the cost of that headroom is always part of the decision.

questions.prompt: Harbor Tickets runs a seat-hold service for concert sales. Each instance handles 300 requests per second at a 70 percent load target, so its usable capacity is 210 per second. The expected on-sale peak is 800 requests per second. Step 1: usable capacity is 300 times 0.70, which is 210 per second. Step 2: divide 800 by 210, which gives about 3.8. Step 3: ___. Step 4: set the autoscaler minimum near the sized figure and the maximum somewhat above it, for surprises. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Set the maximum to exactly 4 so the group can never grow beyond the sizing
Round 3.8 up to 4 instances, so the fleet can carry the full peak
Multiply 210 by 4 and compare that once to 800, without rounding
Round 3.8 down to 3 instances, since fewer machines saves cost
questions.why: Rounding up to the next whole instance is needed because a fraction of a machine cannot be deployed, and rounding down would leave the peak under capacity.

questions.prompt: A payroll portal runs on one server that is already at the largest size its provider offers. Next year's forecast is three times today's load. Which approach fits this growth requirement?
choices: Resize that same server to the next larger size during a planned maintenance window, and repeat each year
Keep the single server and raise the CPU alert threshold so it looks less busy on dashboards
Wait until the forecast peak arrives before adding any capacity, since the server handles today's load
Run several stateless portal instances behind a load balancer, with user session data held outside them
questions.why: Vertical scaling hits a ceiling and needs downtime, while horizontal scaling with stateless instances behind a load balancer can keep growing with the forecast.

questions.prompt: A school enrollment portal adds six new web servers behind its load balancer ahead of registration week. The new servers show low CPU use, yet students report long waits and timeouts. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The new servers should be made bigger vertically, since adding more of them cannot fix queueing
The shared database or another single component is the bottleneck, so adding web servers alone does not relieve the queue
The new servers are too powerful, so the load balancer is sending them too little work
Autoscaling is working correctly, and rising latency is expected with any growth in traffic
questions.why: When the web tier has spare CPU but requests still queue, the constraint has usually moved to a shared component such as a database, which scaling the web tier cannot fix.

questions.prompt: A parcel-tracking API expects a peak of 1,200 requests per second. Each instance handles 400 requests per second, and the team sets a 60 percent load target for comfortable operation. What is the minimum number of instances needed to carry the peak?
questions.why: Usable capacity per instance is 400 times 0.60, which is 240 per second, and 1,200 divided by 240 is exactly 5, so 5 instances are needed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to cloud why a design that scales horizontally needs stateless instances, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on autoscaling to meet a growth requirement.
lessons.modelAnswer: Horizontal scaling means adding more identical instances behind a load balancer, and the balancer can send any request to any instance. That only works if no instance holds information the next request needs, such as a user's login session stored in its memory. If it does, a request routed to a different instance fails or the user gets logged out, so the design must move that state to a shared store or keep it with the client. The tradeoff with autoscaling is that it reacts after demand rises. New instances take time to start, and a sudden spike can overwhelm the existing ones first. Autoscaling also has a maximum set by budget, so for a known holiday peak you should set a minimum already sized for it rather than rely on scaling to catch up.
rubricPoints: Horizontal scaling adds identical instances behind a load balancer.
Instances must be stateless, or session data must live in a shared store.
Autoscaling reacts after demand rises, so spikes can outrun it.
Set the minimum from the forecast peak and the maximum from the budget.
The shared database or a single component often becomes the next bottleneck.

suggested.rationale: A planned autoscaling engine would let the learner tune scaling policies against a growth forecast, which is the core skill this objective tests.

lessons.plain: Performance is how quickly and how smoothly a system does its work. Latency is the wait between asking for something and getting the answer, usually measured in milliseconds. A system can have plenty of capacity and still feel slow if every request has to travel a long distance or wait in a line. When you design for performance and latency, you decide where things run, how close they sit to the people using them, and which answers can be kept ready instead of recalculated. Think of a shop that places its popular goods near the front door instead of in a far warehouse.
lessons.guessPrompt: A mobile app's users are in Sydney, but its only servers are in Virginia, and each screen feels slow. Before any teaching, what is one change you would make first to speed up each screen, and why do you think it would help?
lessons.teach:
Latency is the time one request takes from start to finish. It is usually measured as a round trip: the request travels out, the work happens, and the reply travels back. Throughput is how many requests a system completes per second. The two are different. A system can handle many requests per second and still make each one wait. Performance design cares about both, but this objective focuses mostly on latency.

Distance sets a floor. Signals in fiber cables travel at a fixed speed, so a server far away adds delay that extra hardware cannot remove. The main levers are: place the workload in a region close to its users, keep chatty calls inside one region, keep answers ready with caching (storing a result so the next caller gets it without recomputing), and send reads to read copies of data so the primary copy is not the bottleneck. A load balancer, which spreads incoming requests across several servers, helps throughput and stops any single server from building a queue.

Worked example. A map screen makes 10 calls to a backend on another continent, each with a 150 ms round trip, made one after another. Step 1: 10 times 150 ms gives 1,500 ms before the screen is complete. Step 2: batch the 10 calls into one request that the backend answers together. That is one 150 ms trip plus 50 ms of work, so 200 ms. Step 3: move the backend to a nearby region so the trip drops to 20 ms, giving 70 ms in total. The same feature went from 1.5 seconds to under a tenth of that.

Common mistake: designing for the average response time. Users feel the slow tail, the slowest one in a hundred requests. A design that averages 80 ms but has 3-second tails still feels broken.

In a running system, a chain of sequential calls multiplies latency, and under load the queues grow, so the tail gets worse first.

questions.prompt: A ticketing app's seat-picker page makes 5 calls to a booking database in a region 120 ms away, made one after another, so the page is waiting on each round trip in turn. Step 1: 5 calls at 120 ms each is 600 ms. Step 2: a cache stores the seat map, so 2 of those 5 calls are answered from memory and never travel to the database. Step 3 (you do this step): assuming only the remaining database round trips count toward time, and they are still made one after another, what is the new total time for the page?
choices: 480 ms
600 ms
240 ms
360 ms
questions.why: Caching removes 2 of the 5 round trips, leaving 3 sequential calls at 120 ms each, which is 360 ms.

questions.prompt: A payments service handles 2,000 requests per second, but each individual request takes 4 seconds from start to finish. Which statement best describes this system?
choices: Its throughput is low because each request takes 4 seconds
Throughput and latency always move together, so a 4-second request means only 0.25 requests per second are completed
It has high throughput and high latency at the same time, which is possible because the two measures are different
Its latency is low because it handles many requests per second
questions.why: Throughput counts completed requests per second and latency measures time per request, so a system can score high on one and poorly on the other.

questions.prompt: A team reports that their search service averages 60 ms per response, so they consider it fast. However, 1 in 100 requests takes 2.5 seconds, and users complain about it. What is the best explanation for the complaints?
choices: The average is calculated incorrectly and the 60 ms figure should be ignored
The service has low throughput, which causes the average to rise
Load balancers cause the 2.5-second responses, so the search service itself is not responsible
Users feel the slowest requests, and an average hides the slow tail, so the design is not meeting the users' experience
questions.why: The teaching text warns that designing for the average misses the slow tail, which users notice even when the average looks good.

questions.prompt: A reporting service makes 4 sequential calls to a database that sits 90 ms away in another region, and each call is a full round trip. The team moves the database to a nearby region where the round trip is 15 ms, and keeps all four calls chained one after another. Ignoring the time spent on the work itself, what is the new total time for the four calls?
choices: 60 ms
75 ms
360 ms
15 ms
questions.why: Four sequential calls at 15 ms each total 60 ms, because moving the workload closer shortens each trip, which is the distance lever the text describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a good average response time can still produce a slow app, and name one tradeoff you accept when you cache results to reduce latency.
lessons.modelAnswer: An average blends fast and slow requests together, so a few very slow requests can hide behind a good number. Users remember the slow ones, especially when one screen makes several calls and waits for the slowest. So I would track the tail, the 95th or 99th percentile, not just the mean, and design to bring those down. The main levers are placing the workload near its users, batching or parallelising calls, and caching answers. Caching has a real tradeoff: the cached answer can be stale, so users may briefly see old data, and we have to decide how old is acceptable and how we will expire or refresh the cache. Speed gained from a cache is only worth it if the freshness cost is one the business accepts.
rubricPoints: Explains that averages can hide slow tail requests that users actually notice
Names at least one latency lever such as regional placement, batching, or caching
States a concrete tradeoff of caching, such as stale data and how freshness is managed

suggested.rationale: The design exercise on the vehicle-position ingest and map read path makes the learner reason about where latency comes from in a real read path.

lessons.plain: Gemini Cloud Assist is an AI helper built into the Google Cloud console. You type a question in ordinary language, such as why a service is slow or what a particular setup does, and it reads the context of your project and answers, sometimes suggesting changes. Think of a well-read colleague who has not sat in your meetings: useful for drafting options and spotting gaps, but its answers still need checking against what the business actually needs and the trade-offs you are responsible for.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you ask an AI assistant which database to use for a new service and it answers confidently in two sentences. What would you check before accepting that answer in a design review?
lessons.teach: Gemini Cloud Assist is a generative AI assistant built into the Google Cloud console, the web interface for managing cloud resources. Generative AI means a model that produces new text from a prompt, which is a request written in ordinary language. Cloud Assist can answer questions about your projects and resources, explain how an existing setup behaves, help investigate problems, and suggest options or improvements. It is a research and drafting tool, not a decision maker. It helps because an architect often has to compare options quickly, understand unfamiliar configuration, or check whether a design overlooks a risk. It must be checked because a model predicts plausible text, so it can state a wrong fact confidently, and it knows nothing about your business constraints unless you supply them. The Well-Architected Framework is Google's set of six design pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, cost optimization, performance, and sustainability. Worked example: a design must receive order events and hold them for processing. Step 1, write the requirement first: no event may be lost if a processor is down, and traffic may spike tenfold. Step 2, ask the assistant for options that meet that requirement, along with each option's trade-offs. Step 3, check each named product against the official documentation and the requirement. Step 4, record which pillar each choice serves, such as reliability for the queue and cost for its pricing model. Only then decide. Common mistake: pasting the assistant's first answer into the design document as the decision. Consequence: if the suggestion ignored a constraint such as data residency, which is the legal rule about where data must be stored, the flaw surfaces in production, where fixing it means a migration rather than an edit to a document. The assistant speeds up the search for options, but the architect owns the decision and its justification.

questions.prompt: Harbor Print Co. stores customer proof files, about 6 TB in total, that must stay inside Germany because of data residency, the legal rule about where data must be physically kept. The architect wrote the requirement first: files stay in a German region, and a customer can download a proof within a few seconds. She asked Gemini Cloud Assist for storage options along with their trade-offs, and it suggested three. She checked the first option against the official documentation and found that its default location is a multi-region spanning several countries, so she rejected it. She recorded that the second option serves the security pillar through its access controls, and that the third serves the cost pillar through its lower storage price. Before deciding, what step is still missing?
choices: Check the second and third options against the official documentation and the requirement
Write down which pillar each option serves after the decision is signed off
Ask Cloud Assist to re-check its own three suggestions until the answers agree with each other
Compare only the monthly storage prices of the remaining options
questions.why: Each named product must be checked against the official documentation and the requirement before the decision, and the architect has only done this for the first option, so the second and third must still be verified.

questions.prompt: In the teaching text, what is the main role of Gemini Cloud Assist in architecture design?
choices: A drafting and research aid that suggests options, which the architect must then check
A replacement for the official documentation when a product is unfamiliar
A tool that enforces every Well-Architected pillar automatically on each project
A decision maker that selects the final product for the design document
questions.why: The text describes Cloud Assist as a research and drafting tool that does not make decisions, so its suggestions must be checked and owned by the architect.

questions.prompt: Lumen Books must never lose a checkout event if its billing service is offline, and traffic spikes during sales. The architect chooses a durable managed message queue that holds events until billing recovers. Which Well-Architected pillar does this choice primarily serve?
choices: Cost optimization, because the queue charges only per event
Reliability, because held events survive a billing outage
Sustainability, because the queue uses less energy than a database
Performance, because the queue makes each request faster
questions.why: The requirement is that no event is lost when a processor is down, and holding events durably until processing recovers is a reliability decision, even though cost and performance may also be affected.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Clinics needs patient scans kept inside its own country. An architect pasted an assistant suggestion that stores the scans in a region outside the country into the design document, without checking the residency rule. Nothing in the document flagged the problem. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Nothing happens, since the assistant's suggestions are always checked by Google before they reach the console
The flaw surfaces in production, where fixing it means migrating the data
The design is corrected automatically once the security pillar is recorded
The design improves on cost, because that region is usually cheaper
questions.why: The assistant ignored a business constraint it was never given, and because the error was accepted without checking, it appears in production where the fix is a data migration rather than an edit to a document.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Gemini Cloud Assist is useful for during architecture design, and name one limit or trade-off you would watch for before letting its suggestion shape a decision.
lessons.modelAnswer: Gemini Cloud Assist is the generative AI helper in the Google Cloud console. During design I would use it to get quick options, to explain an unfamiliar configuration in our project, or to check for gaps such as a missing failover path. The limit is that it generates plausible text, so it can be confidently wrong, and it does not know our business constraints unless we state them. So before a suggestion goes into the design, I restate the requirement it must meet, verify any product claim against the documentation, and check which Well-Architected pillar the choice serves and what it costs us. For example, if it proposes a single-region setup to save money, I would test that against the availability requirement before accepting it. The assistant speeds up the search; the decision and its trade-offs stay with the architect.
rubricPoints: Describes Gemini Cloud Assist as a generative AI helper in the Google Cloud console that answers questions and suggests options.
Names a useful design task, such as comparing options or explaining an existing setup.
States the limit: outputs can be plausible but wrong, and the assistant lacks the business constraints.
Says the architect verifies claims against the requirement, the documentation, and the relevant pillar and trade-off.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a design situation where a plausible AI suggestion must be checked against requirements adds the most, and no listed mission covers this directly.

lessons.plain: Backup and recovery design means deciding, before anything breaks, how you will get your data and services back after a mistake, a failure, or a deleted resource. A backup is a copy of data kept separately so it can be restored. Recovery is the act of bringing the system back. The design question is how much work you can afford to lose and how long you can afford to be down. Those two limits shape the whole solution, so a good design writes them down first and then chooses copies, timing, and locations that meet them, instead of adding backups as an afterthought.
lessons.guessPrompt: An orders database is damaged by a faulty script at 4 PM. Its last backup ran at midnight. Before any teaching: what does the backup timing decide, and what two questions would you ask the business before choosing how often to back up?
lessons.teach:
A backup is a separate copy of data, kept so it can be restored. Recovery is the process of getting a system working again from those copies or from a standby. Designing for it means choosing two targets before choosing any tool. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data, measured as time, that the business can afford to lose. An RPO of one hour means losing up to an hour of writes is acceptable. The recovery time objective (RTO) is the longest the service can be down while being restored. Both are business decisions, and they drive every technical choice that follows.

Why it works: once the RPO is known, backup frequency is constrained, because anything written since the last copy is at risk. Once the RTO is known, the restore method is constrained, because restoring from an archive takes far longer than starting a standby copy that is already running. Standby options range from cold (data copied but infrastructure must be rebuilt), to warm (infrastructure ready, data restored on demand), to hot (a live replica that can take over quickly). Each step toward near-zero downtime costs more money.

Worked example. An orders database gets a full backup at midnight. A faulty script deletes rows at 16:00. Step 1: the data lost is everything written from midnight to 16:00, about 16 hours, so the real RPO is 16 hours. Step 2: restoring from the midnight copy takes about three hours, so the real RTO is about three hours. Step 3: if the business needs a one-hour RPO, the design must add frequent backups or continuous change logs, then check the new restore time against the RTO.

Common mistake: keeping backups in the same project and region as the live data, so one bad deletion or regional outage destroys both. Another is never performing a test restore, so the first real restore becomes the first proof that it does not work.

In a running system, a restore usually means writes stop or are redirected, and the team must decide how to merge any data written after the copy was taken. A restore plan is not finished until it has been tested.

questions.prompt: A small booking platform keeps its reservations in one database. The business owners say they can afford to lose at most 30 minutes of bookings, so their recovery point objective (RPO, the most data measured as time that can be lost) is 30 minutes. They also say the site must be back within 2 hours, so their recovery time objective (RTO, the longest the service can be down while being restored) is 2 hours. Today the team takes one full backup each night into a storage bucket in the same project and region as the database. Step 1: the worst case loss is almost 24 hours, so the current setup misses the RPO. Step 2: the team adds a backup every 30 minutes. Step 3: what must the team do next?
choices: Keep the nightly full backup, because the RTO only measures how long the backup takes to create.
Relax the RPO to 24 hours so it matches the nightly schedule.
Check that restoring from the newer copies still finishes within the 2-hour RTO, and run a test restore to prove it.
Move the 30-minute backups into a second project so the RPO is met.
questions.why: Once the RPO sets backup frequency, the restore method must still be checked against the RTO, and only a tested restore shows whether it fits both targets.

questions.prompt: A museum's ticketing system must be back online within 4 hours after a failure, and the business accepts losing up to 15 minutes of sales. Which statement correctly describes the 4-hour figure?
choices: It is the longest the service can be down while being restored.
It is the most data, measured as time, that the museum can afford to lose.
It is the time the restore process takes on a standby copy that is already running.
It is how often backups must be taken.
questions.why: The recovery time objective is the longest acceptable downtime during restoration, while the amount of data that may be lost is the recovery point objective, which is a different target.

questions.prompt: A logistics company keeps its production storage and its backups in the same project and the same region. Which single event would most likely destroy both copies at once?
choices: A single corrupted file in production that is noticed the next morning.
A nightly reporting script that fails with an error.
A backup job that runs twenty minutes late.
A regional outage that makes the one region holding both copies unavailable.
questions.why: When the live data and the backups share a region, an event that affects that region removes both, which is the common mistake the teaching text warns about.

questions.prompt: A team takes backups every six hours and believes its disaster recovery is covered. Nobody has ever restored from those backups. What is the most important gap in their design?
choices: Six hours is too short an interval for any backup to be useful.
They should have used a standby that is always running instead of backups.
Backups do not need to be stored separately from the live data if they are taken often enough.
They have no tested restore, so they do not know whether the copies work or how long a restore takes against their RTO.
questions.why: A restore plan is not finished until it has been tested, because an untested backup gives no proof that it can be restored in time.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why the team should agree on RPO and RTO before choosing backup schedules and storage, and name one tradeoff that a tighter RPO or RTO adds in cost or complexity.
lessons.modelAnswer: We agree on RPO and RTO first because they are the business's answer to two questions: how much data can we lose, and how long can we be down. Backup frequency follows from the RPO, since anything written after the last copy is gone. The restore method follows from the RTO, since a cold copy that must be rebuilt takes far longer than a warm or hot standby. Without these numbers we would be guessing at both. The tradeoff is cost and complexity. A tighter RPO means more frequent backups or continuous change logs, which costs more storage and adds operational work. A tighter RTO usually means keeping standby infrastructure running all the time, which costs money even when nothing fails. This choice mainly serves the Reliability pillar of the Well-Architected Framework, and it must be balanced against cost.
rubricPoints: RPO is the maximum tolerable data loss measured in time, and it sets backup frequency.
RTO is the maximum tolerable downtime, and it sets the restore method or standby level.
A tighter RPO or RTO raises cost or operational complexity, which is the real tradeoff.
Backups should be stored apart from the live system and tested with real restores.

suggested.rationale: The disaster-recovery planner engine would let the learner set RPO and RTO targets and see which backup and standby choices meet them, which is the core reasoning of this objective.

lessons.plain: Many companies keep some systems in their own data centre and run others in one or more cloud providers. Designing integration means deciding how those separate places talk to each other safely and reliably: how traffic travels between them, how each side finds the other by name, how addresses avoid clashing, and who is allowed to connect. Think of it like linking two offices in different cities. You need a road, a map that tells traffic which way to go, unique street addresses, and a gate that checks visitors. Every choice affects speed, safety, and cost, so the architect must pick the link type that matches the business need.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company runs an order system in its own data centre and wants a cloud service to call it every minute. Name two things you would need to agree on before any traffic flows, and say why each matters.
lessons.teach:
Hybrid means some workloads run on premises (in a data centre your organisation owns or rents) and others run in the cloud. Multicloud means workloads span more than one cloud provider. Integration design answers three questions: how packets travel between the environments, how addresses and names resolve across them, and how identity and firewall rules decide who may connect.

For the travelling part there are two broad link types. A VPN (virtual private network) builds an encrypted tunnel over the public internet. It is quick to set up and inexpensive, but bandwidth is limited and latency varies with internet conditions. A dedicated or partner interconnect is a private physical link into the cloud provider's network. It gives steadier latency and higher bandwidth at a higher price and a longer lead time. Routing protocols such as BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) let the two sides exchange which address ranges they own, so routes update without hand edits. In Google Cloud, the component that performs this exchange is called Cloud Router.

Worked example. An on-premises ERP uses the range 10.20.0.0/16. The cloud network is also created with 10.20.0.0/16. Step 1: a cloud service sends a request to 10.20.5.10, the ERP. Step 2: the cloud sees that address as one of its own local subnets, so the packet never leaves the cloud. Step 3: the request silently fails. The fix is to plan non-overlapping ranges before building anything.

Common mistake: sizing the link by average office traffic and ignoring nightly batch jobs or peak load, or assuming a VPN is always good enough. In a running system, saturated links and overlapping routes cause timeouts that look like application bugs, so the design must be verified with path tracing and realistic load before cutover.

Integration is a set of trade-offs between cost, lead time, performance, and security, not a single correct product.

questions.prompt: A warehouse company runs its inventory server on premises at 192.168.10.44, inside the range 192.168.10.0/24. The company builds a cloud network and gives it the same range, 192.168.10.0/24. A reporting job in the cloud is then tested. Step 1: the job sends a request to 192.168.10.44. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: the request fails with no error reaching the job. Which statement correctly fills the missing step?
choices: The VPN tunnel encrypts the packet, so the inventory server cannot decrypt it and drops it.
The cloud network sees 192.168.10.44 as its own local subnet, so the packet stays inside the cloud.
The inventory server receives the request and rejects it because the reporting job has no service account.
Cloud Router withdraws the inventory route, so the packet waits in a queue until the link recovers.
questions.why: Because the cloud network uses the same range as the on-premises server, the cloud treats that address as one of its own local subnets and keeps the packet inside, which is why the request silently fails.

questions.prompt: A team needs a link into the cloud with steadier latency and higher bandwidth, and it can accept a longer lead time and higher cost. Which link type fits this requirement best?
choices: A dedicated or partner interconnect
A single routing table entry with no link
A VPN tunnel over the public internet
A shared office broadband line
questions.why: A dedicated or partner interconnect is a private physical link that gives steadier latency and higher bandwidth at a higher price and longer lead time, which matches the stated trade-off.

questions.prompt: An on-premises system uses the range 10.50.0.0/16. Which cloud range can be planned without overlapping it?
questions.why: The range 10.5.0.0/16 covers different addresses from 10.50.0.0/16, so routes will not collide, while the other three options each include addresses already used on premises.

questions.prompt: A team sized its VPN using average office traffic. Nightly batch jobs then cause timeouts that look like application bugs. What should the team have done before cutover?
choices: Removed the batch jobs so the VPN would not be stressed
Tested with realistic peak and batch load and verified the path before cutover
Switched to Cloud Router so that routes update automatically
Assumed the VPN was good enough because average traffic was low
questions.why: The teaching text says a design must be verified with realistic load and path tracing before cutover, because saturated links cause timeouts that mimic application bugs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would connect an on-premises network to a cloud network, and name one limit or trade-off of the option you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by checking the address ranges on both sides and making sure they do not overlap, because identical ranges mean the cloud cannot route to the on-premises machines even when the link is up. Then I would choose the link type. An encrypted VPN over the internet is fast to set up and cheap, but its bandwidth is capped and its latency varies, so it suits moderate or non-critical traffic. A dedicated or partner interconnect gives steadier latency and more bandwidth, but it costs more and takes longer to order. The trade-off I would name to the team is cost and lead time against steadiness of performance. Route exchange, name resolution between the two sides, and firewall rules come next. I would verify the path with a trace and a load test before moving real traffic.
rubricPoints: Check that address ranges on both sides do not overlap before anything else
Compare VPN and dedicated or partner interconnect on cost, lead time, bandwidth, and latency
Name a concrete trade-off of the chosen link type
Mention route exchange, name resolution, or firewall rules as part of the integration
Describe verifying the path with tracing or load testing before cutover

suggested.rationale: Tracing the path a packet takes across two networks is the hands-on way to see routes, overlapping ranges, and firewall blocks.

lessons.plain: This lesson is about choosing the right kind of AI building block for a business problem. Some options are ready-made models you call over the internet, such as a text writer or summarizer. Some are a catalogue of many models you can compare and deploy. Some are toolkits for building a chatbot that answers from your own documents. Some are very large pools of specialized computers for training or running big models yourself. The architect's job is to match the need, such as speed to market, data privacy, control, or cost, to the right option, and to state what that choice gives up.
lessons.guessPrompt: A retailer wants a chatbot that answers customer questions using only its own product manuals, and its team has no machine learning staff. Before reading anything, would you build a model from scratch, use a ready-made model through a managed service, or rent a large cluster of accelerators to train one? Give your first choice and one reason.
lessons.teach:
A large language model (LLM) is a model trained on very large amounts of text to predict and generate language, so it can answer questions, summarize, or draft text. Gemini is Google's family of models, some of which also accept images and other inputs. You reach Gemini through Vertex AI, Google Cloud's managed AI platform, so you do not host the model yourself. Model Garden is a catalogue inside that platform where you browse and deploy many models, including Google's own, open, and partner models, so you can compare them. Agent Builder is a set of tools for building conversational agents and search experiences that ground answers in your own data, so the model answers from your documents rather than only from what it learned in training. AI Hypercomputer is an integrated infrastructure of accelerator chips, fast networking, storage, and software for training and serving very large models at scale. It is the infrastructure layer, not a chatbot.

The design logic is simple: the less you build and operate, the faster you ship, but the less control you keep. A managed model call needs no servers to patch, yet your prompts travel to a provider endpoint, so data location and governance must be checked. Running an open model yourself gives more control over data and tuning, at the cost of operating it.

Worked example. Step 1: the requirement is answers grounded in manuals, with no ML staff. Step 2: rule out AI Hypercomputer, because training from scratch is unnecessary and the team cannot run it. Step 3: choose a Gemini model reached through Agent Builder, which indexes the manuals and grounds responses in them. Step 4: record the trade-off: data handling and per-use cost of a managed service must be checked against the privacy requirement.

Common mistake: choosing the largest or newest model by default. A smaller model may meet latency and cost goals, and a bigger one raises both.

Consequence: if the chatbot is called on every page view without grounding, cost and latency climb and wrong answers reach customers, so quotas, monitoring, and evaluation belong in the design. Each choice here serves security, cost, and reliability pillars, and each one carries a named trade-off.

questions.prompt: A regional logistics firm wants short daily summaries of shipment exceptions, such as late or damaged parcels, written from its own tracking records. It has two application developers and no machine learning staff, and its contract requires that customer shipment records stay in the European Union. Step 1: the requirement is readable summaries of exception records, with no ML team to operate anything. Step 2: rule out AI Hypercomputer, because the firm does not need to train a model from scratch and cannot run that infrastructure. Step 3: choose a Gemini model reached through Vertex AI, and pass each day's exception records in the request itself, since the summaries use only those records and need no separate search index. Step 4: [missing] Which action completes the design before any real records are sent?
choices: Check the data location and handling of the managed model endpoint against the European Union requirement.
Turn off request logging and monitoring to reduce the per-call cost of the summaries.
Benchmark the largest model in Model Garden so the summaries have the highest possible quality.
Reserve AI Hypercomputer accelerators so that summary generation has the lowest possible latency.
questions.why: The managed endpoint means prompts travel to a provider, so the data location and handling must be verified against the stated residency rule before records are sent, which the other options do not address.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is Model Garden within Vertex AI?
