choices: A training cluster of accelerator chips and fast networking used to build very large models from scratch.
A set of tools that connects a conversational agent to a company's documents so answers are grounded in them.
A monitoring dashboard that records how often each deployed model answers a request and how long it takes.
A catalogue inside the platform where you browse and deploy many models, including Google's own, open, and partner models, so you can compare them.
questions.why: Model Garden is the catalogue where you browse and deploy many models to compare them, while the other options describe AI Hypercomputer, Agent Builder, and a monitoring tool.

questions.prompt: A furniture retailer wants a model to suggest short product tags for a catalogue of tens of thousands of items, and the tags must appear within a fraction of a second on the product page. The team's first instinct is to pick the newest and largest model available. Which outcome best describes the risk of that choice in this design?
choices: A larger model tends to raise both latency and cost, and a smaller model may already meet the speed and budget goals.
Choosing the largest model removes the need for quotas and monitoring.
The largest model guarantees correct tags, so no evaluation is needed.
The largest model will be cheaper per call, so the budget improves.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that a bigger model raises cost and latency, and a smaller model may meet the goals, so the largest-by-default choice works against the stated requirements.

questions.prompt: A bank wants a language model to summarise internal credit memos. Its compliance team insists that memo text never leave infrastructure the bank controls, and it has engineers who can operate model servers. Which design trade-off does the bank accept by running an open model itself rather than calling a managed Gemini endpoint?
choices: It gains a managed service that needs no patching, but its prompts travel to a provider endpoint.
It must rely on Agent Builder to ground every answer, which it cannot do with an open model.
It gives up all control over tuning, but cost per call drops to zero.
It keeps control over data and tuning, but it takes on the work of operating the model.
questions.why: The teaching text states that running an open model yourself gives more control over data and tuning at the cost of operating it, which is exactly the trade-off the bank accepts.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how you would choose between calling a Gemini model through a managed service, using Agent Builder for grounded answers, and running an open model yourself. Name the main limit or trade-off of the option you would not pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with what the business needs. If the team wants answers from its own documents quickly and has no ML staff, I would use Agent Builder with a Gemini model, because it handles grounding in our data and removes server operation. The trade-off is that prompts and responses go to a managed service, so I would check data residency and governance first, and per-use cost grows with traffic. Running an open model from Model Garden on our own infrastructure would give more control over data and tuning, but I would not pick it first, since we would have to operate and scale it ourselves. AI Hypercomputer only makes sense when we train or serve very large models at a scale that justifies dedicated accelerators.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes a managed model service from hosting or building a model yourself.
Explains that Agent Builder grounds answers in the organization's own data.
Names a real trade-off such as data handling, control, or per-use cost.
Notes that AI Hypercomputer is infrastructure for very large training or serving, not a default choice.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission covers AI service selection, so a catalogue read followed by a case-study scenario to reason through is the best fit.

lessons.plain: Cloud networking design is deciding how your servers, containers, and services connect to each other and to users, and who is allowed to talk to what. Think of a building: a private network is the internal corridors, firewalls are locked doors with rules about who may pass, load balancers are receptionists sending visitors to whichever office has room, and routing is the signposts that show traffic the way. Architects make these choices so the system is reachable by the right people, stays private where it should, and keeps working as traffic grows.
lessons.guessPrompt: Imagine a public website and a database that should only be reached by that website. Without looking anything up, what would you place between them so the database cannot be reached from the internet, and why?
lessons.teach:
A virtual private cloud (VPC) is your own isolated network inside a cloud provider: a private address space where your machines get internal addresses and talk to each other without touching the public internet. In Google Cloud a VPC is global, while the subnets inside it are regional. A firewall rule allows or denies traffic into or out of resources based on source, destination, port, and protocol. A load balancer accepts traffic on one address and spreads it across healthy backends. Routing is how packets find their next hop. Peering connects two separate VPCs so they can reach each other privately, but peering is not transitive: if A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B. Shared VPC lets one host project own the network while service projects attach resources to its subnets, so a platform team controls network rules while product teams deploy. Private Service Connect gives a consumer a private endpoint inside its own network that forwards to a service elsewhere, without exposing whole address ranges.

Worked example: a web tier in subnet 10.0.1.0/24 must call a database at 10.0.2.5 in the same VPC. Step 1: both sit in one VPC, so routing between subnets is automatic. Step 2: add an ingress firewall rule allowing TCP port 5432 only from the web tier's network tag. Step 3: the database has no public address, so the internet cannot reach it directly. Step 4: any other source hits the implicit deny rule and is dropped.

Common mistake: opening a rule to all sources, 0.0.0.0/0, to fix a connection error quickly. The database then becomes reachable from the internet, a security failure that often surfaces only during an audit or incident.

In a running system, one over-broad or misplaced rule can silently break a checkout path or expose customer data, so every rule should trace back to a named source and a named purpose.

questions.prompt: Bluewater Logistics runs an API tier in subnet 10.20.5.0/24 of VPC api-vpc. Its reporting service at 10.30.1.10 lives in a separate VPC, reporting-vpc, so the two networks are not connected yet. Work through the fix step by step. Step 1: the two VPCs are separate networks, so nothing connects them by default. Step 2 (missing): ___. Step 3: add an ingress firewall rule on reporting-vpc allowing TCP port 8443 only from the API tier's network tag, so the source and purpose are named. Step 4: any other source hits the implicit deny rule and is dropped. Which statement correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Create a peering between api-vpc and reporting-vpc so they can reach each other privately
Give the reporting service a public IP address so the peering is not needed
Open the reporting firewall to 0.0.0.0/0 on port 8443 so the API can connect
Make reporting-vpc a Shared VPC service project so it joins the API tier's network
questions.why: Peering is the step that connects two separate VPCs privately, and the firewall rule in Step 3 then limits which source may use it.

questions.prompt: A company has VPC-A peered with VPC-B, and VPC-B peered with VPC-C. A virtual machine in VPC-A tries to reach a virtual machine in VPC-C and the connection fails. What is the most likely reason?
choices: Peering is not transitive, so VPC-A needs its own direct peering with VPC-C
The traffic must pass through a load balancer before it can cross a second peering
Google Cloud VPCs are regional, so VPC-A cannot see any VPC outside its region
VPC-A and VPC-C must each be a Shared VPC host, which is not allowed
questions.why: Peering is not transitive, so a route through VPC-B does not give VPC-A access to VPC-C; a direct peering is needed.

questions.prompt: A retail platform team wants a central group to own network rules while separate product teams deploy their own services. Which description of Shared VPC best fits this need?
choices: Each product project keeps a private copy of the network, and the platform team merges the copies monthly
One host project owns the network and its subnets, while service projects attach their resources to those subnets
A peering is created between each product project and the platform project so routes can be exchanged
The service projects own the firewall rules, and the host project only holds billing records
questions.why: In Shared VPC the host project owns the network and service projects attach resources to its subnets, which splits network control from deployment.

questions.prompt: A firewall rule allows TCP port 3306 into database instances tagged db, but only from instances tagged app-servers. A new batch VM tagged batch needs to read from the database. A developer adds a rule allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on port 3306 to fix it quickly. What is the best correction?
choices: Give the database a public address so the batch VM can reach it directly over the internet
Add an ingress rule allowing TCP port 3306 only from the batch tag to the db tag, so the source and purpose are named
Keep the 0.0.0.0/0 rule because the port is limited to 3306 and the traffic stays inside the network
Move the batch VM into the app-servers tag so the existing rule matches it without any new rule
questions.why: A narrow rule that names its source and purpose keeps the database closed to everything else, whereas 0.0.0.0/0 opens it to any source.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how you would connect a public web tier to a private database that lives in a different project in the same company, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would put the web tier and the database in a Shared VPC so the platform team owns the network and its firewall rules, while the web and data teams deploy into their own service projects. The database gets only a private address, and a firewall rule allows the database port only from the web tier's tag. If the database lives in a separate, unrelated network instead, I would use VPC peering or Private Service Connect. The tradeoff is that Shared VPC centralizes control, so the platform team becomes a dependency for network changes, and peering is not transitive, so a third network cannot reach the database through the first one. I would also note that every firewall rule I add needs a named purpose, because a broad rule added during an outage is the most common way private data ends up reachable.
rubricPoints: Names a mechanism to connect the two networks, such as Shared VPC, peering, or Private Service Connect, and says why it fits.
Explains that firewall rules limit traffic to the specific source and port needed.
States a real limit or tradeoff, such as centralized ownership, non-transitive peering, or address range overlap.
Notes the risk of overly broad rules and why each rule needs a stated purpose.

suggested.rationale: A virtual network path tracer would let the learner see which firewall rules and routes allow or block a path, which is the core skill of this networking objective.

lessons.plain: Choosing a data processing solution means deciding how a business turns raw data, such as sales records, sensor readings, or clicks, into something useful like totals, reports, or alerts. The central question is timing: does the work happen in scheduled batches, or continuously as each piece of data arrives? It also means deciding who runs the machinery. You can operate the servers yourself, use a managed service that scales for you, or reuse tools your team already knows. Think of a bakery that bakes one big tray each night versus making each loaf as orders come in. Both work. They differ in speed, cost, and how much staff effort they need.
lessons.guessPrompt: A retailer wants a sales dashboard that is accurate by 7 am each day, and sales data arrives all day long. Would you process the data as it arrives, or once each night in one large job? Give one reason for your choice.
lessons.teach:
A data processing solution is the set of services that reads incoming data, transforms it, and produces results. The first decision is timing. Batch processing collects data and handles it together at a scheduled time. Stream processing handles each record, or a small window of records, as it arrives. Batch is usually cheaper per record and simpler to reason about. Streaming keeps results fresh, meaning the delay between an event happening and its result appearing is short. That delay is called latency.

Why this matters: freshness costs money and effort. A stream pipeline keeps workers running all day, while a batch job runs for a few hours and then stops. Managed services move the operational work to the provider. Dataflow is Google Cloud's managed service for batch and stream pipelines, and it handles scaling for you. Dataproc runs managed Apache Spark and Hadoop clusters, which suits teams that already have that code. BigQuery can transform and query stored data with SQL, which suits analysis questions.

Worked example: a retailer's stores send sales events all day. Step 1: the requirement says the dashboard must show yesterday's totals by 7 am. Step 2: minute-level freshness is not required, so batch fits. Step 3: the team already has Spark jobs, so a managed Spark service runs them with little rewriting. Step 4: the result is one scheduled nightly job, with no always-on workers.

Common mistake: choosing streaming because it sounds modern, then paying for constant capacity to produce results nobody reads before morning.

Consequence in a running system: a stream pipeline that falls behind builds a backlog, and lag grows until it catches up. A batch job that fails halfway must be rerun, so its steps should be safe to repeat.

Choosing a data processing solution means matching timing, cost, and existing skills to the business need.

questions.prompt: Northwind Parcels has vans that send a scan event each time a parcel is loaded or delivered. Requirement: the fleet manager must see a late-delivery alert within 2 minutes of a scan. Step 1: the requirement sets a 2-minute limit, so minute-level freshness matters, which points to stream processing rather than batch. Step 2: stream processing keeps results fresh, so the alert pipeline handles each scan as it arrives. Step 3: ___ Step 4: the result is an always-on pipeline that alerts within the 2-minute target. Which completion fills Step 3?
choices: The team has no cluster-management skills and wants the provider to handle scaling, so pick a managed pipeline service such as Dataflow that runs stream pipelines.
Store every scan in BigQuery and query it once a day to find late deliveries.
Batch is always cheaper, so run a nightly batch job and assume the 2-minute target is still met.
The team already runs Spark jobs, so keep using a managed Spark cluster for the alerts.
questions.why: Managed services move scaling and operations to the provider, and a managed pipeline service that handles streams fits a team with no cluster skills and a 2-minute freshness need.

questions.prompt: In data processing, what does the term latency mean?
choices: The number of records a pipeline handles per second.
The number of unprocessed records waiting in a queue.
The delay between an event happening and its result appearing.
The scheduled time at which a batch job is started.
questions.why: The teaching text defines latency as the delay between an event happening and its result appearing, which is the sense of freshness being discussed.

questions.prompt: A bank must reconcile each day's card transactions and have the results ready by 6 am. The team already has working Spark code for this. Which design best fits the requirement and the team's existing skills?
choices: Stream pipeline with always-on workers, since streaming is the more modern choice.
Rewrite the Spark code into a new stream design before deciding the timing.
Scheduled batch run on managed Spark, reusing the existing code.
Stream every card transaction into a live dashboard, because reconciliation must always be fresh.
questions.why: A 6 am deadline does not require fresh results, so a scheduled batch run is enough, and a managed Spark service runs the existing code with little rewriting.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a weekly job that generates invoices. The job fails at 60 percent completion and must be rerun. What design property prevents a rerun from causing harm?
choices: Make it a stream so it never needs a rerun.
Add more always-on workers so the job cannot fail halfway.
Make each step safe to repeat, so a rerun does not duplicate invoices.
Skip the failed invoices and never rerun, since batch results are only approximate.
questions.why: The teaching text notes that a failed batch job must be rerun, so its steps should be safe to repeat, which means a rerun must not duplicate work or results.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between batch and streaming processing for a new reporting feature, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the business requirement for freshness. If the report must be correct by a set morning time and nobody acts on it during the day, batch is the better fit. It is usually cheaper, because a scheduled job runs for a short time and stops, while a streaming pipeline keeps workers running around the clock. I also check what the team already knows. If they have existing Spark code, a managed Spark service avoids a costly rewrite. The tradeoff with streaming is that it is more complex to operate and costs more to keep running. If I did choose streaming, I would need to watch for backlog, because if processing falls behind, results grow stale. Batch has its own limit: results are only as fresh as the last run, so it is the wrong choice for alerts that must fire within seconds.
rubricPoints: Ties the choice of batch or streaming to a stated freshness requirement
Names cost or operational effort as the main tradeoff of continuous processing
Considers existing skills or code as a factor in choosing a managed service
States a concrete limit of the option not chosen first

suggested.rationale: This design exercise makes the learner choose how vehicle-position data is ingested and processed, which practises the same timing and cost reasoning this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Cloud storage comes in three broad shapes. Object storage keeps whole files, called objects, each with a name and some metadata, in a flat pool you reach over the network. Think of a warehouse of labelled boxes that you fetch whole. File storage presents a shared folder tree that several machines can mount and edit at once, like a network drive in an office. Database storage holds structured records that you search, update and protect with rules about consistency, like a ledger you query. Choosing the right shape starts with the business requirement: how the data is accessed, how often it changes, and who must share it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team stores thousands of customer invoice PDFs that are written once and read occasionally, and also keeps a live table of account balances that many services update at the same moment. Which storage shape fits each, and why would swapping them cause trouble?
lessons.teach:
Object storage holds whole units of data, called objects, each found by a key (its name inside a bucket, which is a container you create). You write an object in one go and read it back in one go; you do not edit a few bytes in the middle. Its strengths are very large scale, low cost per gigabyte, and access by many clients over the network, with lifecycle rules that move old objects to cheaper tiers. It suits media, backups, logs and static assets.

File storage presents a directory tree that machines mount as if it were a local disk, using ordinary file operations. Several virtual machines can share the same files. Choose it when existing software expects a mounted filesystem or when several servers share working files. It costs more per gigabyte and scales less freely than object storage.

Database storage keeps structured records that you query by their fields. Transactions make a group of changes apply completely or not at all, and consistency means every reader sees a coherent answer. Choose it when you must find rows by conditions, update related items together, or keep concurrent writers in agreement.

Why it works: the access pattern decides the shape. Object storage trades fine-grained editing for scale and cheapness; databases trade some raw scale and cost for queries and consistency.

Worked example: a dispatch app stores each driver's live position. Step 1: the position changes every few seconds and is read by driver id, so a database fits. Step 2: route photos are uploaded once and never edited, so object storage fits. Step 3: a legacy tool that expects a shared mounted folder of route templates points to file storage.

Common mistake: putting a frequently updated record into object storage because it is cheap, then rewriting the whole object on every change. This is slow and offers no safe way to handle two writers at once.

Consequence: a retry that rewrites a whole object can overwrite a newer copy from another writer, so the wrong version becomes live. The storage shape sets the cost, the consistency guarantees, and how the system fails under load.

questions.prompt: Harbor Tickets sells seats for live events. Seat holds change many times a second and must never let two buyers take the same seat, so the team chose a database. Event trailer videos are uploaded once, never edited, and are watched by many viewers, so they went to object storage. Three kiosk servers at a venue share a folder of seating-map images that they mount and edit with ordinary file commands, so that went to file storage. Step 4 is the refund ledger: each refund must update the order row and add a matching ledger row together, or neither, and finance searches the ledger by date and region. Which storage type fits Step 4, and why?
choices: Object storage, because ledger files are cheap to keep for many years
Object storage with lifecycle rules, because old ledger rows can move to a cheaper tier
Database storage, because the order and ledger changes must apply together and finance must query rows by date and region
File storage, because several finance servers can mount the same ledger file
questions.why: The refund and its ledger entry must succeed or fail as one unit and the rows must be found by their fields, which are the two things a database provides.

questions.prompt: Crumb and Co, a bakery chain, writes one temperature log file per oven per day. Each file is written once at closing time and is never changed afterward. A reporting dashboard reads these files by day across 300 ovens. Which storage type fits best?
choices: Database storage, because the files must be updated together for each oven
Database storage, because every reading is a structured record
Object storage, because each whole file is written once and read back in one go at low cost
File storage, because the dashboard expects a mounted folder
questions.why: Whole units written once and read back in one go, at large scale and low cost, match the object storage pattern described in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: A stadium parking app keeps a live count of free spaces in each of 12 lots as cars enter and leave. The count changes several times a minute, and several gate computers update it at the same time. The team stores the count as a whole object and rewrites that object on every change. What is the most likely problem?
choices: Object storage cannot hold numbers, so the app will crash at startup
Each rewrite is slow, and two gate computers can overwrite each other with an older count, so the wrong number goes live
The object will be too large to store because counts grow over time
The lot counts will be cheaper but unreadable by the gate computers
questions.why: Rewriting a whole frequently changed object is slow and gives no safe way for concurrent writers to agree, so a stale copy can replace a newer one.

questions.prompt: Lantern Studio runs an editing suite where six workstations mount the same project folder. Editors save small changes to project files many times a day, and the editing software opens files with ordinary local-disk commands. Storage needs are about 80 TB. Which storage type should the team choose for the active projects?
choices: Database storage, because each small change must be a transaction
Object storage with lifecycle rules, because active projects can later move to a cold tier
File storage, because the software expects a mounted directory tree that several machines share
Object storage, because it is the cheapest per gigabyte for 80 TB
questions.why: The software expects a mounted filesystem and several machines must share working files, which is the case the teaching text assigns to file storage even though it costs more per gigabyte.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between object, file and database storage for a new feature. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you are most tempted to over-use.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from how the data is used, not from the product. If the data is whole files that are written once and read back whole, such as uploads, backups or logs, I use object storage, which scales cheaply and lets lifecycle rules age data into colder tiers. If several servers must share a working directory through normal file operations, I use file storage, but I accept that it costs more per gigabyte and grows less freely. If we need to query records by their fields, update related rows together, or keep one consistent answer under concurrent writes, I use a database. The option I am most tempted to over-use is object storage, because it is cheap and simple to start with. Its limit is that you cannot change part of an object without rewriting all of it, so frequently changing records belong in a database.
rubricPoints: Object storage holds whole objects reached by key, and suits write-once or read-whole data at large scale.
File storage gives a shared, mounted directory tree to several machines, at higher cost and lower scale.
Databases suit structured records that are queried and need transactions and consistency.
The access pattern and how often data changes drive the choice, not habit or price alone.
The answer names a real tradeoff of the chosen option, such as rewrite cost, cost per gigabyte, or consistency.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a storage shape is best checked by reasoning through a mixed-workload scenario where the access pattern decides the answer.

lessons.plain: When you rent computers in the cloud, you choose their size and kind. This objective covers three choices. A Spot machine is spare capacity the cloud provider sells cheaply, but it can take the machine back with very little warning. A custom machine type lets you pick exactly how many processor cores and how much memory you need, instead of a fixed package that may leave you paying for capacity you never use. A specialized workload needs hardware built for a narrow job, such as graphics processors for machine learning or a dedicated physical host for licensing rules. The skill is matching each choice to a business need: how much interruption the work can tolerate, how predictable its size is, and what hardware it truly requires.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job splits into 400 independent pieces, and each piece can be safely redone from scratch if it fails. Would you run it on a cheap machine the provider can reclaim at any moment, or on a standard machine that is never taken away? Explain why in a sentence or two.
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A virtual machine (VM) is a rented computer running in a provider's data center. A Spot VM is a VM priced well below normal, built from spare capacity. The provider can stop it, which is called preemption, when it needs that capacity back, usually with a warning of about 30 seconds. A machine type is the combination of virtual CPUs (vCPUs, which are processor cores presented to the VM) and memory a VM gets. A predefined machine type is a fixed package of those two numbers. A custom machine type lets you set the vCPU count and memory within allowed limits. A specialized workload needs accelerators (GPUs or TPUs, chips built for parallel math) or isolation, such as a sole-tenant node, which is a whole physical server reserved for you alone.

Why it works: cost follows what you reserve and how interruptible the work is. Spot trades the guarantee that a machine stays running for a lower price, so it fits work that can stop and restart. Custom types remove the waste of an oversized predefined package.

Worked example: a nightly job must transcode 400 video segments. Each segment is independent and can be retried. Step 1: the work tolerates interruption, so Spot is viable. Step 2: each segment writes its output only when finished, so a preempted segment is simply re-queued. Step 3: each worker needs 4 vCPUs and 6 GB of memory, so a custom type of that size avoids paying for a larger predefined package. Step 4: the savings multiply across all 400 segments.

Common mistake: putting a checkout service or a database with no failover on Spot because it is cheap. A single point of failure, meaning one component whose loss stops everything, then becomes an outage customers feel immediately.

Consequence in a running system: when the cloud reclaims a Spot VM, anything held only in its memory or local disk is lost, so the design must handle that before you choose the price. Choose the compute to fit the work's tolerance for interruption, not the lowest price on the page.

questions.prompt: A regional insurer runs a nightly batch that recalculates renewal premiums for 12,000 policies. Each policy is calculated independently and its result is saved only when that policy finishes. Step 1: the batch can tolerate interruption, so Spot VMs are viable for the workers. Step 2: a policy whose worker is reclaimed mid-calculation has saved nothing, so it is simply put back on the queue. Step 3: each worker needs 2 vCPUs and 8 GB of memory, so a custom machine type of that size is chosen rather than a larger predefined package. Step 4 (the one missing step): before accepting Spot for the whole batch, identify the component that, if reclaimed, would stop all 12,000 policies from being queued and tracked, and decide where it runs. Which completion correctly finishes the reasoning?
choices: Move all 12,000 policy calculations onto a sole-tenant node so that none of them can be preempted.
Choose the largest predefined machine type so the batch finishes sooner and the custom type is no longer needed.
Run the queue scheduler that hands out and re-queues policies on a regular, non-Spot VM, because it is the single point of failure for the whole batch.
Save two copies of every policy result so that a reclaimed worker never loses a finished calculation.
questions.why: The scheduler is the one component whose loss stops everything, so it belongs on a VM that will not be reclaimed, while the interruptible workers can stay on Spot.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is preemption in the context of a Spot VM?
choices: The VM is moved onto a dedicated physical server that only one customer may use.
The provider automatically lowers the VM's vCPU count to reduce what the customer pays.
The provider can stop the VM when it needs the spare capacity back, often after a short warning.
The customer permanently deletes the VM once its job has finished running.
questions.why: Preemption is the provider stopping a Spot VM to reclaim capacity it lent out, which is why Spot suits only work that can stop and restart.

questions.prompt: A university runs a weekly job that regenerates thumbnails for 80,000 archived images. Each image is independent, and its new thumbnail is written only after it is complete. Which workload is the best fit for Spot VMs?
choices: The weekly thumbnail regeneration, where an interrupted image can simply be retried.
The primary gateway that routes all incoming web traffic to the rest of the application.
The live login service that authenticates students every time they open the learning portal.
The enrolment database, which has no replica and holds the only copy of student records.
questions.why: Thumbnail regeneration tolerates interruption because each image is independent and retryable, which is the property Spot requires, while the other three cannot tolerate an outage.

questions.prompt: A team configures a custom machine type with 3 vCPUs and 10 GB of memory for a session service on a Spot VM. Session data is held only in the VM's memory. After a reclaim, all active sessions vanish. What is the root cause?
choices: The session data lived only in memory on an interruptible VM, and the reclaim removed it, so the design ignored preemption.
The custom machine type was invalid, so the VM restarted with default settings that cleared sessions.
Spot VMs always keep memory on a separate disk, so the data should have survived and the storage client must have failed.
The 10 GB of memory was too large, so the operating system swapped session data out to disk and lost it.
questions.why: Anything held only in a Spot VM's memory or local disk is lost when the provider reclaims it, so the design needed to store sessions somewhere durable before choosing Spot.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would place a batch workload on Spot VMs and when you would refuse to, and name the main limit of Spot that drives that decision.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would put a batch job on Spot VMs when each unit of work is independent, idempotent, meaning it can be redone without harm, and writes its result only when complete. Then a preemption just means the unit goes back into the queue, and the savings can be large. The main limit is that Spot capacity can be reclaimed at short notice, so there is no guarantee any given machine will still be running later. I would refuse Spot for anything that holds state only in memory, has a single point of failure, or serves live customers where an interruption is an outage. In those cases I would use standard VMs, possibly with a custom machine type so I do not pay for unused memory. The decision is a trade between cost and reliability, and I would state that trade in the design document.
rubricPoints: Spot VMs are cheaper because they use spare capacity and can be preempted with a short warning.
Work suited to Spot can be stopped, restarted and re-queued without harm.
Work with a single point of failure or state that cannot be lost should stay on standard VMs.
Custom machine types match vCPU and memory to the real need and avoid paying for unused capacity.
Specialized hardware such as GPUs or sole-tenant nodes is justified by the workload or licensing needs, not by habit.

suggested.rationale: Choosing compute well means reasoning through a situation where interruption tolerance, cost and hardware needs pull in different directions, which an exam-style scenario trains better than reading alone.

lessons.plain: When a company moves a working system to the cloud, the new piece rarely works alone. It still has to talk to the billing database, the login service, or the stock system that stays on older servers for now. Integrating a new solution with existing systems means deciding how those connections are made during the move, so data and requests keep flowing correctly the whole time. A good plan answers which systems must keep talking, in which direction, for how long, and what happens when one side is slow or down. Think of rewiring a house one room at a time: the lights must keep working while the new circuits go in.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop moves its checkout service to the cloud, but the list of prices still lives in an office server. What would you need to work out before moving checkout, and why might moving it first cause problems?
lessons.teach:
Integrating a new solution with existing systems means connecting the new piece to the systems already running the business, such as an older database, a payment service, or an internal inventory tool, so data and requests keep flowing. An existing system is any component already in production that the new one relies on. A dependency is a case where the new piece cannot do its job without that system. In a migration plan, this work is an ordering problem: which connections must exist before the move, which can be retired afterward, and which must run side by side for a while. Coexistence is the period when old and new run together. During coexistence, each record needs a source of truth, meaning the one copy that wins when two copies disagree. Cutover is the moment traffic switches from the old path to the new one.

Why it works: the work moves in slices, and each slice keeps every dependency reachable, so the business never has to stop. Worked example: a retailer moves its price-calculation service to the cloud, but the product catalogue stays in an on-premises database. Step one, list every call the service makes to the catalogue. Step two, build a private network link between the two sites and measure the round-trip delay. Step three, keep the catalogue as the source of truth and let the cloud service read a copy. Step four, test under peak load, then cut over one region at a time while the old path stays ready to take traffic back.

Common mistake: moving the service first and treating its links as a later problem. Every call then crosses the public internet, requests time out during peak hours, and customers may see wrong prices.

In a running system, an unmapped dependency is the usual reason a cutover fails. Plan the links first, then move the workload.

questions.prompt: A regional logistics firm is moving its route-planning tool to the cloud. The tool depends on a fleet-tracking database that stays in the firm's own data centre. The firm works through the migration in order. Step 1: list every call the route tool makes to the fleet database, which turns up 14 distinct query types. Step 2 is missing and you must supply it: connect the two sites with a private network link and measure the round-trip delay under expected load before any traffic moves. Step 3: keep the fleet database as the source of truth and let the route tool read a copy. Step 4: cut over one depot at a time while the old path stays ready to take traffic back. Which option best describes what the missing Step 2 is for?
choices: It confirms each dependency stays reachable over a private path with acceptable delay before the move, so requests don't time out at peak.
It retires the fleet database as soon as the route tool has a copy, so only one system remains during cutover.
It lets the route tool write its own copy of fleet records so the cloud side becomes the source of truth.
It moves the route tool to the cloud first, so the link can be checked later once traffic is already flowing.
questions.why: The missing step builds and measures the private link before the move, which keeps every dependency reachable and is the slice-by-slice ordering the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: A bank runs its old card-authorisation system and its new one side by side for three weeks while both process live transactions. What is this overlap period called?
choices: Cutover
Source of truth
Coexistence
Dependency mapping
questions.why: Coexistence is the period when old and new systems run together, which is exactly what the bank is doing; cutover is the single moment traffic switches.

questions.prompt: A hotel chain moves its booking website to the cloud. The team lists the website's calls to its payment service and its inventory service, but never lists the loyalty-points service the website also calls. At cutover, bookings start failing for members. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The loyalty-points service was an unmapped dependency, so the new path could not reach it.
The coexistence period was too short for the new site to warm up.
The source of truth for bookings was set to the old website's database.
The cloud provider's region was chosen without checking the price list.
questions.why: An unmapped dependency is the usual reason a cutover fails, because a link that was never planned is not built before the traffic moves.

questions.prompt: During coexistence, a museum's old ticketing database shows 412 visitor passes for a Saturday slot, while the new ticketing service shows 398. The museum has declared the old database as the source of truth for that slot. Which count should the team use for the slot?
choices: 398, because the newer system is always the more accurate of the two copies.
412, because the designated source of truth is the copy that wins when two copies disagree.
Whichever count the staff member on duty prefers at the time.
The average of 405, since disagreeing copies should be merged numerically.
questions.why: The source of truth is the single copy that wins on disagreement, and here that is the old database, so its count of 412 is the one to use.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should move the checkout service to the cloud first and sort out its links to the old inventory system later. Explain to them how you would integrate the new service with existing systems during the migration, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing every system checkout depends on, such as inventory, pricing and payments, and marking which ones must stay on the existing side for now. Then I would set up a private, measured link between the old and new environments before moving any traffic, because public-internet calls at peak hours would time out. For each shared record I would name a source of truth, usually the inventory system, and let checkout read a copy. The move would happen in stages, with the old path kept ready for a fast fallback. The tradeoff is cost and complexity: while old and new run side by side, we pay for both environments, keep two data paths in sync, and maintain the private link until the last dependency is moved. That is the price of a move with no downtime.
rubricPoints: Identifies the existing systems and dependencies before moving the new service
Explains a secure, measured connection between old and new environments
Names a source of truth for shared data during coexistence
Names a real tradeoff such as duplicate cost, sync complexity, or a long-lived link

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a phased-migration scenario with competing constraints teaches this objective better than reading alone, and no listed mission or planned engine covers migration sequencing directly.

lessons.plain: Before you move a company's servers and databases into the cloud, you need an accurate picture of what exists: which machines are running, what each one does, what it depends on, and how heavily it is used. Migration Center is a Google Cloud service built to gather that picture. It helps you judge which systems are ready to move, how large they should be in the cloud, and roughly what they would cost to run there. Think of it as taking inventory and writing a moving plan before loading the truck, so you do not discover halfway through that a warehouse depends on a server nobody listed.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has 200 old servers and wants them in the cloud by spring. Before any server moves, what is the first piece of information you would want, and why would moving servers without it be risky?
lessons.teach:
Discovery means automatically finding the machines and services in an existing environment and recording what they do and how they behave over time, such as CPU use, memory use, and which other machines they talk to. Assessment means turning that raw record into decisions: whether each workload is ready to move, what size of cloud resource it needs, and what it might cost. A dependency is a link where one system relies on another, for example an application that reads from a database on a different machine. A migration wave is a group of systems moved together, because moving one part of a dependency chain alone can break it. Right-sizing means choosing cloud capacity that matches measured demand instead of copying the size of the old hardware.

The approach works because decisions made from measured data are more reliable than decisions made from memory or old purchase orders.

Worked example: an order-intake server has 16 CPU cores, but its average CPU use over thirty days is 12 percent, and its peak is 40 percent. Discovery records that it calls a database server on another machine. Assessment flags that link as a dependency and suggests a smaller cloud instance sized to the peak plus a margin. The plan then places the order server and its database in the same migration wave, so the traffic between them stays inside the cloud network.

Common mistake: trusting a sizing suggestion built from a short observation window that misses a monthly peak, such as a month-end billing run. The cloud instance then ends up undersized.

Consequence: when the month-end run arrives, the migrated order service slows or times out, even though the assessment said it was fine.

An assessment is only as good as the period it observed and the dependencies it found, so the plan has to check both before a workload moves.

questions.prompt: Harbor Bike Rentals runs a booking API on a server with 8 CPU cores. Step 1: discovery records 30 days of CPU use, averaging 18 percent, with a peak of 52 percent on a Saturday. Step 2: discovery finds that the booking API calls a pricing service on a separate machine. Step 3: assessment flags that call as a dependency and suggests a cloud instance sized to the 52 percent peak plus a margin. Step 4 is missing. The plan must decide which migration wave each of the two machines goes into. Which choice completes the plan correctly?
choices: Size the booking API from its 18 percent average, so the monthly cost stays low.
Leave the pricing service out of the plan, because a single small machine does not need a wave of its own.
Place the booking API and the pricing service in the same migration wave, so the traffic between them stays inside the cloud network.
Move the booking API in wave 1 and the pricing service in wave 3, so the first move is as cheap as possible.
questions.why: A dependency link breaks if only one side moves, so the two systems that depend on each other belong in the same wave.

questions.prompt: Lumen Clinic runs an appointment reminder service on a machine with 4 CPU cores. Discovery observed it for six weeks: average CPU use was 9 percent, and the highest peak was 30 percent, on Monday mornings. Which sizing basis best matches the principle of right-sizing?
choices: Size to the 9 percent average, because it is the most typical figure.
Keep 4 cores, because that is what the old hardware had.
Size to the price on the original purchase order, because that is the verified cost.
Size to the measured peak of 30 percent plus a margin, because the window covered the weekly peak.
questions.why: Right-sizing uses measured demand, here the 30 percent peak plus a margin, rather than the old hardware size or the average.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm assessed its payroll tool using only 10 days of data, taken from the middle of the month. The data showed low CPU use. What is the most likely result after the tool moves to the cloud?
choices: The tool will be cheaper than the assessment predicted, with no other effect.
The tool will show the same low use at month-end, because CPU use is steady all month.
The tool will slow or time out at the month-end payroll run, because the window missed that peak.
Discovery will automatically resize the instance during the month-end run.
questions.why: An assessment is only as good as the period it observed, and a window that misses a month-end peak leads to an undersized instance that slows at that peak.

questions.prompt: A dispatch app on machine A reads its data from a database on machine B. A separate reporting job on machine C also reads from machine B. Why should machine A and machine B be placed in the same migration wave?
choices: Because moving a cheaper machine first reduces the total cost of the whole migration.
Because moving one side of a dependency alone can break the link between them, so both must move together.
Because discovery can only record one machine's behaviour at a time, so the two must be grouped.
Because machines that share a database must always be sized to the same number of cores.
questions.why: A migration wave groups systems that depend on each other, since moving one side alone can break the link.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should lift every server we own into the cloud this quarter at the sizes they run at today, since the assessment already produced numbers. Explain how you would use discovery and assessment before moving anything, and name one limit of those numbers that they should not ignore.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not move anything until discovery has run long enough to cover a full business cycle, including month-end or seasonal peaks. Discovery records what each machine actually uses and which other machines it talks to. Assessment turns that into a readiness view and a suggested cloud size for each workload. I would group systems that depend on each other into the same migration wave so their connections stay intact. The limit to respect is that the numbers only describe the period they were observed in and only the dependencies the tool could see. A batch job that runs quarterly, or a link to a partner system outside the scanned network, can be missing entirely. So the sizes are a starting point to verify with a test workload, not a final decision, and copying today's oversized hardware one-for-one would throw away the cost benefit the move was meant to deliver.
rubricPoints: Explains discovery as measuring actual usage and dependencies, not relying on memory or old specs
Explains that assessment yields readiness, sizing, and cost estimates to inform decisions
Groups dependent systems into the same migration wave to avoid breaking links
Names a limit: observation window may miss peaks, and some dependencies may be invisible

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine walks through discovery and assessment, so this objective is best learned by reading the product's concepts and reasoning about the outputs.

lessons.plain: Moving a working system into a new data center or cloud is harder than it looks. This objective is about planning that move before you start. You decide how much of each system to change (move it as-is, adjust it a little, or rebuild it), prove it can handle real load in a trial run, check that its network addresses and connections still work in the new place, and map which systems depend on which so you move them in a safe order. A good plan turns a risky all-at-once switch into small, reversible steps.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has an old order system that talks to a billing database and a reporting server. Before moving it to the cloud, what would you want to know first, and why would moving only the database on Monday be risky?
lessons.teach:
A migration methodology is a named approach for deciding what happens to each system during a move. The common choices are rehost (move it as-is onto virtual machines, which is fastest but keeps old problems), replatform (make small changes, such as switching to a managed database, while keeping the code mostly the same), and refactor (redesign the application to use cloud-native services, which is slowest but gains the most). Workload testing means running the system under realistic or heavier load in a trial environment before cutover, so you learn its limits while rolling back is still cheap. Network planning means choosing IP address ranges that do not overlap with the existing network, deciding how traffic flows between old and new sites, and estimating how much data must cross the link. Dependency planning means listing what each system calls and what calls it, so that no service moves while something it needs is still left behind on the far side of a firewall or slow link.

The reason this works is that each step shrinks the blast radius. You move a small group, test it, and keep the old copy running until the new one is proven.

Worked example: a retailer has an order API, a pricing service, and a database. First, map dependencies: the API calls pricing and the database. Second, choose methods: rehost the API and replatform the database to a managed service. Third, test: a load test at twice peak traffic shows the connection pool saturates at 150 requests. Fourth, check networking: confirm the new subnet does not overlap the store network and open only the ports needed. Fifth, cut over pricing and the database first, then the API, keeping the old API on standby.

Common mistake: moving the database alone because it looks like the bottleneck, while the application that depends on it still runs on the old side of a slow link. Every query now crosses the network, and latency jumps.

In a running system, that latency change appears as customer-facing timeouts even though nobody changed the application code, which is why dependencies must move together or be planned around.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company moves three pieces: a seat-reservation service, a payments adapter, and a session cache. The team maps dependencies first: the reservation service calls the payments adapter and reads the session cache, and nothing else reads the cache. It then chooses methods: it rehosts the reservation service, replatforms the cache to a managed in-memory service, and rehosts the payments adapter. A load test at three times Saturday peak shows the adapter's retry queue passes 400 messages at 2,000 requests per minute. Step four is missing. Step five is: cut over the cache and adapter first, then the reservation service, keeping the old reservation service running on standby. Which choice correctly fills step four?
choices: Write down the rollback trigger before cutover: if production retries pass the tested limit, route traffic back to the old adapter, which stays running.
Delete the old session cache servers as soon as the managed cache starts, to free capacity.
Enlarge the new network to a /16 range so later services fit without any further planning.
Move the reservation service first because it has the most code, then move the cache and adapter.
questions.why: The old copy stays running until the new one is proven, so the rollback condition and path must be set in advance to keep reversal cheap.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches a replatform migration as the teaching text defines it?
choices: Keep the code mostly the same while making a small change, such as moving to a managed database.
Shut the system down for a weekend and rebuild it from a blank project without a trial run.
Copy each virtual machine image unchanged onto cloud machines and stop there.
Redesign the application around cloud-native services, accepting the longest timeline.
questions.why: Replatforming keeps the code largely intact and makes a small change such as switching to a managed database, which is what the text describes.

questions.prompt: A team plans to move a fraud-scoring service, but that service calls a customer-profile API which will stay on the old side behind a firewall that blocks the port the service uses. What does dependency planning direct the team to do?
choices: Move the scoring service now, since the firewall only affects the old side, and fix the port later.
Increase the scoring service's memory so it can wait longer for each blocked call.
Skip the dependency list because firewalls are handled by the network team after cutover.
Move the profile API with the scoring service, or map and open the traffic path before cutover.
questions.why: Dependency planning means listing what each system calls so that no service moves while something it needs is left behind somewhere it cannot reach well.

questions.prompt: A team reserves 10.0.0.0/16 for a new cloud network, but its office network already uses 10.0.128.0/17, which sits inside that same block. What is the main planning problem?
choices: The new network is too small to host any virtual machines at all.
The load test cannot run until the office network is renumbered to a public range.
Each cloud service will be charged extra for traffic that stays inside its own range.
The two ranges overlap, so routing cannot tell which addresses belong on which side; choose a non-overlapping range before building.
questions.why: Network planning requires IP ranges that do not overlap with the existing network, and this pair does because 10.0.128.0/17 falls entirely inside 10.0.0.0/16.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to cloud how you would plan moving a legacy reporting system into the cloud. Name one trade-off of the migration approach you choose and one thing you would check before cutover.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by mapping dependencies: what the reporting system reads from, what reads from it, and which scheduled jobs call it, because a move that ignores a nightly job breaks someone else's work. Then I would pick a methodology per component. The report engine could be rehosted quickly to meet a deadline, while the aging file-based data store might be replatformed to a managed database. The trade-off of rehosting is speed against carrying old problems into the cloud. Before cutover I would run a workload test with last quarter's peak report volume in the new environment, confirm the IP ranges do not clash with existing networks, and check that the data transfer window fits. I would move the data store and reports together, keep the old system read-only as a fallback, and retire it only after a week of clean runs.
rubricPoints: Maps dependencies before choosing what to move
Explains the migration approaches in own words with a trade-off for at least one
Describes workload testing under realistic or peak load before cutover
Covers network planning such as non-overlapping IP ranges and data transfer capacity
Keeps a rollback path until the new system is proven

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine has the learner plan a migration, so explaining the methodology, test, network, and dependency choices back is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: When a company moves an application from its own servers into the cloud, the software on those servers usually comes with license terms: a permission, often tied to a physical machine or to a number of processor cores. Those terms do not disappear when the workload moves. Some licenses can be carried over to cloud machines, some require buying a new license from the cloud provider, and some require dedicated hardware that only your organization uses. Money follows from these choices. A license you already own may save a lot, while a license you must repurchase, or a machine that must sit alone, can raise the bill. Checking this before the move is part of planning the migration, because it can change which option is cheapest.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company owns a database license priced per processor core, and it wants to move that database onto a cloud virtual machine with 16 cores. Before reading further, what would you check first to learn whether the license can be reused there, and what that choice might cost?
lessons.teach:
A software license is the permission, set out in the vendor's terms, that says how many copies of a product you may run and on what hardware. Two common pricing models matter here. A per-core license charges for each processor core a machine exposes. A per-socket license charges for each physical processor chip. Bring your own license, usually shortened to BYOL, means you reuse a license you already own on a cloud machine instead of paying the cloud provider for a license bundled into the hourly price. Some vendors allow BYOL only on sole-tenant nodes, which are physical servers reserved for your organization alone, because their license counts physical chips or cores that would otherwise be shared on multi-tenant hosts.

Why this matters: the cloud charges you for running time and capacity, while the vendor charges for the right to run the software. Put those two meters side by side. The true migration cost is the cloud bill, plus any new licenses, plus dedicated-hardware premiums, plus one-off work such as testing and dual running, where old and new systems run together during cutover.

Worked example: an on-premises database runs on two 8-core processors and is licensed per core, so 16 cores are licensed. Step one: confirm the vendor permits BYOL on cloud virtual machines. Step two: check whether the license counts physical cores, which would force a sole-tenant node. Step three: price a cloud machine with 16 vCPUs, noting that vCPUs may be counted differently from physical cores. Step four: add two weeks of dual running. Compare the total with a machine that includes the license in its price.

Common mistake: assuming a license you own transfers automatically to any new environment. The consequence in a running system is that an audit finds unlicensed use, and the cost of missing licenses plus penalties can wipe out the savings the migration was supposed to deliver. Read the license terms before you price the move.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dental runs a practice-management database on an on-premises server with two physical processor chips. The vendor licenses per socket, so the count is 2 licenses. The vendor allows bring-your-own-license use only on sole-tenant nodes. Step 1: confirm the vendor allows BYOL on sole-tenant nodes. Step 2: because the license counts physical chips, a sole-tenant node is required. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: compare the migration-period total with a bundled-license machine that costs $3,600 per month including the license.
choices: Switch the count to per-core licensing, which lowers the number of licences to one.
Price the sole-tenant node at $2,800 per month and add the two-month dual-running cost, then total the whole migration period.
Ignore dual running, because the overlap is temporary and does not count toward the total cost.
Confirm the license transfers automatically to any new virtual machine, so no further licence cost is needed.
questions.why: The missing step is to price the dedicated node and add one-off dual-running work so the total covers the full migration period, which is what the comparison in step 4 needs.

questions.prompt: A vendor licenses its product per socket. A server has 4 physical processor chips, each with 8 cores. How many licences does the vendor count for this server?
choices: 32 licences, one per core
1 licence, because the server is one machine
8 licences, one per core on a single chip
4 licences, one per physical chip
questions.why: Per-socket licensing charges for each physical processor chip, so 4 chips means 4 licences regardless of how many cores each chip has.

questions.prompt: A team owns per-core licences for software that runs on shared multi-tenant cloud hosts. The vendor allows bring-your-own-license use only on sole-tenant nodes. What is the main risk if the team moves the software to shared hosts and reuses its licences?
choices: The team's per-core count will drop to zero, so the licences become free to use.
Using owned licences on shared hosts may be unlicensed use, which an audit can find and penalise, so the terms must be checked first.
The cloud provider will automatically bill the team for a bundled licence at the same rate.
Nothing changes, because owned licences always transfer to any new environment.
questions.why: Vendors that restrict BYOL to sole-tenant nodes do not permit reuse on shared hosts, so running there risks unlicensed use and penalties.

questions.prompt: A firm compares two cloud options over a 3-month migration. Option A is a bundled-license machine at $1,200 per month. Option B is a BYOL machine at $900 per month using a licence the firm already owns, plus a one-off $1,000 for one month of dual running. Which statement about the 3-month totals is correct?
choices: Option B is cheaper by $900, because the only cost is the monthly machine price.
Option A is cheaper by $100, because Option B totals $3,700 once dual running is included.
Option B is cheaper by $200, because the owned licence removes the licence cost entirely.
The two totals are equal, because the dual-running cost offsets the licence saving.
questions.why: Option B totals $2,700 for machine time plus $1,000 dual running, which is $3,700, while Option A totals $3,600, so the bundled option is $100 cheaper.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that moving our licensed database to the cloud will cut costs because cloud compute is cheap per hour. Explain to them, in your own words, which license and financial questions must be answered before the move, and name one trade-off that could make the move cost more.
lessons.modelAnswer: Hourly cloud prices are only one part of the picture. First we need to know whether our existing license allows reuse on cloud virtual machines, because bring your own license terms differ by vendor. Next, we check whether the license counts physical cores or chips. If it does, the vendor may require a sole-tenant node, which costs more than a shared host. We then add the costs that often get missed: any new licenses, the dedicated hardware premium, testing time, and a period where old and new systems run side by side during cutover. The trade-off I would raise is that keeping our own license saves money now but ties us to a fixed licensing model and makes the environment harder to change later. A licence-included machine costs more per hour but is simpler to scale and audit. We should compare total cost over the expected life of the system, not the hourly rate.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes the license cost from the cloud compute cost and adds them together
Explains that BYOL eligibility and hardware requirements depend on the vendor's license terms
Names a hidden cost such as dedicated hardware, dual running, or new licenses
States a trade-off between reusing an owned license and flexibility or simplicity

suggested.rationale: A cost model in fictional credits lets the learner practice comparing a BYOL setup against a license-included setup, including one-off migration costs.

lessons.plain: Cloud services and the tools around them keep changing. Providers add better options, change prices and limits, and eventually retire older products. Anticipating these improvements means designing a system now so that later changes are cheap to absorb instead of forcing a rebuild. Think of a house built with standard pipe sizes and removable interior walls. You cannot predict every future renovation, but you can avoid choices that turn each renovation into a demolition. For a solution architect, this means preferring managed services that the provider keeps updated, keeping business logic separate from the specific products it runs on, and reviewing regularly what the platform now offers. The goal is not to predict the future perfectly but to keep your options open.
lessons.guessPrompt: A reporting system uses a message service that its provider announces will be switched off in two years. Option A is to wrap every call to that service behind one internal function now. Option B is to leave the calls scattered across the code and migrate when the deadline arrives. Which option has the lower total cost, and why?
lessons.teach:
Anticipating improvement means designing so that change later is cheap. Three forces keep moving under any solution: the provider retires products (deprecation, meaning an announced end of support with a date), releases better or cheaper versions, and changes prices and limits. A design that anticipates these forces does three things. First, it draws an abstraction boundary, a line in the design where business logic talks to a stable internal interface rather than directly to one product's specific behaviour, so swapping the product touches one module instead of the whole system. Second, it prefers managed services, where the provider handles the underlying software upgrades and scaling, so the team inherits improvements without starting a project. Third, it sets a review cadence, a recurring date on which the team checks announced deprecations, new offerings, and pricing against the design.

Why it works: change arrives at a rate you can roughly predict, so it can be budgeted. A retirement announced with a year's notice is a planned task if the dependency is isolated, and an emergency if the dependency is woven through twenty services.

Worked example: a dispatch team calls a queue product directly from fifteen services. The provider announces the product's retirement in 18 months. Step 1: list the callers, which is fifteen. Step 2: estimate the rework per caller, about one day each. Step 3: total roughly fifteen days, spread across teams with competing priorities. Had the team placed one publish function in front of the queue, the same change would be one module plus a test run.

Common mistake: assuming that upgrading later is free. Each unisolated dependency adds cost every year, and that cost stays hidden until a deadline arrives.

Consequence: when a retired interface stops responding, every caller fails at once, so the outage lands on live dispatch instead of inside a planned migration window.

questions.prompt: A regional ticketing company has nine services that call a hosted seat-map rendering product directly. The provider announces that the product's old endpoint will stop responding in 12 months. Step 1: count the direct callers, which is nine. Step 2: estimate rework per caller, about half a day each. Step 3: ?? The team then has to decide whether the work can be done before the deadline.
choices: Total the rework to about 4.5 days and check that total against the 12-month window, given other work.
Replace the seat-map product this week, because any change costs the same no matter how many callers exist.
Assume the endpoint will keep working past the date, since it has never failed before in production.
Count the number of seat-map features in use, since features are what the provider retires.
questions.why: Step 3 turns the per-caller estimate into a total and compares it with the time available, which is the planning check the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: In the context of a provider's product lifecycle, what does it mean when a vendor announces that an API version is deprecated with an effective date of March 1?
choices: The vendor has released a faster version and is raising the price of the old one.
The API has been merged into a newer product and no action is needed by the customer.
The vendor has announced an end of support for that version, with a date by which it stops being supported.
The API will be removed the same day without any notice to customers.
questions.why: Deprecation means an announced end of support with a date, so the correct choice describes that announcement and its date, not an immediate removal or a price change.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit sends donation receipts. Its four web pages and two nightly batch jobs each call a managed PDF rendering service directly. The team wants a design that will be cheap to change if the service is retired. Which choice best anticipates that change?
choices: Leave all six direct calls as they are, since the service is managed and will be upgraded automatically.
Rewrite all six callers to a different PDF product now, before any retirement is announced.
Add a cache in front of each caller so that fewer calls reach the service.
Place one rendering function between the six callers and the service, so the service is called from one module.
questions.why: An abstraction boundary, a single internal function that the callers use, isolates the dependency so a later swap touches one module instead of six callers.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain runs its order database on servers it patches by hand, reasoning that a managed database costs more per month. Over several years, which consequence best describes the risk of this choice?
choices: The provider will automatically move the chain's data to a cheaper region without telling the team.
The database's price will fall at the same rate as hardware, so the chain gains nothing from managed services.
The database will never need upgrading, so the team saves the full cost of the software over time.
The team carries every software upgrade itself and misses improvements that a managed service would have delivered without a project.
questions.why: A managed service means the provider handles upgrades and scaling, so self-patching shifts that recurring work and the lost improvements onto the team.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says: 'We should just pick the newest managed service and build directly on it, so we never have to think about future changes.' Explain to them, in your own words, what anticipating platform change means for this design, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would take instead.
lessons.modelAnswer: Anticipating change doesn't mean predicting it. It means arranging the design so that a likely change is a small task rather than a rebuild. I agree that managed services are a good default, because the provider carries patching and scaling and we inherit its improvements. But newest is not the same as stable, and building directly against one product's interface spreads that dependency across every service. I would keep the product calls behind one internal interface and review announced deprecations and pricing on a fixed schedule. The tradeoff is real: the wrapper adds some up-front code and one more component to maintain. For a short-lived prototype that cost may not be worth paying, but for a system expected to run for years, I would accept it.
rubricPoints: Anticipating change means designing so likely changes are cheap, not predicting them exactly.
Isolate product-specific calls behind a stable internal boundary so a swap touches one place.
Prefer managed services that inherit provider upgrades, while watching deprecation notices.
Name the tradeoff: up-front complexity and maintenance versus later change cost, which may not pay off for short-lived systems.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the idea and its tradeoff back to a teammate is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: Cloud-first design means that when you plan a new system, you start by asking whether a cloud service can do the job before you plan your own servers. A cloud service is something a provider runs for you, such as storage, a database, or a message queue. The approach treats the cloud's built-in strengths, like adding capacity on demand and not buying hardware up front, as the normal starting point. You can still run your own machines when you have a good reason, such as a rule about where data must live or a program that cannot move. The key habit is to write down every departure from the cloud default and its reason, so the choice can be revisited when the cloud offers something better.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team must receive bursts of vehicle location messages and keep them until they are processed. One option is to run its own message software on rented servers it patches itself. The other is a managed queue that the provider runs and scales. Under a cloud-first approach, which should be the starting default, and what is the main reason?
lessons.teach:
Cloud-first design is a default, not a rule. Before you design a component, you ask whether a managed service can meet the requirement. A managed service is one the provider operates for you, including patching, failover, and capacity, so your team owns less of the work. The default exists because managed services offer elasticity, meaning capacity that grows and shrinks with demand, and they move routine operating work away from your team. Each hour engineers spend keeping servers alive is an hour not spent on the product, and a service that scales itself removes a class of capacity guesses.

Worked example. A ride app receives position updates from 20,000 vehicles every few seconds. Step 1: list the requirements: accept bursts of messages, keep them until processed, and never silently lose one. Step 2: ask the cloud-first question: does a managed queue meet these? Yes, it accepts bursts and retains messages. Step 3: check for exceptions: no rule forces on-premises hosting, so there is none. Step 4: record the decision with its reason, such as managed queue because it scales with bursts and removes broker upkeep, so a future team knows why it was chosen.

Common mistake: treating cloud-first as move everything unchanged onto cloud machines. Copying an old on-premises layout keeps the same operating burden and pays for idle capacity. A real exception, such as a licence bound to a physical machine, should be a recorded decision, not a silent habit.

Consequence: if the queue is self-hosted on fixed machines, a traffic surge can fill its disk and drop positions, so dispatchers see stale maps exactly when demand is highest. A cloud-first default with a written reason for every exception keeps that risk visible at design time.

questions.prompt: A regional library wants scanned book page images stored durably and served to readers, with traffic spiking during exam week. Step 1: list the requirements: keep every scan durably, serve bursts of reads, and never lose an image. Step 2: ask the cloud-first question: does a managed object storage service meet these? Yes, it stores durably and scales reads on its own. Step 3: check for exceptions: the scanning workstation's software is licensed to one physical machine in the library, so the scan intake stays there as a recorded exception, while storage and serving stay cloud-first. Step 4: the library's design review asks for the record. Which entry completes step 4?
choices: Record only the vendor name, since the reason for choosing it is obvious to the next team.
Skip recording the scanner exception, because a licence is a procurement matter rather than a design matter.
Record managed object storage as the choice, with the reason it scales reads and removes disk upkeep, and note the scanner licence as a documented exception with its reason.
Re-host the image storage on library-owned disks so the exception list stays empty.
questions.why: Step 4 is to record the decision with its reason, including every exception, so a future team can see why each choice was made.
