questions.prompt: Which statement best describes cloud-first design as a default?
choices: Never self-host anything, because self-hosted parts are always more expensive.
Every component must run on cloud virtual machines that the team patches itself.
Before designing a component, check whether a managed service can meet the requirement, and write down a reason for any exception.
Move each existing server onto the cloud unchanged so nothing has to be redesigned.
questions.why: Cloud-first is a default that starts with asking whether a managed service fits, and each exception is recorded with its reason rather than treated as a silent habit.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency with 300 buses sends location pings every few seconds. The team proposes running its own message broker on three fixed servers sized for average load. Which response best applies the cloud-first approach?
choices: Drop the location feature entirely so that no message broker is needed.
Ask whether a managed queue can accept bursts and keep messages; if it can, choose it and record the reason, noting that fixed servers sized for average load can overflow at peak.
Approve the three fixed servers, since owning hardware gives the team full control of capacity.
Buy five more fixed servers so the average-sized design never has to handle a peak.
questions.why: The cloud-first step is to check the managed option first, and the fixed-server design risks losing or delaying messages when load peaks, which the recorded decision should make visible.

questions.prompt: A team moved its old on-premises layout onto cloud virtual machines, keeping the same number of servers. After the move, the bill rose and the team still patches every server by hand. What best explains this outcome?
choices: The team copied the old layout, which keeps the same operating burden and pays for capacity that sits idle, instead of checking managed services first.
Elasticity was switched on automatically, which increased the number of servers beyond what the team needed.
Patching by hand is required on the cloud, so the team did the right thing and the bill is simply normal.
Cloud virtual machines always cost more than physical servers, regardless of how they are used.
questions.why: Copying an old layout keeps the same operating work and idle capacity, which is the common mistake the cloud-first default is meant to prevent.

lessons.explainPrompt: A colleague says we are cloud-first, so we never run our own servers. Explain to them in your own words what cloud-first design actually asks for, and name one limit or trade-off of defaulting to managed services.
lessons.modelAnswer: Cloud-first means that for each new requirement we first check whether a managed cloud service meets it, and only then design our own machines. It is a default, not a ban. The main gain is operational: the provider handles patching, failover, and scaling, which mainly serves the reliability and operational excellence pillars, and we pay for what we use. The limit is that a managed service sets the rules. We get less control over versions, configuration, and some tuning, and moving data out later can be costly, so that lock-in trade-off belongs in the decision record. When a requirement such as a licence or a data residency rule pulls us away from the default, we keep the exception and its reason written down so we can revisit it when the cloud offers a better fit.
rubricPoints: Describes cloud-first as a default that is checked per requirement, not a blanket ban on servers
Names a managed service as the first option and explains the operational benefit
Names at least one real trade-off such as less control or lock-in cost
Says exceptions must be recorded with their reason so they can be revisited

suggested.rationale: This design exercise on the vehicle-position path makes you choose cloud components and justify each departure from the default, which practises this decision directly.

lessons.plain: Your company already runs servers in its own office or data centre, and now some of its work is moving to the cloud. Extending the network to on-premises means connecting those two places so machines on each side can reach each other using private addresses, as if they sat on one office network. Think of it as building a secure road between your building and a new warehouse, with a clear map of which addresses live on which side. The work is choosing how the road is built, making sure the two address plans do not clash, and telling each side where the other side's addresses are.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office network uses the addresses 10.0.0.0 to 10.0.255.255, and the cloud network you want to reach also uses 10.0.0.0 to 10.0.255.255. Before reading on, what problem do you expect when you connect them, and what would you change first?
lessons.teach:
On-premises means the computers you own or rent space for yourself, such as an office server room or a data centre, as opposed to cloud resources. A hybrid network joins those on-premises machines to cloud networks so they can talk privately. In Google Cloud, a VPC network is your own private software network, made of subnets, which are address ranges such as 10.20.0.0/16. Every network that talks to another needs unique addresses, because a router cannot tell two identical addresses apart.

There are two main ways to build the link. Cloud VPN sends encrypted traffic through tunnels over the public internet; HA VPN uses two tunnel interfaces so a single failure does not drop the link. Cloud Interconnect is a dedicated private connection into Google's network at a physical facility, which gives steadier speed and latency but costs more and takes longer to order. Cloud Router is the managed piece that exchanges routes with your on-premises router using BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol, which is how two networks announce which address ranges they can reach.

Worked example: the office uses 192.168.10.0/24 and the VPC subnet is 10.20.0.0/16. Step one: confirm the ranges do not overlap. Step two: create HA VPN tunnels between the office gateway and the VPC. Step three: Cloud Router and the office router open a BGP session; the cloud side announces 10.20.0.0/16 and the office side announces 192.168.10.0/24. Step four: a VM at 10.20.1.5 sends to 192.168.10.20, the learned route points at the tunnel, the packet is encrypted, and the office gateway decrypts and delivers it.

The common mistake is overlapping address ranges, or forgetting that cloud firewall rules must allow traffic from the on-premises range. In a running system the result is silent drops or a route that goes nowhere, which often surfaces only during cutover. Good hybrid design plans addresses first and routes second.

questions.prompt: Bakery Co. runs an on-premises network of 192.168.40.0/22 and has a VPC subnet of 10.50.0.0/18. Its team built the link as follows. Step one: they confirmed the two ranges do not overlap. Step two: they created HA VPN tunnels between the bakery gateway and the VPC. Step three: Cloud Router and the bakery router opened a BGP session, with the cloud side announcing 10.50.0.0/18 and the bakery side announcing 192.168.40.0/22. Step four is missing from their notes. A test VM at 10.50.2.7 sent a request to 192.168.40.15 and the request was silently dropped. Which step was skipped?
choices: Create a Cloud Interconnect circuit so the link no longer runs over the public internet
Add a second VPC subnet so the test VM holds two addresses at once
Shrink the bakery range to a single /32 address so BGP can announce it
Add an ingress firewall rule in the VPC that allows traffic from 192.168.40.0/22
questions.why: Cloud firewall rules must explicitly allow traffic from the on-premises range, and without that rule the packets are dropped even though the routes and tunnels are correct.

questions.prompt: In the link between an on-premises network and a VPC network, which statement best describes Cloud Router?
choices: It assigns public IP addresses to virtual machines inside the VPC
It encrypts every packet before it leaves the office and decrypts it on arrival
It keeps a log of every firewall rule that blocked a packet
It exchanges route announcements with the on-premises router using BGP
questions.why: Cloud Router is the managed component that runs BGP to swap the address ranges each side can reach, while encryption is the job of the VPN tunnels.

questions.prompt: A company has an office network of 10.8.0.0/16 and plans a VPC subnet of 10.8.3.0/24. What is the main risk if they connect the two as planned?
choices: Cloud Interconnect will refuse to start, so the team must switch to a different link type
The office router will need a separate BGP session for every single subnet it announces
Traffic will be slower than expected because encryption is applied twice to each packet
Packets sent to the overlapping addresses can be misdelivered or dropped
questions.why: The subnet 10.8.3.0/24 sits inside the office's 10.8.0.0/16, so the two networks use the same addresses and a router cannot tell them apart.

questions.prompt: A startup with a small team needs a secure link from its office to its VPC within one week, and has a modest budget. Which option fits best?
choices: HA VPN tunnels over the public internet, with Cloud Router exchanging routes via BGP
Copying office files to Cloud Storage by hand each night
Giving every office laptop a public IP address and opening all ports
A dedicated Cloud Interconnect circuit ordered through a colocation facility
questions.why: HA VPN is encrypted, quicker to set up and cheaper than Interconnect, which costs more and takes longer to order.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should connect the office to the cloud with a VPN because it is cheaper than a dedicated link, so the network part is done. Explain to them, in your own words, what a VPN connection gives you, what a dedicated interconnect gives you instead, and one limit or tradeoff of the choice you would recommend.
lessons.modelAnswer: A VPN connection sends our traffic through an encrypted tunnel over the public internet. It is quick to set up and cheap, and with two tunnels it can stay up if one fails. Its limit is that performance depends on the internet path, so latency and throughput can vary. A dedicated interconnect is a private physical link into Google's network at a colocation facility. It gives steadier latency and more bandwidth, but it costs more, needs a facility presence, and takes weeks to order. Either way we still need Cloud Router and BGP to exchange routes, and we must check that our address ranges do not overlap. I would recommend starting with HA VPN for the first migration phase because it is fast and resilient, then measuring latency and traffic. If the workload needs steady throughput, we should move to interconnect. Cost is only one part of the decision.
rubricPoints: Explains VPN as an encrypted tunnel over the public internet with variable performance
Explains dedicated interconnect as a private physical link with steadier latency and higher cost
Notes that routes must be exchanged, typically with Cloud Router and BGP
States a concrete tradeoff such as cost versus performance or setup time
Mentions that non-overlapping address ranges are required

suggested.rationale: Tracing how a packet crosses a hybrid link through tunnels and learned routes is the skill this objective depends on, and the planned path tracer would practise it.

lessons.plain: A cloud network is a private network made of software, where your servers reach each other by address. Multicloud means one application runs across more than one cloud provider, for example Google Cloud plus another cloud, and its pieces still need to talk privately. Extending the network topology means deciding how these separate private networks connect: which addresses can reach which, over what kind of link, and how the routes are learned. Think of several office buildings, each with its own internal phone system. You can link them with a private cable or through an encrypted line over the public road. The work is choosing the link, making sure the address books do not clash, and keeping traffic private where it must be.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose network A and network B are linked privately, and both use the subnet 10.0.0.0/24. What would you expect a VM in A to experience when it sends traffic to 10.0.0.5, and why?
lessons.teach:
Start with the terms. A VPC network (virtual private cloud, a private network you define inside Google Cloud) holds subnets, which are address ranges such as 10.0.1.0/24. A route is a rule saying which destination range goes to which next hop. Cloud Router is the Google Cloud component that learns and announces routes automatically with BGP (Border Gateway Protocol, the protocol networks use to tell each other which address ranges they own). A VPN tunnel carries encrypted traffic over the public internet. An Interconnect is a dedicated private physical link.

For Google Cloud to Google Cloud there are three common patterns. VPC Network Peering joins two VPC networks, even across projects, so their internal addresses reach each other directly. Peering is not transitive: if A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B. Shared VPC lets a host project own one network that several service projects use. Private Service Connect exposes one specific service through a private endpoint address without merging the networks.

Between clouds, you typically build a VPN or dedicated link with Cloud Router and BGP, and the other cloud configures its side to exchange routes. It works because each side announces the ranges it owns, so packets follow learned routes.

Worked example: Google Cloud network uses 10.10.0.0/16 and the other cloud uses 10.20.0.0/16. A VM sends to 10.20.5.7. Cloud Router has learned 10.20.0.0/16 over BGP, so the route points at the tunnel. The packet is encrypted, carried across, and delivered. The reply follows the reverse route.

Common mistake: overlapping address ranges. If both sides use 10.0.0.0/16, the router cannot tell which side owns a destination, and traffic goes to the wrong place or nowhere. Plan non-overlapping ranges before building.

Consequence: if a tunnel drops, its learned routes disappear and that path is down until BGP reconverges, so production designs use redundant tunnels across separate links.

Non-overlapping address plans are the first condition for any multicloud or cross-network path to work.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain runs its web servers in a Google Cloud VPC using 172.16.0.0/16. Its warehouse system sits on another cloud using 192.168.20.0/24, and the two are joined by a VPN tunnel with Cloud Router. Trace a request from a web server to 192.168.20.9. Step 1: the server's packet has destination 192.168.20.9, and the VM's route lookup is made. Step 2: ___ Step 3: the packet is encrypted, carried across the tunnel, and delivered. Step 4: the reply follows the reverse route. Which completes Step 2?
choices: Cloud Router has learned 192.168.20.0/24 over BGP from the other cloud, so the route for that range points at the tunnel.
VPC Network Peering is created automatically between the two clouds, so the packet reaches 192.168.20.9 directly without a route.
The packet is sent over the public internet without encryption because the warehouse range is treated as a static address.
The warehouse subnet 172.16.0.0/16 is announced to the other cloud by Shared VPC, so the other cloud knows where to send replies.
questions.why: Cloud Router learns the destination range over BGP, which creates a route pointing at the tunnel, and that learned route is what sends the packet into the tunnel.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's Google Cloud network holds subnets 172.31.4.0/24 and 172.31.8.0/24. It needs its on-premises network to exchange routes with it automatically. Which Google Cloud component learns and announces those routes using BGP?
choices: Private Service Connect
VPC Network Peering
Cloud Router
Shared VPC
questions.why: Cloud Router is the component that learns and announces routes automatically with BGP, while the other three options are patterns for connecting networks or exposing services rather than exchanging routes.

questions.prompt: Two clouds are linked by a tunnel. Both sides use the address range 192.168.0.0/16 for their workloads. What is the most likely result when a workload on one side sends traffic to an address in that range?
choices: The router cannot tell which side owns that destination, so traffic goes to the wrong place or nowhere.
The tunnel refuses to form until a BGP timer expires and then the duplicate routes are removed.
Traffic is encrypted automatically and both copies of the range are used equally, so every packet arrives.
The routes are merged into one larger range and traffic is split evenly between the two clouds.
questions.why: Overlapping address ranges leave the router unable to decide which side owns a destination, so packets are misdelivered or lost, and non-overlapping address plans must be made before building.

questions.prompt: A retailer has project A linked to project B with VPC Network Peering, and project B linked to project C with another peering. A VM in project A needs to reach a server in project C. Which statement is correct?
choices: Yes, traffic relays through project B automatically once both peerings exist.
Only if a Shared VPC host project is configured across all three projects.
No, peering is not transitive, so project A cannot reach project C through project B.
Yes, but only when all three projects are placed in the same region.
questions.why: Peering is not transitive, so each peering only connects the two networks it joins, and A cannot reach C through B.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would connect a Google Cloud VPC to a network in another cloud, and name one limit or tradeoff of the method you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use a Cloud VPN tunnel or a dedicated Interconnect, with Cloud Router on the Google Cloud side and the matching router or gateway on the other cloud. Both sides exchange their address ranges over BGP, so each learns the routes to the other and traffic follows them. First I would confirm the two address plans do not overlap, because a clash makes routing ambiguous. The tradeoff with VPN is that traffic crosses the public internet inside an encrypted tunnel, so bandwidth and latency vary. A dedicated link is more predictable but costs more and takes longer to order. For Google Cloud to Google Cloud inside one organization, I would consider VPC peering, but I would remember it is not transitive, so a third network needs its own peering.
rubricPoints: Names a link (VPN tunnel for an encrypted internet path, or dedicated Interconnect) and Cloud Router with BGP to exchange routes.
Checks that the address ranges on both sides do not overlap before connecting.
States the tradeoff: VPN is quicker and cheaper but variable over the internet; dedicated links are predictable but costlier.
Notes that VPC peering links Google Cloud networks directly and is not transitive.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet hop by hop across routed and peered networks practises the route and overlap reasoning this objective depends on.

lessons.plain: Think of a building. Walls and locked doors decide who may walk in, a guard checks who is at the door, and cameras notice when someone behaves oddly inside. Network security does the same job for connections between computers. A firewall is a set of rules that allow or block traffic by source, destination and port. Intrusion protection watches for attacks that get past the first line. Access control decides which identities may reach which services at all. Building these protections into the layout of the network from the start is far cheaper than adding them after something goes wrong.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web application runs on servers with no public IP address, and the firewall allows no inbound connections from the internet. Can an attacker on the internet still reach these servers directly, and what might they try instead?
lessons.teach:
A firewall is a filter that decides, for each connection, whether to let it through. In Google Cloud the everyday form is a firewall rule attached to a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC), which is your private software network. Each rule names a direction (ingress, traffic coming in, or egress, traffic going out), a source or destination range of IP addresses, a protocol and port such as TCP 22 for SSH, an action (allow or deny), and a priority number. Lower numbers are checked first, so priority 100 beats priority 1000. A rule can apply to all machines or only to those carrying a network tag or a service account.

Two defaults matter. Ingress is denied unless a rule allows it, and rules are stateful, so replies to an allowed outbound connection return automatically. Intrusion detection watches a copy of traffic for attack patterns and raises alerts; intrusion prevention sits in the path and can block. Access control asks who is connecting. Identity-aware tools check the user's identity before a request reaches the application, so an IP address alone is not treated as trust.

Worked example: a bastion host tagged admin-bastion accepts SSH on TCP 22 from the office range 203.0.113.0/24 through an allow rule at priority 1000. A laptop at 198.51.100.7 tries SSH. Step one: the connection is ingress, so ingress rules apply. Step two: the rules are checked in priority order, and the allow rule's range does not contain 198.51.100.7, so it does not match. Step three: no other rule allows it, so the implied deny blocks the connection before any login is attempted.

Common mistake: opening SSH to 0.0.0.0/0 for a quick test and forgetting it, so every scanner on the internet can try passwords. The consequence is a flood of failed logins and any weak credential becomes a way in, which is why alerting on failed-login spikes belongs alongside the rule.

A firewall narrows who can reach a port, identity controls who may act once connected, and detection shows when something gets through anyway.

questions.prompt: Larkspur Dental runs a Postgres database on a VM tagged db-tier in its VPC, listening on TCP 5432. Two ingress rules apply to that tag. Rule A denies TCP 5432 from 10.20.0.0/16 at priority 200. Rule B allows TCP 5432 from 10.20.4.0/24 at priority 300. A connection arrives from 10.20.4.15 on TCP 5432. Step one: the connection is ingress, so ingress rules apply. Step two: rules are checked in priority order, so Rule A is checked before Rule B. Step three: [missing]. Step four: the connection is blocked and never reaches the database.
choices: Rule B is checked and its allow wins because its range is smaller and more specific.
Rule A's range contains 10.20.4.15, so Rule A matches first and its deny decides.
Rule A does not match because a source must equal the full /16 range, so Rule B decides.
Because rules are stateful, the connection is allowed since it looks like a reply to an earlier request.
questions.why: Rule A is checked first and its range contains the source address, so it is the first match and its deny action decides the outcome.

questions.prompt: A new VPC has no ingress rules at all. A browser on the internet tries HTTPS on TCP 443 to a web VM in that VPC. What happens?
choices: The connection is blocked, because ingress is denied unless a rule allows it.
The connection is blocked only if an egress rule also denies it.
The connection is allowed until an intrusion detection alert fires.
The connection is allowed, because web servers accept HTTPS by default.
questions.why: Ingress is denied by default, so with no rule allowing the traffic the connection is blocked.

questions.prompt: A VM tagged worker makes an outbound HTTPS call to a payment API at 192.0.2.50. The only rule touching that VM is an egress allow for TCP 443 to 0.0.0.0/0. Does the response need its own ingress rule to reach the worker?
choices: No, because rules are stateful and the reply to an allowed outbound connection returns automatically.
Yes, but only if the egress rule has a priority number above 1000.
No, because replies from outside the VPC bypass firewall rules entirely.
Yes, every reply needs a separate ingress allow rule using the same port.
questions.why: Rules are stateful, so the reply to an allowed outbound connection comes back without a separate ingress rule.

questions.prompt: Larkspur wants its internal admin dashboard protected. The team says a firewall rule limiting the dashboard port to the office range is enough. Which addition best covers the other two layers described in the teaching text?
choices: Adding an egress deny rule so the dashboard cannot send replies to hosts it does not recognise.
Identity-aware access control plus intrusion detection alerts.
Lowering the priority number of the existing allow rule so it is checked before other rules in the set.
Raising the priority number of the existing allow rule so it is checked after every other rule in the set.
questions.why: The firewall narrows who can reach the port, identity controls who may act once connected, and detection shows when something gets through anyway, so the other two layers are identity-aware access and detection.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes opening SSH to the whole internet on the bastion so engineers can log in from home without a VPN. Explain to them in your own words what a firewall rule does here, what it cannot protect against, and what you would add to reduce the risk.
lessons.modelAnswer: A firewall rule decides which source addresses can reach which port on which machines. Opening SSH to 0.0.0.0/0 means any address on the internet can attempt a login, so the bastion faces constant password guessing and any unpatched SSH flaw. The firewall only filters by address, port and protocol. It cannot tell a legitimate engineer from an attacker who has a permitted address, and it does not inspect allowed traffic for attack patterns. I would narrow the source to known ranges where possible, or put access behind an identity-aware gateway so the engineer's account is checked before the connection is allowed. I would also enable intrusion detection, alert on bursts of failed logins, and allow key-based logins only. The tradeoff is convenience for remote staff against a larger attack surface, so the decision should be explicit and reviewed.
rubricPoints: Explains that a firewall rule filters traffic by source, port and protocol, and that ingress is denied by default.
Names the risk of exposing a management port to the whole internet.
States the limit: a firewall cannot verify identity or inspect allowed traffic for attacks.
Proposes a mitigation such as narrowing sources, identity-aware access, or detection and alerting.
Names the tradeoff between convenience for remote staff and a larger attack surface.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a connection through ordered firewall rules to see which one allows or blocks it is the core skill for this objective, and the planned net-trace engine would practise it directly.

lessons.plain: This is about deciding how the private network your cloud resources live in is laid out, and how traffic from users and other systems reaches them. Think of a company building: the network is the building's internal corridors, subnets are the floors, and a load balancer is the receptionist who takes each visitor and sends them to a free desk. Some visitors come from the public street, some come from inside the company, and some are internal services that should never touch the street at all. The core job is choosing the right entry point and the right private path for each kind of traffic.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you run three copies of a web app on separate machines, and visitors from around the world all use one address. What do you think should happen to each visitor's request before it reaches a machine, and why would one central address be useful?
lessons.teach:
A VPC network (virtual private cloud) is your own isolated network inside Google Cloud, and it is global: one VPC can span every region. A subnet is an address range carved out of a VPC, and each subnet lives in exactly one region. The split matters for topology design because the VPC holds the routing across regions, while a subnet is where a machine's private address comes from.

A load balancer is a managed entry point that accepts traffic on one address and spreads it across a pool of backends, the machines or services doing the work. Health checks are periodic probes the balancer sends to each backend; a backend that fails is removed from rotation. Balancers work at different layers. Layer 4 balancers route on network details such as IP address and port. Layer 7 (application) balancers read the HTTP request itself and can route by host name or path. Each balancer is either external, with an internet-facing address, or internal, reachable only from inside your VPC.

Worked example: a web app's backends sit in subnets in two regions. A user in Europe opens the site. A global external Application Load Balancer answers on one anycast address (an address advertised from many points at once), so the user connects to a nearby entry point. The balancer checks which backends are healthy, picks the closest healthy region, and forwards the request there. The backends have no public IPs, so they reach the internet for updates through Cloud NAT, a managed service that lets private machines make outbound connections only.

Common mistake: giving every machine a public IP and pointing DNS at each one. A failed machine keeps receiving traffic, and there is no single place to manage encryption or health checks.

For calls to Google APIs or managed services, Private Google Access and Private Service Connect keep that traffic on Google's network rather than the public internet.

A running system feels this choice directly: when a backend fails its health check, the balancer routes around it, and users see no error.

questions.prompt: Lumen Labs runs an internal reporting API on backends in two subnets of one VPC, one subnet in europe-west1 and one in asia-east1. The API must be reachable only from inside the VPC, so Lumen Labs puts an internal load balancer in front of it. Trace one analyst request. Step 1: the analyst's workstation, inside the VPC, sends the request to the internal balancer's address. Step 2: the balancer has already been probing each backend with health checks. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: a healthy backend answers, and the analyst sees no error. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: The balancer copies the subnet's region into the request so the backend knows where the request came from.
The balancer sends the request to every backend at once and returns whichever reply arrives first.
The balancer gives each backend a public IP address so the analyst can connect to it directly.
The balancer selects a healthy backend from its pool and forwards the request to that backend.
questions.why: A balancer forwards each request to a backend it considers healthy, which is the step that lets it route around a failed machine without the analyst noticing.

questions.prompt: A media company builds a VPC with two subnets, one in us-central1 and one in us-east4. Which statement about these subnets and the VPC is true?
choices: A subnet spans every region the VPC spans, so one subnet covers both regions.
Each subnet belongs to exactly one region, while the VPC handles routing across all regions.
A single subnet can be split across two regions to balance load between them.
The VPC is limited to one region, and each subnet can be global.
questions.why: A VPC is global and holds routing across regions, while each subnet is an address range tied to exactly one region.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Clinics has four backend machines behind an external balancer. One machine fails and stops answering its health check. What happens to user traffic next?
choices: Users see errors for every request until the whole balancer is restarted.
Each user is moved to a fixed machine by DNS, and the failed machine keeps receiving those users.
The balancer stops routing new requests to the failed machine and sends them to the healthy ones, so users see no error.
The balancer keeps sending about a quarter of requests to the failed machine until an administrator removes it by hand.
questions.why: Health checks detect the failed backend, and the balancer removes it from rotation so requests go only to backends that pass.

questions.prompt: A retailer wants requests for /api to go to one backend pool and requests for /images to go to another, all on the same host name. Which kind of balancer does this, and why?
choices: A Layer 7 application balancer, because it reads the HTTP request and can route by path.
An internal balancer, because path-based routing requires a private address.
A Layer 4 balancer, because it routes on IP address and port alone.
Private Google Access, because it keeps the traffic on Google's network.
questions.why: Only a Layer 7 application balancer reads the HTTP request itself, so it is the layer that can route by path on one host name.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between an external and an internal load balancer for a service that only other internal services call, and name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use an internal load balancer for a service that only other services inside our VPC call. It gets a private address from a subnet in one region, so nothing on the internet can reach it, and callers in the same VPC or connected private networks use that address. The tradeoff is that it only serves clients that can route to that private range. A partner outside our network, or a browser on a laptop, cannot use it without a separate external entry point. A regional internal balancer also serves backends in one region, so cross-region failover needs deliberate design rather than happening automatically. Health checks still decide which backends get traffic, so I would confirm those before calling the setup production-ready.
rubricPoints: Internal load balancers get a private address and serve only clients that can reach the VPC.
External load balancers have internet-facing addresses and suit public traffic.
Tradeoff: an internal balancer excludes clients outside the private network.
Health checks determine which backends receive traffic.

suggested.rationale: A virtual network path tracer would let the learner follow a request through VPC routes, subnets and balancers, which is the core skill this objective tests.

lessons.plain: Allocating data storage means deciding where a system's data will live, what kind of storage holds it, and how much room to give it before the system needs it. Think of a warehouse: you choose between shelves for loose boxes, numbered lockers for organized items, and a big open yard for bulky goods, and you reserve space for what you expect to store. On Google Cloud the choice is between object storage for whole files, block disks attached to virtual machines, shared file systems, and managed databases. Getting it right means matching the storage to how the data is read, written and shared, and sizing it with some headroom.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web app must save user-uploaded videos that are read whole and rarely edited, and several servers also need to read the same shared configuration files. Which kind of storage would you pick for each, and why?
lessons.teach:
Object storage keeps whole files, called objects, inside buckets, which are containers with a globally unique name. You reach an object by name over the network; you never mount a bucket as a disk. Block storage presents a raw disk to one virtual machine (VM), which is a rented computer. Persistent Disk and Hyperdisk are Google's block products, and you choose each disk's size when you create it. File storage is a shared network file system that several machines mount at the same time; Filestore is the managed version. Managed databases such as Cloud SQL, Spanner, Bigtable and Firestore store structured records and handle indexing and replication for you.

Why it works: each type trades flexibility against access pattern. Object storage needs no sizing and is inexpensive for large, rarely changed data, but it is slow for many tiny edits and cannot change part of a file in place. Block storage is fast for random reads and writes from one machine, but its capacity is fixed until you resize it and then extend the file system inside the VM.

Worked example: a retailer stores product photos, a web server's boot OS, and order records. Step one: photos are whole files read over HTTP, so they go in a bucket. Step two: the boot OS is used by one machine with random small writes, so it gets a 50 GB block disk. Step three: orders need rows, relationships and transactions, so they go in a managed relational database. Each choice follows from how the data is accessed.

Common mistake: putting a database's data files in a bucket, or sizing a disk to exactly today's need with no headroom. Consequence in a running system: a block disk that fills up stops the application from writing, so customers see failed saves, and the cause is easy to miss unless disk usage is watched.

Choosing the storage type is the allocation decision you defend in a design, and sizing it with headroom keeps it running.

questions.prompt: A podcast company, separate from the examples in the teaching text, plans its storage. Step one: finished episode audio files are whole files that listeners download over HTTP, so they go in a bucket, which is a container of objects with a globally unique name. Step two: its transcoding VM, a rented computer, rewrites small temporary chunks at random positions, so its scratch space is a 120 GB block disk, a raw disk attached to one machine, sized for current work with no headroom. Step three is missing: the subscriber ledger holds rows, relationships between customers and plans, and transactions that must succeed or fail together. Which completion finishes the plan?
choices: Store the subscriber ledger as JSON files in a second bucket so listeners can download them.
Replace the transcoding disk with a bucket so the ledger and the scratch chunks share one store.
Store the subscriber ledger in a managed relational database such as Cloud SQL, which handles rows, relationships and transactions for you.
Mount one shared file system on the transcoding VM and place the subscriber ledger in it.
questions.why: Rows, relationships and transactions are access patterns that a managed database is built for, while buckets and shared files are not designed for them.

questions.prompt: Which storage type presents a raw disk to a single virtual machine, and whose capacity is fixed until you resize it?
choices: A managed database such as Firestore
Object storage in a bucket
Block storage such as Persistent Disk or Hyperdisk
Shared file storage such as Filestore
questions.why: Block storage gives one VM a raw disk whose size you choose at creation and must extend later, which matches the description.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm keeps 12 TB of scanned shipment forms. The scans are written once, almost never change, and are fetched whole by name when an auditor asks for them. Which allocation fits best?
choices: A block disk attached to the archive server, sized to the current 12 TB
A managed relational database with one row per scan
A shared file system mounted by every office workstation
Object storage in a bucket, where scans are stored and fetched as whole objects
questions.why: Whole, rarely changed files read by name are the access pattern that object storage suits, and it needs no up-front sizing.

questions.prompt: A VM's application stops saving customer data. The data disk was created at 80 GB and is now completely full, with no headroom ever planned. What is the correct first remedy?
choices: Restart the VM, which frees the disk space automatically.
Resize the disk to a larger size, then extend the file system inside the VM so the added space is usable.
Mount a shared file system on the VM so writes go to the network instead.
Move the application's writes into a bucket so the disk no longer matters.
questions.why: A block disk's capacity is fixed until resized, and the file system inside the VM must then be extended before the new space can be used.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between object storage and a block disk for a new service, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from how the service reads and writes its data. If it stores whole files that are read over the network and rarely edited, such as uploads or exports, that belongs in object storage, which scales without us sizing it and costs less per gigabyte. If the service runs a database engine or needs fast small random writes from a single machine, it needs block storage attached to a VM, and that disk has a fixed size we must choose up front and extend later. The tradeoff of object storage is that you cannot edit part of a file in place and it is slow for many tiny updates, so I would not put a database there. The tradeoff of block storage is that it is tied to one machine and fills up silently, so I would set headroom and an alert on usage before we go live.
rubricPoints: Chooses storage by access pattern: whole-file reads suit object storage, random small writes suit block storage
Names that block disks have a fixed size chosen up front and must be resized and extended
Names that object storage cannot edit part of a file in place and is slow for many tiny updates
Recommends headroom and usage alerts because a full disk causes failed writes

suggested.rationale: Picking a storage type from a short scenario with competing access patterns is best practised as an exam-style reasoning exercise, and no listed mission covers cloud storage directly.

lessons.plain: Data processing means taking a large pile of records, such as logs, sales rows, or sensor readings, and turning it into something useful like totals or a report. Compute is the processing power that does the work, usually virtual machines with CPU and memory that you rent by the hour. Provisioning both together means setting up the machines and the job's data handling as one planned unit: how many machines, how they start, how they grow when work piles up, where the data lives, and what happens to the machines when the job finishes. Getting this right keeps the job fast and keeps the bill from running on after the work is done.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job must read 500 GB of sales records, compute totals, and write a report before 6 am. Would you run one large machine all day, or many machines created only for the job and removed afterwards? Which would you choose, and what would you worry about with your choice?
lessons.teach: A data processing job reads a large set of records, transforms or summarises them, and writes results. Compute is the processing power that runs it: virtual machines with CPU and memory. A cluster is a group of those machines that a processing framework (software that splits the job into tasks and coordinates the machines) runs as one system. One node acts as the manager that hands out tasks, and the others are worker nodes that carry them out. Why it works: a job split into many independent tasks finishes sooner when more workers share them. Keep the input and output in durable object storage, separate from the workers' own disks. Then the compute can be created for the job and deleted afterwards, which is called an ephemeral cluster. Autoscaling adds workers when the queue of pending tasks grows and removes them when the queue empties. Worked example: a nightly job reads 2 TB of logs from storage. Step 1: create a manager and two workers. Step 2: the task queue grows to 400 tasks, so autoscaling adds workers up to a cap of 10. Step 3: tasks finish, the queue empties, and the extra workers are removed. Step 4: results are written to storage and the cluster is deleted, so you pay for compute only while it runs. Common mistake: writing results only to a worker's local disk. Deleting the cluster then destroys the output. The consequence on a running system is data loss at exactly the moment cleanup saves money, which is why the output belongs in durable storage.

questions.prompt: A weather analytics firm, Brightwater Labs, runs a daily job over 800 GB of station readings. Its processing cluster has one manager node and three worker nodes, and autoscaling is capped at 6 workers. Step 1: the task queue grows to 90 pending tasks, so autoscaling adds workers up to the cap of 6. Step 2: the workers read the readings from durable object storage and work through the queue. Step 3 is missing: it is the step that must finish before the cluster is deleted, and it writes the daily summary files. Step 4: once the queue is empty, the extra workers are removed and the cluster is deleted to stop compute charges. Which action fills the missing Step 3?
choices: Write the summary files to durable object storage so they survive when the cluster is deleted
Scale the cluster down to one worker so the disks stay attached and the results can be read later
Nothing is needed, because deleting the cluster only removes idle workers and keeps their disks
Copy the summary files onto the manager node's local disk so they stay with the cluster
questions.why: Deleting an ephemeral cluster destroys the disks on its nodes, so results must be written to durable object storage before Step 4 deletes the cluster.

questions.prompt: In a processing cluster that runs as one system, what is the role of the manager node?
choices: It hands out tasks to the worker nodes and coordinates them
It holds the only durable copy of the job's results
It does all of the transform work while the workers only store data
It is the disk that workers write their outputs to before deletion
questions.why: The manager node hands out tasks and the workers carry them out, so the manager coordinates rather than storing results or doing the bulk of the work.

questions.prompt: A team runs a batch job where each task writes its output to the local disk of the worker that ran it. Once the task queue empties, the team deletes the whole cluster. What happens to the output?
choices: The output is copied to the manager node's disk automatically at deletion time
Autoscaling keeps the output, because the queue emptied before the deletion
The output is lost when the cluster is deleted, because the workers' local disks are removed with it
The output survives, because local disks are only removed after the job is reported finished
questions.why: Local disks belong to the cluster's nodes, so deleting the cluster destroys anything written only there, which is why output belongs in durable storage.

questions.prompt: A job is split into 50 independent tasks and runs on a cluster whose autoscaling cap is currently 4 workers. Which change most directly shortens the total time to finish the job?
choices: Keeping the cluster running permanently so it never has to be recreated
Storing the input on a larger disk attached to each worker
Raising the worker cap so more workers can share the pending tasks
Adding a second manager node, since the manager is what limits progress
questions.why: Independent tasks finish sooner when more workers share them, so allowing more workers to be added is the change that directly speeds the job.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would provision compute for a nightly data processing job so that the cluster can be deleted when the job finishes, and name one limit or tradeoff of that approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would keep the input and output in durable object storage, not on the machines, and create a small cluster just for the nightly run: one manager and a few workers, with autoscaling set between a minimum and a cap. The framework splits the job into tasks, and autoscaling adds workers while the task queue is long and removes them when it empties. When the results are written back to storage, the cluster is deleted, so we pay only for the hours it works. The main tradeoff is startup time: creating a cluster takes minutes, so a job that must finish in seconds, or many small jobs run back to back, may be better served by a longer-lived cluster. Also, the cap on workers limits how fast the job can go, so it must be set against the deadline.
rubricPoints: Compute and data should be kept separate so the cluster can be removed safely.
Autoscaling adds and removes workers based on pending work.
Results must be written to durable storage before the cluster is deleted.
A limit such as cluster startup time or the worker cap must be named.

suggested.rationale: The autoscale engine would let the learner watch workers grow and shrink against a task queue, which is the core behaviour of this objective.

lessons.plain: Storage systems hold your data: files, backups, logs, and database exports. Security and access management for storage means deciding who or what may read, write, or delete that data, and keeping those decisions narrow. Think of a locked filing room: you need a key, the key opens only certain cabinets, and the building records who came in. In cloud platforms, the rules about who may do what are attached to the storage resource as permissions, and the stored data is usually encrypted so that someone who copies the underlying disks cannot read it. Getting this right means granting only the permissions a person or program actually needs, and never making a whole storage container public by accident.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job copies monthly reports into a shared storage bucket, and a dashboard service only needs to read those reports. Should the dashboard service also be allowed to delete files in that bucket, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A principal is whoever or whatever asks for access: a person, a group of people, or a service account, which is an identity that a program uses instead of a human login. A permission is one allowed action, such as reading an object (a stored file) or deleting one. A role is a named bundle of permissions, so you grant a role rather than listing every action. A policy binding attaches a role to a principal on a specific resource, such as one bucket. Least privilege means giving each principal the smallest set of roles that lets it do its job. Encryption at rest means stored data is encrypted on disk; customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) are keys you control in a key service rather than keys the provider holds alone. A signed URL is a time-limited link that grants temporary access to one object without a user account. Public access prevention is a setting that blocks any binding to everyone on the internet.

Worked example. Bucket monthly-reports holds report files. The dashboard service account is bound to the viewer role on that one bucket only. Step 1: the dashboard asks to read report.csv. Step 2: the platform looks for bindings on monthly-reports for that identity. Step 3: it finds the viewer role, which includes the read permission. Step 4: access is allowed. If the same service tries to delete report.csv, no role bound to it includes delete, so the request is denied.

Common mistake: granting a broad project-wide editor role because it is quicker than finding the right narrow role. Then every service in the project can modify every bucket.

Consequence: a bug in the dashboard that calls a delete command would erase backups it was never meant to touch. Narrow bindings limit the damage a bug or stolen credential can do.

questions.prompt: Harbor Pantry Co-op keeps supplier invoices in a bucket called pantry-invoices. The service account ledger-sync is bound to the reader role on that one bucket only. The reader role includes read and list permissions but not delete. Here is the check for a request by ledger-sync to delete old-2023-03.pdf. Step 1: ledger-sync asks to delete old-2023-03.pdf. Step 2: the platform collects the bindings on pantry-invoices that belong to ledger-sync and finds the reader binding. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: no role that the identity holds on this bucket includes delete, so the request is denied. Which missing step completes the check?
choices: It checks whether the bucket is public, and if it is, allows the delete because anyone may act on it.
It creates a time-limited signed URL for old-2023-03.pdf so the delete can go through without a binding.
It checks whether any role bound to ledger-sync on pantry-invoices includes the delete permission, and finds none.
It falls back to the project-wide editor role, since the bucket itself has no delete role to check.
questions.why: The platform decides by looking only at the permissions inside roles bound to that principal on that specific resource, and none of them include delete, so the check fails.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is the difference between a permission and a role?
choices: A permission and a role are the same thing, and the words are used interchangeably in policies.
A permission is one allowed action such as deleting a file, and a role is a named bundle of permissions that you grant as a unit.
A role is the identity asking for access, and a permission is the resource it is trying to reach.
A permission is a named bundle of actions, and a role is one single allowed action.
questions.why: A permission is a single allowed action, and a role groups permissions under one name so you can grant them together.

questions.prompt: Kestrel Logistics wants a driver's phone to view one delivery photo for two hours, with no Google account on the phone. Which mechanism fits, and what is the main risk to watch for?
choices: Give the driver's personal email a viewer binding on the whole photo bucket and remove it after the delivery.
Create a signed URL for that one object with a two-hour expiry; the risk is that anyone who holds the link can use it until it expires.
Grant the driver's phone the project editor role for the day, since it is the simplest option available.
Make the bucket public so the link works everywhere, then rely on the file name being hard to guess.
questions.why: A signed URL is a time-limited link to one object that needs no user account, and anyone holding it can use it until expiry, so its lifetime must be kept short.

questions.prompt: A Kestrel administrator adds a binding that gives the viewer role to all users on the internet for a bucket holding internal audit files. Which setting is designed to block this kind of binding?
choices: Public access prevention, which blocks any binding to everyone on the internet.
Customer-managed encryption keys, which stop outsiders from reading encrypted data.
Least privilege, which reduces the number of roles any principal holds.
Service accounts, which replace human logins so no public identity can exist.
questions.why: Public access prevention is the setting that blocks bindings to everyone on the internet, while the other options address different concerns such as encryption or identity type.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would give a reporting service read access to one storage bucket and no more. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would create a dedicated service account for the reporting service, so it has its own identity rather than sharing a person's login. Then I would bind only the viewer role for that specific bucket to that account. The viewer role lets it read and list objects, but it cannot write or delete, and binding at bucket level means it cannot see other buckets. The tradeoff is maintenance: every new bucket the service needs means another explicit binding, and someone has to review those bindings periodically. Ideally the bucket is also protected by public access prevention, so the only way to read it is through an identity we granted. If the service only needs to hand a file to one outside recipient, I would use a signed URL with a short expiry instead of a standing grant.
rubricPoints: Explains principal, role, and policy binding in plain terms
Shows that access is granted at the narrowest resource and role that works
Names a tradeoff such as maintenance overhead of many narrow bindings or the risk of broad roles
Notes that public access prevention or time-limited links reduce exposure

suggested.rationale: The planned authorization policy evaluator would let the learner test whether a principal's bindings allow or deny a storage action, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Moving data into and around a cloud system takes time. The time depends on how much data there is, how fast the connection is, and how far the data has to travel. Latency is the delay before a piece of data arrives, usually measured as round-trip time: the time for a request to go out and a reply to come back. Configuring data transfer and latency means choosing how data reaches the cloud, where it is stored, and how close it sits to the people and machines that use it, so a job finishes before its deadline and users do not wait. Architects make these choices before anything is built, because they are costly to change later.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company must copy 200 terabytes of archived video from a data centre to the cloud, and the copy must finish within two weeks. Before reading further, which would you worry about more: the speed of the internet link, or the distance between the data centre and the cloud region? Why?
lessons.teach:
Bandwidth is the maximum rate a connection can carry, such as 1 gigabit per second. Throughput is the rate you actually achieve, which is always at or below bandwidth because the link is shared with other traffic and protocols add overhead. Latency is the delay for one round trip, and it grows with physical distance because signals take time to travel and every hop adds some processing. A cloud region is a geographic location containing data centres; a zone is an isolated site inside a region. Egress means data leaving a cloud, which is usually billed.

Worked example: 200 terabytes is about 1.6 x 10^15 bits. Divide by a fully used 1 gigabit per second link (10^9 bits per second) and you get 1.6 x 10^6 seconds. Divide by 86,400 seconds per day and you get roughly 18.5 days, and that assumes the link never slips below full speed. The two-week deadline is therefore impossible over that link, and the fix is either more bandwidth or a different method, such as a shipped offline appliance for one-off bulk moves, or a managed transfer service for recurring scheduled copies.

The common mistake is to read the advertised link speed as the achieved speed, or to place storage in one region while the compute that reads it runs in another. The second error adds latency to every read and creates egress charges. In a running system, a web app that reads from a distant region shows slow page loads, and a nightly sync that was sized on paper overruns into business hours.

The right transfer method depends on volume, deadline, and whether the copy repeats, and the right placement keeps data in the same region as the workloads that use it.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm must copy 50 terabytes of archived scans to Google Cloud over a dedicated 500 megabit per second link that stays fully used. Step 1: 50 terabytes is 50 x 8 x 10^12 = 4 x 10^14 bits. Step 2: dividing 4 x 10^14 bits by 5 x 10^8 bits per second gives 8 x 10^5 seconds. Step 3 is missing: convert 8 x 10^5 seconds into days, then decide whether a 14-day deadline is met.
choices: Divide 8 x 10^5 by 1,000 to get 800 days, which fits within the 14-day deadline.
Multiply 8 x 10^5 by 86,400 to get about 69 million days, so the deadline is missed.
Divide 8 x 10^5 by 86,400 to get about 9.3 days, so the deadline is missed because the link is slower than 1 gigabit.
Divide 8 x 10^5 by 86,400 to get about 9.3 days, which fits within the 14-day deadline.
questions.why: Seconds become days by dividing by 86,400, giving about 9.3 days, which is inside the 14-day deadline on the assumption the link never drops below full speed.

questions.prompt: A learner says a 2 gigabit per second link will always deliver 2 gigabits per second of data to an application. Which statement corrects this?
choices: Bandwidth is the achieved rate, so the application does receive 2 gigabits per second.
Egress is the rate at which data enters a cloud, which makes throughput equal to bandwidth.
Latency equals bandwidth, so a 2 gigabit link has a 2 millisecond delay.
Throughput is the achieved rate and sits at or below bandwidth, because the link is shared and protocols add overhead.
questions.why: Bandwidth is the maximum capacity, while throughput is what is actually achieved, which is always at or below that maximum because of shared traffic and protocol overhead.

questions.prompt: A product team places its database in one region and its application servers in a different region. Which consequence is most accurate?
choices: Latency is removed because the data is held in a separate geographic location.
Zones inside each region automatically make cross-region reads faster.
Every read pays extra delay for the distance, and the cross-region traffic can incur egress charges.
Only the bill changes; reads are as fast as before because bandwidth is unaffected.
questions.why: Latency grows with distance, so reads across regions are slower, and data leaving a cloud is usually billed as egress.

questions.prompt: A retailer must copy 5 terabytes of point-of-sale files to cloud storage every night on a fixed schedule. Which transfer method best fits this repeating job?
choices: A single copy over the link, with no further copies needed because the first one is enough.
A one-off shipped offline appliance, sent again by hand each night.
A managed transfer service that runs scheduled copies.
Storage placed in a different region from the nightly analysis jobs, to save transfer time.
questions.why: A managed transfer service is designed for recurring scheduled copies, whereas a shipped appliance suits one-off bulk moves and the other options ignore the repeating schedule or the placement rule.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between a network transfer and a physical offline transfer for a large one-time data move, and name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the volume and the deadline, then divide the volume by the realistic throughput of the link, not its advertised bandwidth, to estimate the time. If the estimate misses the deadline by a wide margin, a physical offline device is usually the better choice, because shipping time is fixed and independent of link speed. If the copy repeats on a schedule, or only needs to move changed files, a managed online transfer service is the better fit, since it handles retries and scheduling. The tradeoff with offline shipping is that the data is out of the network for days and the copy is only as current as the day it was loaded, so you need a catch-up plan for changes made meanwhile. The tradeoff with online transfer is that it competes with production traffic on the same link, so I would schedule it off-peak and cap its rate.
rubricPoints: Estimates transfer time from volume divided by achieved throughput, not advertised bandwidth
Chooses online transfer for recurring or incremental moves and offline shipping for large one-time moves
Names a tradeoff such as data being offline during shipping or competing with production traffic
Keeps storage and the workloads that read it in the same region to control latency and egress

suggested.rationale: Choosing a transfer method and placement from volume, deadline, and latency is an exam-style reasoning task that benefits most from working through scenarios.

lessons.plain: Data retention is how long you must keep information before it is allowed to disappear, and lifecycle management is the set of automatic rules that move or delete that information as it ages. Think of a records room in an office: some files must stay for seven years, some can be shredded after a month, and some should be moved to a cheaper back room once nobody opens them. In a cloud, you write these rules once on the storage itself, so the system applies them without a person remembering to. Getting this right saves money and keeps you on the right side of legal and business promises, while getting it wrong either deletes something you needed or keeps paying for data nobody wants.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company must keep customer invoices for seven years, but its application log files are only useful for 30 days. Without looking anything up, where would you put the seven-year rule and the 30-day rule, and what could go wrong if you only relied on someone remembering to delete logs by hand?
lessons.teach:
A retention policy sets a minimum period during which stored data must be kept, so it cannot be deleted or overwritten before that time passes. A lifecycle rule is an automatic instruction attached to a storage location (in Google Cloud, a bucket of objects, where an object is one stored file) that fires when an object meets a condition, such as being older than a set number of days. The action can be to delete the object or to change its storage class, which is the price and access tier for how rarely it is read.

Why it works: the conditions are checked against metadata the storage system already holds, such as creation time, so the rule runs without human effort. Lifecycle changes are evaluated in the background, typically within about a day, so do not expect deletion at the exact moment a rule first matches.

Worked example: a bucket holds application logs. Rule one: when an object is older than 30 days, move it to a colder, cheaper class. Rule two: when an object is older than 365 days, delete it. A log written on day 0 stays in the standard class. On day 31 the background process changes its class. On day 366 the delete rule matches and the object is removed, unless the bucket also has a 400-day retention policy, in which case the delete attempt fails and the object survives until day 400.

Common mistake: treating a lifecycle rule as a retention promise. Lifecycle rules delete on schedule and can be edited by anyone with permission to change the bucket, while a retention policy blocks deletion for its full period. If the retention policy is locked, the change is permanent: even the owner cannot shorten it, and the bucket cannot be deleted until its objects age out.

Consequence: on a running system, a locked seven-year retention on invoices means an accidental deletion cannot be undone, so the period should be tested on an unlocked bucket before anyone locks it.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Podcasts stores raw audio masters in one bucket. Rule A: when an object is older than 60 days, change it to a colder class. Rule B: when an object is older than 2,555 days, delete it. The bucket also has an unlocked retention policy of 2,600 days. Trace one master file created on day 0. On day 61 the background process changes its class, since lifecycle checks run within about a day of a match. On day 2,556 Rule B matches, but the retention policy blocks the delete, so the attempt fails. Step left for you: state the earliest day the master can actually be removed, and why.
choices: Day 2,555, because the delete rule matches then and lifecycle rules override retention policies.
Day 2,600, but only if the bucket is locked, since unlocked retention policies never block deletion.
Never, because a retention policy that has been set cannot expire on its own.
Day 2,600, when the retention period ends, and a later background pass can then delete it.
questions.why: The retention policy blocks deletion for its full period, so the file becomes removable once that period ends, and the background process then evaluates the delete rule again.

questions.prompt: A compliance team locks a 10-year retention policy on a bucket of tax records. Which statement is correct?
choices: The bucket can be deleted as soon as its newest object is 10 years old.
Nobody can shorten the lock, and the bucket cannot be deleted until its objects have aged past the period.
The owner can shorten the period later if the team changes its mind.
Lifecycle rules can override the lock and delete objects early.
questions.why: A locked retention policy is permanent, and the bucket cannot be deleted until its objects have aged out of the retention period.

questions.prompt: A media team sets a delete rule at 20 days on an unlocked bucket that also has a 90-day retention policy. A file is 25 days old and is still present. Which explanation fits best?
choices: The retention policy blocks deletion until the file is 90 days old, so the delete rule's match does not remove it.
The delete rule is broken and must be recreated from scratch.
Lifecycle rules only apply to files uploaded after the rule was created.
Lifecycle rules run only when the bucket is locked.
questions.why: A retention policy blocks deletion for its full period regardless of a lifecycle delete rule matching earlier, so the file at 25 days is still protected.

questions.prompt: A build team's bucket has a rule that deletes objects older than 45 days. An artifact was created on March 1 in a non-leap year. Which expectation is most accurate?
choices: It is never deleted, since the rule only applies to objects created after the rule was set.
It is deleted on March 16, because the rule counts from the start of the month.
It becomes eligible around April 15, and the deletion itself happens in a background pass, typically within about a day.
It is deleted at the first moment of April 15, because rules are evaluated instantly.
questions.why: Forty-five days after March 1 is April 15, but lifecycle actions run in the background and typically complete within about a day rather than at that exact moment.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a lifecycle rule and a retention policy on cloud object storage, and name one limit or tradeoff of locking a retention policy.
lessons.modelAnswer: A lifecycle rule is a scheduled housekeeping instruction: when an object reaches an age or matches a condition, the storage either deletes it or moves it to a cheaper storage class. A retention policy is a guarantee: for a set period, nobody, including admins, can delete or overwrite the object. The two work together. For example, a bucket might carry a seven-year retention policy for audit records, while a lifecycle rule moves them to a colder class after 90 days to save money. The tradeoff of locking a retention policy is that it becomes permanent: you cannot shorten it, and the bucket cannot be removed until the period ends. A wrong period in a locked bucket therefore costs real money and cannot be undone, which is why teams usually test the period on an unlocked bucket first.
rubricPoints: A lifecycle rule automatically deletes or changes the storage class of objects based on a condition such as age.
A retention policy prevents deletion or overwriting for a minimum period and applies even to administrators.
Lifecycle rules run in the background, so deletion is not instant.
Locking a retention policy is irreversible, so a wrong period cannot be shortened or undone.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between a lifecycle rule, a retention policy, and a locked policy in a realistic scenario tests the reasoning more than reading or a single existing mission does.

lessons.plain: Planning for data growth means asking, before data piles up, how much information a system will hold next month and next year, and whether the storage and its layout can keep up without becoming slow or expensive. Think of a filing cabinet in a growing office. You estimate how many new folders arrive each week, then decide whether to add cabinets, move old folders to an archive room, or switch to a warehouse with shelves that expand on demand. In a cloud, most of these choices come from a few numbers: how fast data arrives, how long it must be kept, how often it is read, and how much you are willing to pay. The goal is a plan that survives growth you did not expect, not a perfect forecast.
lessons.guessPrompt: A logging service writes 2 GB per day today, and the business expects that volume to double every six months. Without any tools, what would you need to know before deciding whether today's storage will still be fine in two years, and what would you check first?
lessons.teach:
Data growth planning is the habit of estimating how much data a system will store over a chosen time horizon, such as one or two years, and then choosing storage that fits that estimate. The growth rate is how much the volume increases per period. The retention period is how long you must keep each piece of data before you may delete it. The access pattern describes how often data is read: hot data is read constantly, while cold data is rarely touched. A storage class is a pricing and performance tier suited to one access pattern. A lifecycle rule is an automatic policy that moves or deletes objects as they age.

The plan works because total stored data is roughly the daily intake multiplied by the retention period, and that total grows with every new day. Growth is usually compounding, so the last months of a long horizon dominate the total. Small changes in the rate change the answer a lot.

Worked example. Intake starts at 2 GB per day and doubles every six months. In the first half-year it averages about 3 GB per day, which is roughly 550 GB. In the second half it averages about 6 GB per day, adding roughly 1100 GB. Year one therefore needs about 1.6 TB. If you keep all of it in the fastest tier, you pay for cold data as if it were hot. Instead, keep the last 30 days in a hot tier, roughly 240 GB at the late-year rate, and let a lifecycle rule move older data to an archive class.

A common mistake is sizing for today's volume and forgetting that retention turns every day of intake into stored data for months. A running system that ignores this fills its disks, or its bill climbs without warning, and queries slow as tables grow past what the design expected.

Planning for data growth means forecasting volume from intake rate and retention, then matching each slice of that data to a storage tier and a lifecycle rule.

questions.prompt: Lumen Parcel Logistics stores scanner logs. Intake is 3 GB per day for the first 182 days of a one-year horizon and 4 GB per day for the remaining 183 days, so year one stores about 1,280 GB in total. Their retention period is 90 days, meaning each day's logs must be kept for 90 days before deletion. The hot tier should hold only the logs that must stay readily available, which is the most recent 90 days of intake at the late-year rate. What is the size of that hot-tier slice?
choices: 360 GB
270 GB
90 GB
questions.why: The hot slice is the last 90 days of intake at the late-year rate of 4 GB per day, so 4 times 90 equals 360 GB, while the other options use the wrong rate, the total, or the day count alone.

questions.prompt: In data growth planning, what does the retention period mean?
choices: The price tier that a dataset is assigned to
The number of gigabytes written per day
How often each piece of data is read by applications
How long each piece of data must be kept before it may be deleted
questions.why: The retention period is the length of time data must be kept before deletion is allowed, which is distinct from access frequency, price tier, or daily intake.

questions.prompt: A telemetry service writes 6 GB of new data each day, and each day's data must be retained for 120 days. Assuming intake stays flat, roughly how much data is stored at steady state?
choices: 120 GB
6 GB
840 GB
720 GB
questions.why: Total stored data is roughly daily intake multiplied by the retention period, so 6 GB times 120 days equals 720 GB.

questions.prompt: A team sizes its disks for the 2 TB of data the system holds today, even though intake is doubling every quarter and retention is long. What is the most likely consequence on the running system?
choices: Data will be deleted automatically once it passes the retention period, so capacity is never exceeded
Read speed improves as data accumulates, so the original sizing becomes more than enough
Storage fills before the planned horizon ends, since growth compounds and the later months dominate the total
The disks will be fine because the plan only needs to cover the current volume
questions.why: Because growth compounds and every day of intake stays stored for the whole retention period, sizing for today's volume leaves the disks short well before the horizon, which the other options wrongly dismiss or reverse.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would plan storage for a service whose data grows every month. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by measuring how much data arrives per day and how long we must keep it, then project that forward over a horizon like one or two years, using a growth rate we can justify. That gives a total volume to size against. Next I would split the data by how often it is read. Recent data that is queried often goes in a hot tier, and older data goes to a cheaper archive tier with a lifecycle rule that moves it automatically. The main tradeoff is that the forecast is only as good as its growth assumption. If the real growth is faster, the plan needs revisiting, so I would set alerts on actual volume against the forecast and review the numbers every quarter. Archive tiers also cost more to read back and have minimum storage periods, so cheap storage is not free when data is needed again.
rubricPoints: Estimate volume from intake rate, growth rate and retention over a stated horizon
Separate hot from cold data by access pattern and match each to a storage tier
Use lifecycle rules to move or delete data automatically as it ages
Name a tradeoff, such as forecast error or retrieval cost from archive tiers

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a growth scenario with retention, access patterns and tiers adds more than a read-only catalogue, and no listed mission covers capacity forecasting directly.

lessons.plain: Backup and recovery means keeping extra copies of your data, plus a tested way to get a working system back when data is lost, damaged, or deleted by mistake. A backup is a copy taken at a point in time. Recovery is the process of restoring that copy and getting the service running again. It is a bit like keeping a spare key somewhere safe and knowing exactly how to use it when you lock yourself out. The hard questions are how old a copy you can tolerate losing, and how long you can afford to be down while you restore it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop backs up its order database every night at 2 a.m. At 6 p.m. a bad update corrupts the orders. Roughly how many hours of orders could be missing from the restored copy, and would the shop accept that?
lessons.teach:
Two numbers drive every backup design. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum amount of data, measured as time, that you are willing to lose. An RPO of one hour means the newest usable copy may be up to an hour older than the failure. The recovery time objective (RTO) is how long the service may stay unavailable while you restore.
