Backups are the mechanism; RPO and RTO are the requirements that the mechanism must meet.

Google Cloud offers several mechanisms that map onto these ideas. Disk snapshots are point-in-time copies of a disk, and after the first one they store only changes. Managed database backups, with point-in-time recovery, let you restore a database to a moment between scheduled backups by replaying logged changes. Object versioning in Cloud Storage keeps older versions of a file when it is overwritten or deleted. Backup and DR Service centralizes scheduled backups and restores for supported workloads. Retention settings decide how long each copy survives.

Worked example: an order database takes a full backup every night at 02:00 and has point-in-time recovery enabled, with a stated RPO of 15 minutes. At 14:10 a bad migration deletes a table. Step 1: pick the target moment, 14:09. Step 2: restore the 02:00 backup into a new instance, leaving production untouched. Step 3: replay logged changes up to 14:09. Step 4: check the restored data, then switch traffic over. The restore takes most of an hour, which is your real RTO, and you should measure it rather than assume it.

Common mistake: treating a backup as protection just because it exists. Copies kept in the same place as the original, or never restored in a test, often fail when they are needed. Deleted copies can also disappear if the same account can remove them, unless retention locks are set.

Consequence: if the RPO is 15 minutes but backups run only once a day, the system has quietly accepted up to 24 hours of lost orders.

questions.prompt: Tidewell Logistics keeps a shipment-tracking database with point-in-time recovery turned on. A nightly full backup runs at 01:30, and the stated RPO is 10 minutes. At 09:40 a faulty script overwrites the status column for many rows. The team follows these steps. Step 1: choose the target moment, 09:39. Step 2: restore the 01:30 backup into a new instance, leaving production untouched. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: check the restored data, then point the application at the restored instance.
choices: Take a fresh snapshot of the production disk so the damage is captured
Delete the corrupted rows from production before restoring anything
Replay logged changes from 01:30 onward directly into production
Replay logged changes on the new instance up to 09:39
questions.why: After restoring the nightly backup, the logged changes must be replayed onto the new instance only up to the chosen target moment, so the copy reflects the state just before the fault without touching production.

questions.prompt: A file-sync service states an RPO of 6 hours. Which statement correctly describes what that number means?
choices: Each backup copy is kept for 6 hours before it is deleted
The restore process is allowed to run for at most 6 hours
The service must be back online within 6 hours after a failure
The newest usable copy may be up to 6 hours older than the failure
questions.why: RPO is the maximum amount of data, measured as time, that may be lost, so a 6-hour RPO means the newest usable copy can be up to 6 hours older than the failure; the other options describe RTO or retention instead.

questions.prompt: An engineer accidentally deletes a monthly sales report stored as an object in a Cloud Storage bucket. Object versioning was enabled on the bucket before the deletion. Which statement is correct?
choices: Versioning keeps earlier versions, so a prior version can be restored if it was retained
The report must be recreated from the source spreadsheet because versioning only protects overwrites
The report can be recovered only if a disk snapshot of the bucket was taken
The report is gone permanently because deletion removes every stored version
questions.why: Object versioning keeps older versions when a file is overwritten or deleted, so as long as a prior version is still retained it can be restored; the other options misstate what versioning covers or confuse it with disk snapshots.

questions.prompt: A small agency's runbook says a restore takes about 30 minutes. Its last test restore of the same backup took 3 hours and 10 minutes. Which figure should the team use when judging whether it meets its RTO?
choices: The 3 hours and 10 minutes measured in the test, because RTO is the real time the service may stay unavailable
The average of the two figures, since both were measured under different conditions
The 30 minutes in the runbook, because documented estimates are the official RTO
Neither figure, because RTO depends only on how often backups run
questions.why: RTO is how long the service may be unavailable while restoring, so the measured restore time is the figure to plan against, and an unmeasured assumption such as the runbook estimate can hide a real gap.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between RPO and RTO, and name one tradeoff that makes a cheaper backup schedule riskier.
lessons.modelAnswer: RPO is how much data we can afford to lose, measured as time. If our RPO is 15 minutes, the newest copy we can recover from must be no more than 15 minutes older than the failure. RTO is how long the service can be down while we restore. Both are targets set from business impact, and then we choose mechanisms that meet them. The tradeoff is that backing up less often, such as nightly instead of every 15 minutes, lowers storage and operations cost, but it raises the worst-case data loss to nearly a full day, so the RPO is silently broken. Frequent copies or continuous log-based point-in-time recovery shrink the RPO but cost more storage and add complexity. In both cases, a backup only counts once a restore has been tested within the RTO.
rubricPoints: Defines RPO as the maximum tolerable data loss measured in time
Defines RTO as the maximum tolerable downtime during restoration
Names a cost-versus-risk tradeoff, such as backup frequency or storage cost against data loss
Notes that a backup only proves its value once a restore has been tested

suggested.rationale: A planner where learners set RPO and RTO and check whether a backup schedule and restore path meet them would practise this objective directly.

lessons.plain: Provisioning compute resources means deciding what computing power your system runs on and then actually creating it. Compute is the part that executes your code: the processor and memory doing the work. In a cloud, you can rent a virtual computer that you configure yourself, a platform that runs packaged applications, or a service that runs your code only when a request arrives. Provisioning means choosing among these, sizing them, and setting them up so they can be recreated reliably. It is a bit like deciding whether to lease a delivery van, hire a fleet manager, or pay a courier per parcel, and then writing down exactly how each van should be equipped.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small website needs to serve one customer during business hours and almost no traffic at night. Would you rent a fixed server that runs around the clock, or pay per request for code that only runs when someone visits? Which would you choose and why?
lessons.teach:
Key terms first. A virtual machine (VM) is a computer simulated in software on the cloud provider's hardware. You choose its CPU and memory, and its operating system starts from an image. A machine type is the named size of that VM. An image is a saved copy of a disk with an operating system and software already installed, so every new VM starts the same way. An instance template is a stored recipe that bundles a machine type, an image and startup settings. A managed instance group (MIG) is a set of identical VMs created from one template. The group replaces machines that fail health checks and can add or remove copies to match load. A container packages an application with everything it needs to run. A serverless service runs your code on demand and bills per use.

Why it works: the cloud lets you describe compute as data. Writing the recipe once means the tenth server matches the first, and a broken machine can be replaced rather than repaired by hand.

Worked example: an order-status API receives steady traffic. Step 1: pick a machine type that handles one copy's load with some headroom. Step 2: build an image with the web server installed. Step 3: write an instance template that references that image and machine type. Step 4: create a managed instance group of three VMs from that template, so one can fail without an outage. Step 5: when a VM fails its health check, the group deletes it and creates a fresh copy from the template.

Common mistake: guessing at the size of one large VM and then patching it by hand. The servers drift apart, and when that one machine dies, the service goes down with it.

Consequence in a running system: a template is shared by every copy the group creates, so a flawed template makes every replacement inherit the flaw at once.

questions.prompt: Pedal Route runs a bike-availability feed. One VM of the chosen machine type handles 350 requests per minute comfortably, and peak traffic is 900 per minute. Step 1: choose a machine type whose single VM handles 350 per minute with headroom. Step 2: build an image with the feed software installed. Step 3: write an instance template that references that image and machine type. Step 4 is missing from these notes. Step 5: the team creates a managed instance group from the template, and when a VM fails its health check, the group replaces it. Which choice correctly fills in the missing Step 4?
choices: Build a second image so the template can switch between two software versions
Set the group to one large VM and patch it by hand whenever traffic rises
Set the group to 4 VMs created from the template: 900 divided by 350 needs 3 copies, and the spare lets one fail without an outage
Skip the group and deploy one VM from the template, since templates handle load on their own
questions.why: Step 4 is where the team sizes the group: dividing peak load by one copy's capacity gives the number of copies needed, and adding a spare keeps service up when one fails, while the other choices either misuse the template or patch by hand.

questions.prompt: A team's instance template contains a mistake in its startup settings. Their managed instance group has five VMs, and one of them fails its health check. What happens next?
choices: The template corrects its own startup settings before the replacement is made
Nothing happens until an engineer patches the VM by hand
The group deletes the failed VM and creates a fresh copy from the template, so the mistake carries into the replacement
The group repairs the failed VM in place by editing its settings
questions.why: A managed instance group replaces failed VMs by creating new copies from the template it was given, so any flaw in that template is copied into every replacement.

questions.prompt: Why is one large VM that is patched by hand a risky way to run a service?
choices: Health checks cannot be attached to a single VM at all
Its setup exists only as hand edits, so nothing can rebuild an identical copy when it fails
A large VM always runs on slower hardware than a set of smaller VMs
Hand patches make the image smaller, which slows down startup
questions.why: Because the machine's configuration is not captured in a shared template, no recipe can recreate it, and the service has no identical copy ready to take over when it fails.

questions.prompt: A team needs a short piece of code to run only when a new file is uploaded, and they want to pay only for the moments it actually runs. Which kind of compute fits best?
choices: A managed instance group of always-on VMs created from one template
An instance template, which runs the code directly once it is written
A serverless service, which runs code on demand and bills per use
A single VM with a hand-built image that stays running all day
questions.why: A serverless service runs code only when triggered and bills per use, which matches a short task that runs only on upload, while the other options keep machines running continuously or are not compute at all.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a managed group of virtual machines and a serverless service for a new internal API. Name one limit or tradeoff of the choice you would make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the traffic pattern and the level of control the service needs. If requests are steady and the app needs a specific operating system, a long-running process, or custom software, I would use a managed instance group built from an instance template, which gives me consistent copies and automatic replacement of failed machines. If traffic is spiky or mostly idle, and each request is short, I would consider a serverless service, which scales to zero and bills per use. The tradeoff with the managed group is that I pay for the machines even when they sit idle, and I am responsible for patching the image and choosing sizes. The tradeoff with serverless is less control over the environment, and cold starts can add latency on the first request after a quiet period. So my choice depends on those two factors, and I would say so in the design note.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes a managed group of identical VMs from a serverless, pay-per-use service
Links the choice to traffic pattern and required control over the environment
Names a concrete tradeoff for the chosen option, such as idle cost or patching duty
Mentions that a template or image keeps copies consistent and replaceable

suggested.rationale: Choosing a compute model from a described traffic pattern is best practised as a short exam-style scenario, where reasoning about the tradeoff adds the most.

lessons.plain: A virtual machine (VM) is a computer that runs as software on shared physical hardware in a cloud provider's data center, and you rent it by the second or hour. Google Cloud offers two ways to run one. A standard VM costs the full rate and keeps running until you stop it. A Spot VM costs much less, but Google can take it back whenever it needs that spare capacity elsewhere. Choosing between them means trading a lower price for the risk of sudden interruption. The question to ask is whether your work can survive being stopped without warning.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a batch job that takes about ten hours of computing and could be restarted from the beginning with no harm done. Would you run it on the cheapest VM that the provider may stop at any moment, or on a standard VM that runs until you stop it? Say why in a sentence or two.
lessons.teach:
A VM is a virtual computer. Compute volatility is how likely the provider is to interrupt that machine without you asking. A standard VM has a steady price and is not reclaimed for capacity reasons. A Spot VM is sold from spare capacity at a discount, and the discount depends on region and machine type. The price of that spare capacity can change, but the defining feature is that Google may preempt it, meaning stop it, when it needs the capacity back. Before preemption, the VM gets a short warning, roughly thirty seconds, delivered to the operating system as a shutdown signal. Spot VMs have no fixed maximum lifetime, but they can be reclaimed at any time, so there is no guarantee of uptime.

Why it works: you pay less because you accept that the machine is borrowed capacity. That only makes sense when a stop costs you little. The key defence is checkpointing, which means saving progress to durable storage at regular points so that a restart resumes from the last save.

Worked example: a ten-hour transcode job runs on a Spot VM and saves a checkpoint every fifteen minutes. Step one, the job runs for three hours and thirty minutes. Step two, Google preempts the VM. Step three, the last checkpoint was at three hours fifteen minutes, so the job loses only fifteen minutes. Step four, a new VM starts, reads the checkpoint, and continues. Without checkpoints, the same event would discard three and a half hours of work.

Common mistake: placing a customer-facing service that must answer requests on Spot VMs and assuming a few replicas make it safe. If every replica is reclaimed in the same capacity crunch, the service goes down, and any state held only in memory or on local disk is lost.

In a running system, use Spot for fault-tolerant, restartable work such as batch processing, and keep standard VMs for the serving path where an interruption hits users directly.

questions.prompt: Lumen Parcel Co. runs a nightly job that resizes shipping label images. The job needs about six hours on a Spot VM, a discounted virtual machine that Google can stop when it needs the spare capacity back. The job writes a checkpoint, a saved snapshot of progress in durable storage, every 20 minutes. Step one: the job runs for 2 hours and 50 minutes. Step two: Google preempts the VM, meaning it stops the VM. Step three: [missing: work the job must redo]. Step four: a new VM starts, reads the latest checkpoint, and continues from there. What belongs in step three?
choices: Work lost is 2 hours and 50 minutes, because the whole run restarts from zero
Work lost is zero, because the Spot VM keeps its memory when it is stopped
Work lost is 10 minutes, measured from the last checkpoint at 2 hours and 40 minutes to the preemption at 2 hours and 50 minutes
Work lost is 20 minutes, because checkpoints are always a full interval old
questions.why: The last checkpoint was saved at 2 hours and 40 minutes, so only the stretch from that save to the preemption at 2 hours and 50 minutes must be redone, which is 10 minutes.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a Spot VM offer compared with a standard VM?
choices: A permanent machine with a fixed hourly price and no interruptions
A discounted machine taken from spare capacity that Google can stop with a short warning when it needs that capacity back
A guaranteed uptime window that Google will not interrupt for capacity reasons
A machine that runs only in a single zone and is never shared with other customers
questions.why: A Spot VM is cheaper because it is borrowed spare capacity, and Google may preempt it, which means stop it, at any time with only a short shutdown warning.

questions.prompt: A payments API on a retail platform runs five replicas, all on Spot VMs spread across three zones. The team says a single zone outage cannot take it down. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
choices: Zones do not affect Spot VMs, so the placement has no bearing on availability
Five replicas is too few, so the team should have used ten
Spread across zones means the replicas share no capacity pool, so nothing can be reclaimed together
Replicas on Spot VMs can all be reclaimed during the same regional capacity shortage, so spreading them does not protect a request-serving path
questions.why: Spreading replicas guards against a single zone failure, but a capacity crunch can reclaim Spot VMs across many zones at once, and a customer-facing serving path needs standard VMs.

questions.prompt: A worker process on a Spot VM receives the operating system shutdown signal that Google sends before preemption. What should the worker do with the roughly thirty seconds it has?
choices: Ignore the signal and keep processing, since the VM will keep running until the job is finished
Start a brand new VM in the same zone to take over before the old one stops
Delete all its checkpoints so the replacement starts clean and avoids stale data
Write its latest unsaved progress to durable storage so a replacement VM can resume from there
questions.why: The short warning is the window to save progress to durable storage, so the restart can pick up from the most recent point instead of losing that work.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to cloud what Spot VMs are, when it is safe to use them, and the main limit you must design around.
lessons.modelAnswer: A Spot VM is spare capacity sold at a lower price, and Google can stop it at any time when it needs that capacity back. Before the stop, the machine gets a short warning, but there is no guarantee of uptime. So I would only use Spot for work that can be restarted safely, such as batch jobs or rendering. The limit I would design around is loss of progress. Work should checkpoint to durable storage so a preempted job resumes from the last save, not from the start. Anything customer-facing, or any state held only in memory or on local disk, belongs on a standard VM. The price saving is real, but it is paid for with interruption risk, so the decision depends on how much a stop would cost.
rubricPoints: Spot VMs are cheaper because they use spare capacity that Google can reclaim at any time
Standard VMs keep running until stopped and suit work that cannot tolerate interruption
Design Spot workloads to tolerate preemption, for example with checkpointing or retries
Do not put user-facing or stateful serving on Spot without a plan for interruption

suggested.rationale: Comparing the cost of a Spot run against a standard run in fictional credits, including the cost of re-running work after interruptions, would build the tradeoff directly.

lessons.plain: When you run software on rented cloud machines, those machines need a private network address and a way to talk to each other, to the internet, and to other services. This objective is about choosing and wiring that network for each kind of compute: plain virtual machines, containers run by a managed Kubernetes service, short-lived serverless functions, and a whole VMware data center rented from Google. The core question is where a workload sits on the network and which other places it can reach. Get this wrong and an app either cannot reach its database or is exposed to the internet by accident.
lessons.guessPrompt: Imagine two servers in the same cloud project, each placed in a different private network that you created on purpose. Without doing anything else, can server A send a request to server B's private address? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A VPC (virtual private cloud) is a private software network you own inside Google Cloud. Compute resources attach to a VPC, and a subnet is a range of private IP addresses inside one region of that VPC. A route is a rule that tells traffic where to go. Each VPC gets routes for its own subnets automatically, so resources in the same VPC can reach each other by private (internal) IP address. An external IP is a public address that lets the internet reach a resource directly. Peering is a link between two separate VPCs that lets their private addresses reach each other; it does not carry traffic onward through a third network.

A worked example: a web VM sits in subnet 10.0.1.0/24 in the shop-vpc network, and its database sits in subnet 10.0.2.0/24 in the same network. Step 1: the web VM sends a request to 10.0.2.15. Step 2: the VPC's automatic subnet route sends that packet toward the database subnet. Step 3: both are in the same VPC, so no peering is needed. Step 4: if the network's access rules allow it, the request arrives. If the database lived in a different VPC, you would need peering, and the two subnet ranges must not overlap.

The common mistake is assuming that being in the same project means being on the same network, or giving every VM an external IP so that things 'just work'. An external IP exposes the VM to internet scanning. In GKE, each pod takes an address from a secondary range of the subnet, so a range that is too small stops new pods from scheduling during a traffic surge. Overlapping address ranges also break a later peering or VPN connection.

Choose the network first, then the addresses, and only then decide which doors are open.

questions.prompt: Crumb and Co runs a reporting VM in subnet 10.20.0.0/24 of the reports-vpc network. It needs to query an analytics VM at 10.30.0.5, which sits in subnet 10.30.0.0/24 of a separate ledger-vpc network. Step 1: the reporting VM sends its request to 10.30.0.5. Step 2: reports-vpc's automatic routes cover only its own subnets, so the packet has no route into ledger-vpc on its own. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: if the access rules allow it, the request arrives. Which completion fills step 3?
choices: Nothing more is needed, because both VMs belong to the same Google Cloud project.
The analytics VM is given an external IP so the reporting VM can reach it over the internet.
The reporting subnet is widened to a /16 so that its automatic routes cover the ledger network.
A peering link is set up between reports-vpc and ledger-vpc, and their subnet ranges do not overlap.
questions.why: Two separate VPCs need a peering link to pass private addresses between them, and the subnet ranges must not overlap; being in the same project does not connect networks.

questions.prompt: Crumb and Co peers vpc-east with vpc-west, and vpc-west with vpc-central. A VM in vpc-east tries to reach a VM in vpc-central by private IP address. What happens?
choices: It works only if vpc-east and vpc-central happen to use the same subnet range.
It fails, because private addresses cannot cross any VPC boundary at all.
It works, because the two peering links join up automatically into one network.
It fails, because a peering link does not carry traffic onward through a third network.
questions.why: Peering links only two VPCs directly, and traffic does not pass through a middle VPC to reach a third one.

questions.prompt: A GKE team gave its pods a secondary range of 10.90.0.0/26, which holds 64 addresses. During a traffic spike, new pods stop starting while the nodes still have spare CPU. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The nodes have run out of CPU, so the scheduler will not place new pods on them.
The pod address range is nearly used up, because each pod takes an address from it.
The external IPs on the nodes were exhausted by the traffic spike.
The VPC's automatic subnet routes were deleted during the spike.
questions.why: In GKE each pod draws an address from a secondary range of the subnet, so an undersized range stops new pods from scheduling even when compute capacity remains.

questions.prompt: Dana's team runs a batch worker VM in subnet 192.168.40.0/24 that only reads data from other VMs in the same VPC. The team gave it an external IP so that it works. What is the main concern?
choices: The VM now needs a peering link to reach its own subnet.
The subnet's automatic route is removed once an external IP is added.
Internal addresses cannot be used by a VM that needs to read from other VMs.
The VM is exposed to internet scanning even though it never needs internet access.
questions.why: Same-VPC traffic already works over internal addresses, so an external IP adds public exposure without adding any needed capability.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a Compute Engine VM, a GKE pod and a Cloud Run service each get onto a private network, and name one limit or tradeoff of connecting a serverless service to a VPC.
lessons.modelAnswer: A Compute Engine VM attaches directly to a subnet in a VPC and gets an internal IP from that subnet's range. A GKE pod is different: in a VPC-native cluster it takes its address from a secondary range reserved in the subnet, so the cluster needs enough addresses for every pod it will run. A Cloud Run service is serverless and does not sit in a subnet by default; to reach private resources in a VPC it needs a connection such as direct VPC egress or a Serverless VPC Access connector. The tradeoff is that this connection adds configuration and some cost, and the serverless service's traffic then follows your VPC routes, so the destination must be reachable from that network. Overlapping ranges or missing routes will break calls that worked in a test environment.
rubricPoints: A VM gets an internal IP from a subnet inside a VPC.
A GKE pod's address comes from a range sized for the cluster, so the range can run out.
Serverless services reach a VPC through a connector or direct egress, not by sitting in a subnet.
Naming a real tradeoff such as extra configuration, cost, or dependence on routes and non-overlapping ranges.

suggested.rationale: Tracing the path from a compute resource to a destination through routes and subnets practises the network reasoning this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Infrastructure here means the servers, networks and storage a system runs on. Orchestrating it means describing the whole setup in a written file and letting software build and change it the same way every time, instead of clicking through a screen. Configuring resources means choosing the settings each piece uses, such as its size, its labels, or the script that runs when it first starts. Managing patches means applying security and bug-fix updates to the operating systems on those machines on a planned schedule, in stages, so one bad update does not hit everything at once. Together these keep a fleet of machines identical, current, and recoverable, which matters more as the fleet grows.
lessons.guessPrompt: You need the same 12 virtual machines in two regions, and next month one security update must reach all of them. Would you rather rebuild and patch each machine by hand, or keep one written description and apply it everywhere? Why do you think that choice is safer?
lessons.teach:
Infrastructure as code means writing the desired state of your cloud resources in a text file: which virtual machines should exist, their size, their network, and their attached disks. A tool reads that file and creates or changes real resources until they match it. This is called declarative provisioning, because you describe the end state and the tool works out the steps. Orchestration is the coordination of many such pieces in the right order, for example creating a network before the machines that sit on it.

Configuring resources means setting the parameters that shape each piece: machine size, labels, metadata, and a startup script that runs on first boot. Keeping these settings in the file rather than in someone's memory makes the setup reviewable and repeatable.

Patch management is the planned application of operating system updates. A managed patch service groups machines, applies updates in waves (for example a small test group first, then the rest), and can reboot them within a chosen window. Staged waves let you stop the rollout if the first group fails its health checks.

Worked example: a team runs 40 web servers. The file says the group has 40 machines of medium size, patches run Sunday at 02:00, and the first wave is 4 machines. On Sunday the service patches those 4, checks that they are healthy, then patches the other 36. If the 4 fail their checks, the rollout stops and the other 36 keep their current working version.

Common mistake: patching by logging into each machine by hand. The machines drift apart, nobody has a record of what changed, and the next rebuild reproduces an old state.

Consequence: a fleet patched all at once with no stages can take the whole service down with one bad update, and a fleet that has drifted cannot be rebuilt reliably after a failure. Declaring the setup in a file and patching in waves is how you avoid both.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dental runs six appointment-booking machines. Its patch window is Thursday at 01:00, and the rollout is written as: Step 1, patch the first wave of two machines. Step 2, [missing]. Step 3, patch the remaining four machines. Which entry best fills Step 2 so the rollout stays safe?
choices: Check that the two patched machines pass their health checks before going further
Reboot all six machines at once so the window is not exceeded
Patch the remaining four by logging into each one by hand to save time
Copy the four remaining machines' settings into a new file before Step 3
questions.why: Staged waves only protect the service if the first group is checked for health before the next wave starts, so a failing update can stop the rollout while most machines still run the working version.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches declarative provisioning, as the teaching text uses the term?
choices: Logging into each machine and recording the changes in a notebook
Writing a startup script that runs once on first boot and never again
Describing the desired end state in a file and letting a tool work out the steps to reach it
Running one patch on every machine the moment an update is released
questions.why: Declarative provisioning means you state the end state you want and the tool determines the steps, rather than you listing the steps yourself.

questions.prompt: A team runs 20 batch-processing machines and wants a patch rollout that can be stopped early if something breaks. Which plan follows the staged approach described in the teaching text?
choices: Patch all 20 in one step at midnight so the job finishes quickly
Log into each machine one at a time, patch it by hand, and keep no record
Patch 10 machines, then patch the rest without checking since the first 10 were not failing yet
Patch 2 machines, check that they are healthy, then patch the other 18
questions.why: A small first wave followed by a health check, then the remaining machines, lets the rollout stop after the first group fails, which is the purpose of waves.

questions.prompt: An engineer changes the machine size of one server directly in the cloud console instead of editing the file that describes the fleet. Six months later the fleet must be rebuilt after a failure. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The rebuild reproduces the file's settings exactly, so the console change is kept automatically
The file no longer describes the real machine, so a rebuild may not reproduce the working state
The tool notices the change and deletes the file so the two agree
Nothing changes, because the file only matters during the very first build
questions.why: Settings kept outside the file drift away from it, and a rebuild from the file then reproduces an old state rather than the working one.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we describe infrastructure in a file and patch it in stages rather than logging into each machine, and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Writing the setup as a file means every machine comes from the same description, so we can review changes, rebuild after a failure, and know what should be running. Applying patches in stages means a small test group gets the update first, and if its health checks fail the rollout stops before the rest of the fleet is touched. Logging in by hand gives no record and lets machines drift apart over time. The main tradeoff is that the file itself becomes critical: a mistake in it can be applied everywhere at once, so changes need review and a tested rollout plan. Staged patching also takes longer than patching everything at once, and the team must accept that slower rollout for safety.
rubricPoints: Describes infrastructure as a file that a tool applies, so the same setup is repeatable
Explains that configuration settings belong in the file so they can be reviewed
Explains staged patching: a small group first, with a stop if health checks fail
Names a real limit, such as a bad file change spreading everywhere or slower rollouts

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right provisioning layer and mechanism for a fleet-wide change is best practised by reasoning through a realistic exam-style situation, which no listed mission covers directly.

lessons.plain: Imagine packing an app together with everything it needs to run into a sealed box called a container, so it behaves the same on any machine. Now picture hundreds of these boxes. Someone must decide which computer each one runs on, restart any box that crashes, add copies when traffic rises, and roll out a new version without taking the service down. Container orchestration is that managing layer. You describe what should be running, and it keeps reality matching that description, handling placement, healing, scaling and updates. On Google Cloud, the main managed service for this is Google Kubernetes Engine.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team runs 40 copies of a small web app spread across 8 servers. At 2 a.m. one server dies. Without anyone touching anything, what would you want to happen to those copies, and what kind of system should make it happen?
lessons.teach:
A container is an application packaged with the libraries and settings it needs, so it runs the same way wherever it lands. Container orchestration is the job of deciding where containers run across a group of machines and keeping them running as intended. The group of machines is a cluster, and each machine is a node. In Google Kubernetes Engine, a managed cluster service, the control plane stores your intentions and makes decisions, while the nodes actually run the workloads.

You do not tell the system to start a container on node 3. You declare a desired state, such as three copies of version 2 of an app. A controller constantly compares that with what is actually running and acts on any difference by starting, stopping or moving copies. This comparison loop is why orchestration works without a person watching.

Worked example. Your deployment asks for three replicas, meaning three identical copies. Each replica runs as a pod, the smallest unit the scheduler places on a node. Step 1: the controller sees three pods on three nodes. Step 2: node B loses power, leaving two pods. Step 3: the controller notices desired three, actual two. Step 4: the scheduler finds a healthy node with enough free CPU and memory and places a new pod there. Step 5: the cluster is back to three. A service, which is a stable address that routes traffic to healthy matching pods, means clients never need to know which pod moved.

A common mistake is treating pods as permanent servers, storing data inside them or hard-coding their addresses. Pods are replaced freely. Another mistake is omitting resource requests, so the scheduler cannot place pods sensibly and nodes overload.

In a running system, a single replica on a single node means one failure is an outage. Spreading replicas across nodes, and using health checks so traffic only reaches ready pods, is what turns orchestration into real resilience.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain runs its online ordering service as 4 replicas (identical copies of the same app), with each replica running as a pod (the smallest unit the scheduler places on a node) on a different node. Step 1: the controller (the loop that compares declared and running state) sees 4 pods running. Step 2: one node is drained for an operating-system update, so only 3 pods remain. Step 3: the controller notices the declared count is 4 but the actual count is 3. Step 4: [missing step]. Step 5: the cluster is back to 4 pods. Which action fills Step 4?
choices: The service stops routing requests until the update finishes.
The scheduler finds a healthy node with enough free CPU and memory and places a new pod there.
The control plane deletes the drained node from the cluster record.
The deployment lowers its declared count to 3 so that it matches what is running.
questions.why: The scheduler's job is to place pods on healthy nodes with spare capacity, which restores the declared count of 4 without changing the declared intention.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm declares a deployment with 6 replicas. Right now only 4 replicas are running. According to the comparison loop described in orchestration, what happens next?
choices: The controller starts or moves pods until the running count matches the declared six.
The controller deletes all 4 running pods and starts 6 fresh ones.
The controller changes the declared count to 4 so the two numbers agree.
The controller waits for an engineer to notice and file a ticket before acting.
questions.why: The controller continuously compares declared state with actual state and acts on the difference by starting, stopping or moving pods, so it works toward the declared six without deleting healthy copies or altering the declared intention.

questions.prompt: A game studio runs its matchmaking service as 2 replicas on 2 different nodes, and a stable service address routes traffic to ready pods (pods passing their health checks). One node is removed for hardware repair, so one replica is lost, and the surviving replica passes its health check. What should a client application need to do to keep working?
choices: Be updated with the new IP address of the surviving pod, since the old address is now invalid.
Store the pod's local data so it can reconnect after the pod moves.
Nothing, because it keeps using the stable service address while traffic goes only to ready pods.
Stop sending requests until both replicas are restored.
questions.why: A service gives clients a stable address and routes only to healthy, matching pods, so clients keep working without knowing which pod is running.

questions.prompt: A cafe chain stores its order history on the local disk inside a pod, and its mobile app is configured with the pod's specific network address. Which is the main risk of this design in an orchestrated cluster?
choices: Nodes will refuse to run any container that holds order history.
Pods cannot run more than one copy of the same app at a time.
The control plane will delete the app's configuration as soon as it is deployed.
Pods are replaced freely, so stored data and hard-coded addresses can disappear or stop matching the running pod.
questions.why: Pods are treated as disposable, so data kept inside them and addresses tied to a single pod are unreliable; the correct design keeps data outside pods and reaches pods through a service.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says: 'Containers already restart when they crash, so we don't need an orchestrator.' In your own words, explain what an orchestrator adds beyond a restart on one machine, and name one limit or tradeoff of running an orchestrator.
lessons.modelAnswer: A container restart policy only helps on the machine where the container lives. If that machine dies, nothing restarts the container. An orchestrator watches a cluster of machines against a declared desired state, so when a node fails it reschedules the lost copies onto healthy nodes. It also handles scaling the number of copies up or down, rolling out new versions gradually, and routing traffic only to ready pods. The tradeoff is operational complexity: the cluster itself must be configured, upgraded and monitored, and a poorly sized or misconfigured cluster can waste money or fail in new ways. For a single small app on one machine, that overhead may not be worth it.
rubricPoints: A restart policy only works on one machine; an orchestrator recovers from node failure across a cluster
The orchestrator reconciles actual state against a declared desired state
It adds scaling and gradual rollouts, with traffic sent only to healthy pods
Tradeoff: running a cluster adds operational complexity and cost, which may not suit small workloads

suggested.rationale: Deciding whether a given situation needs an orchestrator, and which layer and mechanism it maps to, is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios.

lessons.plain: Serverless compute means you give the platform a piece of code or a container, and it runs copies of that code only when requests or events arrive, adding and removing copies as demand changes. You do not manage the machines underneath. You still have to set the rules: how much one copy handles at once, how many copies may exist, how long a request may run, which identity the code uses, and whether a few copies stay warm. These settings decide whether the service is fast, affordable, and safe during a traffic surge. It is a bit like hiring temporary staff: you decide how many people can work at once, how much work each person may take on, and how long any one job may last.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web service can run up to 10 copies at once, and each copy can process 80 requests at the same time. With no other changes, what is the most requests it can be working on simultaneously, and what do you think happens to the 801st request that arrives during a surge?
lessons.teach:
Serverless compute is a model where you hand the platform a container or function and it runs copies of it on demand, without you managing servers. On Google Cloud, Cloud Run is the main service for containers, and function-based and App Engine standard options follow similar ideas. Configuring a serverless service means choosing the limits and behaviours the platform uses when it scales.

The key terms are these. An instance is one running copy of your code. Concurrency is how many requests a single instance handles at the same time. Max instances is the ceiling on how many copies may exist. Min instances is how many copies stay warm, so the first request does not wait for a cold start, which is the delay while a new copy boots. Timeout is the longest a request may run before it is stopped. A service account is the identity the code uses when it calls other services.

Worked example: a positions API has concurrency 80 and max instances 10. The most requests it can work on at once is 80 times 10, which is 800. Step one, the platform fills existing instances up to 80 requests each. Step two, it starts new instances, up to 10. Step three, request 801 is queued briefly or rejected with a throttling response, so the caller must be ready to retry.

Common mistake: raising max instances to absorb a surge without checking downstream limits. Each new instance may open its own database connections, so 1,000 instances can exhaust a database sized for 50 connections, and the failure moves to a component the scaling setting never showed.

Serverless does not mean unconfigured. These numbers are the cost, speed and safety controls of the service, and each one must be chosen against the systems it calls.

questions.prompt: A stock-photo company runs a thumbnail resizer on Cloud Run with concurrency 20 and max instances 6. Each instance opens 4 connections to a database that accepts 100 connections in total. The team checks the setup in three steps. Step 1: the most requests handled at once is 20 times 6, which is 120. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: 24 is well below 100, so the database has 76 connections of headroom for other clients. Which choice correctly fills the missing step 2?
choices: Multiply max instances by connections per instance to get the worst-case connection count of 24.
Add concurrency and connections per instance together to get 24, then compare that with the request ceiling.
Set min instances to 6 so that connections are opened before traffic arrives.
Divide 100 by 20 to find that each request may use 5 connections.
questions.why: The worst-case connection count is max instances times connections per instance, because every allowed copy may open its own connections at full scale, and step 3 compares that number with the database limit.

questions.prompt: A service has min instances set to 3. What does this setting mainly protect against?
choices: It caps the total number of copies at 3.
It limits each copy to 3 simultaneous requests.
It keeps 3 copies running so a new request does not wait for a copy to boot.
It stops any request that runs longer than 3 seconds.
questions.why: Min instances keeps copies warm so the first request avoids the cold-start delay of booting a new copy, while the other options describe max instances, concurrency and timeout.

questions.prompt: A logistics tracker has concurrency 50 and max instances 4. A burst sends 260 requests at once. How many can be worked on simultaneously, and what happens to the overflow?
choices: 4 at once; the rest wait until concurrency is raised.
250 at once; the overflow starts a fifth instance automatically.
200 at once; the overflow is queued briefly or rejected with a throttling response, so callers should be ready to retry.
200 at once; the overflow is silently dropped with no response to the caller.
questions.why: The ceiling is 50 times 4, which is 200, and requests beyond that are queued briefly or throttled, which is why callers must be built to retry.

questions.prompt: A reporting service allows max instances 500 and each instance opens 2 connections to a database that accepts 40. During a surge, the team raises max instances to 500 to absorb the traffic. What is the most likely result?
choices: Cold starts disappear because the database pre-warms itself.
The request timeout drops automatically to match the connection limit.
It is safe, because max instances only affects the request queue and never the database.
Connections run out at the database once about 20 instances are open, so the failure appears in a component the scaling setting never showed.
questions.why: Each new instance opens its own connections, so 500 instances could demand up to 1,000 connections against a limit of 40, and the database fails before the scaling setting shows any problem.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what concurrency and max instances each control in a serverless service, and name one tradeoff you accept when you raise max instances to handle a traffic surge.
lessons.modelAnswer: Concurrency controls how many requests one instance handles at the same time, so it sets how much work each copy of the code takes on. Max instances sets how many copies the platform may run, so together they give the total simultaneous capacity. If concurrency is 80 and max instances is 10, the service can work on about 800 requests at once, and anything beyond that is queued or rejected. Raising max instances adds capacity during a surge, but the tradeoff is that every new instance can open its own connections to downstream systems such as a database, which can overload something that was never sized for that many clients. Cost also rises with the number of instances. So before raising the ceiling, I check the limits of the systems the service calls.
rubricPoints: Concurrency sets how many requests one instance handles at once
Max instances sets the ceiling on how many copies run
Together they give the total simultaneous capacity of the service
Raising max instances can overload downstream systems such as databases
Cost and downstream limits must be checked before raising the ceiling

suggested.rationale: That mission makes the learner diagnose throttling under a traffic surge, which is where concurrency and instance limits are tested in practice.

lessons.plain: Machine learning work is rarely one action. It is a chain: gather data, clean it, train a model, check how good it is, then put it live. Done by hand, each link is a chance to forget a step or use the wrong file. An ML pipeline is a recipe that writes those steps down once, in order, so a machine runs them the same way every time. Agent Platform Pipelines is Google Cloud's managed service for running such recipes. It keeps a record of every run and can rerun the whole chain when new data arrives. The idea is the same as any workflow orchestrator, applied to building models.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team retrains its fraud model every week by running five scripts by hand. Last month someone skipped the evaluation step and shipped a worse model. What single change would most reduce the chance of this happening again, and why?
lessons.teach:
A pipeline is a defined sequence of steps. Each step is a component: a self-contained task with declared inputs and outputs, such as preparing data or training a model. Orchestration means something else decides when each component runs, passes outputs to the next one, retries failures, and records what happened. Each execution of the pipeline is a run. The files or models a step produces are artifacts. Parameters are values you can change per run, such as a date range or an accuracy threshold, without editing code.

Why it works: because every step declares what it consumes and produces, the platform can work out the order, run independent steps in parallel, and skip a step whose inputs have not changed since an earlier run. That skipping is called caching. Every artifact and parameter is also recorded, so you can later answer which data and settings produced the model now in production. That record is called lineage.

Worked example: a weekly churn model. Step 1 extracts last week's customer rows. Step 2 cleans them into a training table. Step 3 trains a model on that table. Step 4 scores the model on held-out data and outputs an accuracy number. A condition then compares that number with the threshold parameter, 0.85. If accuracy is above the threshold, Step 5 deploys the model. If not, the run ends and the current model stays live. Each run keeps its own inputs and outputs, so next month you can compare runs.

Common mistake: a step that reads a file from a personal path or relies on a variable left over from another step. It works on the author's machine and fails or silently differs in the managed run. Declare every input explicitly.

Consequence: if the evaluation gate is missing or wired wrongly, the pipeline deploys whatever it trains. A bad model reaches live predictions, and no failed run alerts anyone.

A pipeline turns the ML lifecycle into a repeatable, recorded, gated sequence. Its value depends on every step declaring its inputs and outputs honestly.

questions.prompt: A ride-share company runs a pipeline that predicts trip durations. Step 1 pulls yesterday's trip records. Step 2 builds a features table from them. Step 3 trains a duration model on that features table. Step 4 evaluates the trained model on held-out trips and outputs a mean error in minutes. Step 5 deploys the model only if that error is below a parameter called max_error, set to 4.0 minutes. In the draft, Step 4 has no declared inputs. Instead it reads the model from a local folder where the trainer happened to save it. Which fix makes Step 4 correct under the pipeline's rules?
choices: Have Step 4 read the most recently modified model file from a shared bucket by name
Have Step 4 read the features table directly, since the model is derived from it
Keep the local folder path and add a comment saying where the model is saved
Declare the trained model from Step 3 and the held-out trip set as explicit inputs to Step 4
questions.why: Declaring the Step 3 model and the held-out set as explicit inputs lets the platform order the steps, track the artifacts, and record lineage, whereas a local path or a guessed file name is invisible to the orchestrator.

questions.prompt: A parts-distribution company's nightly demand-forecast pipeline started at 02:00 on Tuesday and finished at 02:40. In pipeline terms, what is the record of that one execution?
choices: An artifact
A component
A parameter
A run
questions.why: Each execution of a pipeline is called a run, while components are the reusable steps, artifacts are files or models produced by steps, and parameters are per-run values.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain's pipeline has a parameter min_sales_days set to 30. An analyst wants to test a threshold of 45 without changing any component code. What is the appropriate way to do this?
choices: Pass 45 as the value of that parameter when starting a new run
Copy the forecast artifact from the last run and rename it
Edit the component's source code, then redeploy the pipeline
Delete the cache so the step reruns using the older value of 30
questions.why: Parameters are designed to be changed per run without editing code, so supplying a new value at run time is the intended mechanism.

questions.prompt: A pipeline deployed a model whose evaluation accuracy was 0.71, even though the team set the deployment threshold to 0.85. Which cause best explains this?
choices: Lineage recorded the wrong date, which caused the deploy step to skip the threshold check
The threshold parameter was stored in a different run, so the comparison used a default of zero
The evaluation gate was missing or wired wrongly, so the deploy step ran regardless of the score
The cache reused an older model artifact that had been trained on a larger dataset
questions.why: The consequence of a missing or miswired evaluation gate is that the pipeline deploys whatever it trains, and no failed run alerts anyone, which matches this result; the other options describe mechanisms that do not bypass a correctly wired comparison.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, who has only run training scripts by hand, what an ML pipeline gives you over that approach, and name one limit or tradeoff of using one.
lessons.modelAnswer: A pipeline writes the lifecycle down as ordered components, each with declared inputs and outputs, so the same steps run the same way every time. Compared with hand-run scripts, you get a recorded run history, lineage showing which data and parameters produced each model, caching so unchanged steps are skipped, and a built-in gate such as an evaluation threshold before deployment. The main tradeoff is setup cost and rigidity. Every step has to be packaged as a component with explicit inputs, which takes real effort for messy, exploratory work. Debugging also moves from a script you can run locally to a managed run you inspect after the fact. So pipelines pay off for work that repeats, like weekly retraining, and are often overkill for a one-off experiment.
rubricPoints: A pipeline is an ordered set of components with declared inputs and outputs that runs the same way every time.
It gives recorded runs and lineage, so you can trace which data and parameters produced a model.
It can gate deployment on an evaluation result, preventing a worse model going live unchecked.
A real limit: packaging steps as components takes effort and suits repeatable work more than one-off experiments.

suggested.rationale: The workflow state machine engine would let the learner practise ordered steps, conditional gates and retries, which is the core of pipeline orchestration.

lessons.plain: Before a machine learning service can learn from your information, that information has to be in a place the service can reach, in a shape it can read, and the service has to be allowed to read it. Preparing for data integration means connecting the places where your records already live, such as files, tables, and event streams, to the training service so it can pull examples without someone copying them by hand. Think of a chef who must first bring ingredients from several storerooms into one prep area, labelled and checked, before cooking starts. The chef does not need to own the storerooms, only the right to open them. Getting this step wrong often shows up later as a model trained on stale, partial, or unauthorised data, which is hard to spot after the fact.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team has customer purchase history in a data warehouse in one region and product photos in a file bucket in another region, and a machine learning training job needs both. What would you check before starting the job, and why?
lessons.teach:
A data warehouse is an analytics database that stores data as structured tables, with named columns and fixed types. BigQuery is Google Cloud's example. A bucket is object storage, where files are kept under names and read over the network. Cloud Storage is Google Cloud's example. A region is a geographic location group where resources live. A service account is an identity that a service uses to act on your behalf, separate from any human user. A schema is the agreed list of column names and types that a dataset must match.

Why this matters: a training job reads its inputs over the network. Reads across regions are slower, can cost more, and may be restricted by your organisation's policy. The job also reads as its own service account, so that account needs read permission on every source. Finally, the schema has to agree across sources, or the job misreads or drops fields.

Worked example. Step 1: list the sources. Purchases are in a warehouse table in region A; photos are in a bucket in region B. Step 2: check locations. They differ, so choose one location for the data and the training. Step 3: copy the photo bucket into region A, or move the training job to a location both can reach under your policy. Step 4: grant the training job's service account read access to the table and the bucket. Step 5: check the schema. The photo labels use the column name 'item_id' while purchases use 'product_id', so agree one name and type before training.

Common mistake: assuming that because both sources sit in one project, the training job can read them. The job still needs its own identity granted access, and it fails with an access-denied error if that step is skipped.

In a running system, a job that quietly reads an old export or a second copy trains a model that disagrees with what production actually holds.

questions.prompt: Pinecrest Logistics wants a model that predicts late deliveries. Its route logs sit in a data warehouse table (a database that stores data as structured tables with named, typed columns) in region us-central1. Its dashcam clips sit in a bucket (object storage where files are kept under names and read over the network) in region us-east4. Step 1: list the sources, which are the route table and the clip bucket. Step 2: check locations. They differ, so the team copies the clip bucket into us-central1 so the data and the training job share one region. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: check the schema. The clip index calls the trip key 'trip_ref' while the route table calls it 'trip_id', so one name and one type are agreed before training. What is Step 3?
choices: Increase the training job's machine size so it reads the clips faster across regions.
Delete the route table once the clip bucket has been copied, to save storage cost.
Grant the training job's own service account read access to both the route table and the clip bucket.
Confirm that both sources live in one project, since the job can read anything inside that project.
questions.why: The job reads as its own service account, a separate identity, so that identity needs read permission on every source before the job can run.

questions.prompt: A team says their training job is effectively the same as the engineer who wrote it, because both are 'the account running the work.' Which statement is correct?
choices: A service account is an identity a service uses to act on your behalf, separate from any human user, so the job needs its own grants.
A service account is a region, so the job can only read data that lives in the same geographic group as itself.
A service account is a bucket that holds the job's output files, and it grants no permissions of its own.
A service account is a human user's password, so the job and the engineer share exactly the same access.
questions.why: A service account is a separate identity used by a service, so the job's access must be granted to that identity rather than inherited from a person.

questions.prompt: A training job runs in one project that holds both a warehouse table and a bucket, and both sit in the same region. The job fails with an access-denied error when it reads the bucket. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The bucket's region is wrong, so the job must be moved into a different project.
The table's column names differ from the bucket's file names, which blocks access.
The job's service account was never granted read access to the bucket, even though the bucket shares its project.
The bucket is too large for the job's memory, so the read is refused.
questions.why: Sharing a project does not give the job permission, because the job reads as its own service account, which must be granted access to each source.

questions.prompt: A team plans to train on a bucket of photos whose labels use a text field named 'item_id', and a warehouse table whose matching field is named 'product_id' and stored as an integer. What should they do before training?
choices: Copy the table into a second bucket so the field names no longer need to match.
Drop the photos entirely, since the warehouse table is the only trusted source.
Train on the photos first and let the model sort out the mismatched field names later.
Agree one column name and one type across both sources before the job runs.
questions.why: The schema must agree across sources, or the job misreads or drops fields, so one name and one type must be settled first.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that because the training job and the data are in the same Google Cloud project, the job will automatically be able to read everything. Explain to them what you would check before launching the job, and name one limit or tradeoff of copying data into a single location.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would tell them that a shared project does not grant access. The training job runs as its own service account, so I would confirm that account has read permission on each source, such as the warehouse table and the storage bucket. Then I would check that the sources are in locations the job can reach without slow or restricted cross-region reads, and that the column names and types match the agreed schema. If a copy is needed, the tradeoff is that the copy can go stale: if the source changes after I copy it, the model trains on old data. So I would record which snapshot was used, and set a refresh step if the data changes often.
rubricPoints: Access is granted per identity: the training job's service account needs read permission on each source
Data and training location should be aligned to avoid slow or restricted cross-region reads
Schemas must agree on column names and types across sources before training
Copying data creates a snapshot that can go stale, so record which version was used

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers ML data preparation, so a reasoning situation about choosing sources, locations, and access is the most useful practice.

lessons.plain: An accelerator is a computer chip built to do the heavy number crunching that machine learning needs, much faster than an ordinary processor. Google Cloud offers two kinds: GPUs (graphics processing units), which are general parallel chips made by several vendors, and TPUs (tensor processing units), which Google designed for this kind of math. Training is the slow process of teaching a model from huge amounts of data. Serving, also called inference, is using the finished model to answer requests. Large jobs often need many accelerators working together, and the trick is getting that capacity when you need it, at a price you can afford.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team needs 64 accelerators for three weeks to train a model, but the job can be restarted if it stops. Which would you expect to cost less per hour: guaranteed capacity booked in advance, or capacity you grab only when it happens to be free? Why?
lessons.teach:
Accelerator means a chip that does one type of work, here matrix arithmetic, far faster than a general CPU. GPUs are general parallel chips; TPUs are Google's own design for machine learning. Training adjusts a model's internal numbers, called weights, over a large dataset. Serving (inference) uses the trained model to answer requests, so it cares most about response time and cost per request.

Why it works: a large training job splits its math across many accelerators, and they must exchange data constantly. So the machines are grouped into a cluster joined by a fast network, and the job is scheduled as one unit. Because a single failure can stop the whole job, training saves checkpoints, which are snapshots of model state, so a restart resumes from the last snapshot instead of from zero.

Worked example: a team trains on 64 accelerators. Step 1: they choose a region where that accelerator type is offered. Step 2: they book the capacity as a reservation, a guaranteed allocation, because the job needs all 64 at once. Step 3: they checkpoint every hour, so a failure costs at most an hour of work. Step 4: when training ends, they release the reservation so billing stops.

Common mistake: relying on on-demand capacity for a long, all-or-nothing job, then finding the accelerators unavailable mid-run. Consequence in a running system: the run starts late or stalls, and paid hardware sits idle while the schedule slips.

Consumption choices trade price against certainty. On-demand is pay-as-you-go with no commitment. A committed use discount is a lower rate in exchange for a fixed-term commitment. Spot capacity is cheaper but can be reclaimed at any time, so it suits checkpointed training. Dynamic Workload Scheduler lets you request capacity for a future window, useful when a job can wait for its start.

questions.prompt: A regional news publisher is serving a summarisation model on GPUs. Traffic is steady at about 4 GPUs around the clock, but on breaking-news days it spikes to about 12 GPUs for a few hours. Worked trace: Step 1, classify the workload as serving, because it answers live user requests and is judged on response time and cost per request. Step 2, identify the steady 4-GPU baseline, which runs every hour of every day. Step 3, cover that baseline with a one-year committed use discount to get the lower rate. Step 4 is missing: decide how to cover the extra GPUs needed during the short spikes above the baseline. Which choice correctly completes Step 4?
choices: Book a reservation for 12 GPUs for the full year so the spike capacity is always guaranteed
Buy a one-year committed use discount for 12 GPUs so the peak is covered at the lowest rate
Run the spike GPUs on spot capacity, since spot is the cheapest option available
Run the spike GPUs on on-demand capacity, paying only for the hours they are used, because the spikes are short and unpredictable and there is no commitment to break
questions.why: On-demand is pay-as-you-go with no commitment, which fits short, unpredictable spikes, whereas spot can be reclaimed at any time and would interrupt live requests.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is an accelerator in the context of Google Cloud AI hardware?
choices: A general-purpose processor that runs the operating system and everyday software faster than any other chip
A network switch that moves data between machines in a training cluster at high speed
A storage device that holds model checkpoints close to the compute nodes for quick reads
A chip that performs one type of work, such as matrix arithmetic, far faster than a general CPU
questions.why: The teaching text defines an accelerator as a chip specialised for one kind of work, here matrix arithmetic, that is much faster than a general CPU.

questions.prompt: A forecasting team runs a training job across 32 accelerators and saves a checkpoint every 90 minutes. The job fails at the 4 hour 10 minute mark. Roughly how much completed work is lost, and why?
choices: About 4 hours 10 minutes, because checkpoints only help when the job finishes
About 70 minutes, because the job resumes from the last snapshot at 3 hours and loses work after it
About 90 minutes, because the job restarts from the start of the current interval
About 10 minutes, because the job restarts from the failure point itself
questions.why: Checkpoints are snapshots of model state, so the restart resumes from the most recent one at 3 hours, and everything after that snapshot is lost, about 70 minutes.

questions.prompt: A university lab needs to fine-tune a model on 8 accelerators together for 20 hours. The job can start any time within the next two weeks, but all 8 must be available at once. Which consumption option best fits?
choices: On-demand capacity, retrying the launch each day until all 8 accelerators are free
Spot capacity, because it is the cheapest and the job can be restarted if reclaimed
Dynamic Workload Scheduler, to request the capacity for a future window when the job can start
A three-year committed use discount, because it gives the lowest rate for the long term
questions.why: Dynamic Workload Scheduler lets you request capacity for a future window, which suits a job that can wait for its start but needs all of its accelerators together.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a large model training job on GPUs or TPUs needs a different capacity plan from a small web service, and name one tradeoff of the cheaper consumption option you would consider.
lessons.modelAnswer: A small web service handles independent requests, so it can scale out one instance at a time and tolerate losing one. Large training is different: dozens of accelerators must work together on the same math and exchange data constantly, so the job needs them all at the same moment. That pushes you toward reserved or scheduled capacity, and toward checkpoints so a failure does not waste the whole run. The cheaper option, Spot capacity, can be reclaimed at any time, so a run that depends on it can be interrupted partway. You accept lower cost in exchange for the risk of restarts, and you should only take that risk if checkpointing is in place and a delay is acceptable. Serving is another case: it needs steady capacity to keep response times low, so it is usually planned differently from training.
rubricPoints: Training needs many accelerators at once because they work as one cluster
Checkpoints limit how much work is lost when a machine fails
Cheaper capacity such as Spot can be reclaimed, so it trades cost for interruption risk
Reservations or scheduled capacity give certainty at a higher or committed price
Serving and training have different latency and availability needs

suggested.rationale: Comparing on-demand, committed, and interruptible consumption against a fixed workload is best practised in the planned cost model engine using fictional credits.

lessons.plain: Google Cloud offers ready-made AI services that you call over the network instead of building and hosting a model yourself. They sort into families by the kind of data they handle: text used for searching, back-and-forth dialogue, still pictures, video, and sound. Choosing the right family is one of the first design decisions, because each one is built for a different input and a different output. A search service finds the best matching content in your own documents. A conversation service holds a dialogue and answers in turns. Vision, image, video and audio services each read or create one kind of media. Picking the wrong family can work technically and still be the wrong design.
lessons.guessPrompt: A clinic wants staff to type a question and get an answer drawn only from its own 200 policy documents. A second team wants to upload X-ray photos and have the system flag possible fractures. Which Google AI family would you reach for first for each, and why?
lessons.teach:
An AI API is a managed service: you send it data in a request and it returns a result, while Google runs the model and its infrastructure. You do not train or host the model yourself. The core skill is matching the job to the right family. Search retrieves the most relevant items from a collection you own, such as product pages or policy documents, and can return ranked results or grounded answers. Grounded means the answer is tied to your own documents rather than to what a general model happens to remember. Conversation handles multi-turn dialogue, so the system keeps track of earlier messages and can route the user to an action. Vision reads still images to find labels, objects, or text. Image covers generating or editing pictures from a text prompt. Video analyzes or generates footage, which means it works across frames and over time. Audio covers speech: speech recognition turns spoken words into text, and speech synthesis turns text into spoken words.

The reason this works is that each family is built around one kind of input and one kind of output. So the matching question is simply: what goes in, and what should come out?

Worked example: a retailer wants shoppers to ask about returns and get answers from its own policy pages. Step one: the input is text and the output is an answer grounded in company documents, so the family is Search. Step two: if the shopper must keep chatting, ask follow-ups, and be routed to a refund action, you add Conversation. Step three: if the shopper uploads a photo of a damaged item, the input is an image, so Vision applies, not Search.

Common mistake: reaching for a generative Image or Video service when the task is only analysis, or sending audio to a text-only search flow. Teams also assume one family covers everything.

Consequence in a running system: a mismatched family often returns output that looks plausible but is wrong, such as a generated picture where a label was needed. The error then flows silently into downstream data and decisions.

questions.prompt: Lakeside Bakery wants phone callers to ask whether a cake contains nuts and hear the answer read aloud from the bakery's own allergen sheets. Step one: the caller's spoken question is audio input and the output is a text transcript, so the Audio family's speech recognition applies. Step two: [missing]. Step three: the text answer must be spoken back to the caller, so the Audio family's speech synthesis applies. Which choice correctly fills the missing step two?
choices: Pass the transcript to Search, which returns an answer grounded in the bakery's own allergen sheets.
Skip the step, because Conversation alone answers from the model's general memory.
Pass the transcript to Vision, since the allergen sheets are scanned pages.
Pass the transcript to Image so a new picture of the cake is generated for the caller.
questions.why: Search takes a text query and retrieves an answer tied to documents the bakery owns, which is the missing link between the transcript and the spoken reply.

questions.prompt: A marketing team wants an AI API to create a new banner picture from a written description of a desert sunset. Which family fits this task?
choices: Image, because it generates or edits pictures from a text prompt.
Vision, because it reads still images to find labels and objects in them.
Audio, because it turns written text into spoken words for a voiceover.
Search, because it ranks items from a collection the team already owns.
questions.why: The input is a text prompt and the output is a new picture, which is the job the Image family is built for.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team uploads one still photo of a shelf and asks an AI API to count the boxes on it. Which family fits, and what is the error in choosing a video service?
choices: Video, since counting objects always needs a service that works over time.
Image, since counting boxes means generating a new picture of the shelf.
Vision, since one still image is analyzed for objects, while video works across frames over time.
Search, since the photo can be indexed and ranked against the warehouse catalog.
questions.why: A single still image is analyzed by the Vision family, and a video service is the wrong fit because it expects footage that changes across frames over time.

questions.prompt: A call center holds 4,000 recorded customer calls and wants the spoken words turned into searchable text. Which family and which direction of conversion does this need?
choices: Conversation, since each call involves multiple turns between two people.
Audio, using speech recognition to turn spoken words into text.
Audio, using speech synthesis, since the calls must be re-voiced for analysis.
Audio, using speech synthesis to turn text into spoken words.
questions.why: Turning spoken words into text is speech recognition, which is in the Audio family, while speech synthesis goes the opposite way.
