lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide which Google AI API family fits a new feature, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on a managed AI API instead of building your own model.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the input and the output. If the input is a question over our own documents, I look at Search, and if the answer must be grounded in those documents, I check that the service supports that. If the user needs back-and-forth dialogue with follow-ups or actions, I add Conversation. For photos I look at Vision, for generated pictures at Image, for footage at Video, and for speech in or out at the Audio family. The tradeoff is control: a managed API is fast to adopt and needs no model hosting, but I cannot change the underlying model, and my data handling and output quality depend on the provider's behavior. So I would test the chosen service against real examples from our data before committing to it.
rubricPoints: Matches the family to the input and output type, such as text search, dialogue, image, video, or audio.
Explains that Search grounds answers in the organisation's own documents, while Conversation manages multi-turn dialogue.
Names a real limit of a managed AI API, such as limited control over the model or dependence on the provider.
Recommends validating the chosen service against representative data before relying on it.

suggested.rationale: Mapping a described feature to the right AI family is an exam-style reasoning task that no existing mission covers, so a scenario set adds the most.

lessons.plain: Gemini Enterprise is a company-wide AI assistant platform that employees can use with the company's own information. Two of its parts matter here. An AI agent is a helper that can carry out a multi-step task, such as gathering information from several sources and drafting a result, often with a person approving the result before anything changes. NotebookLM is a research tool where you load your own documents and ask questions that are answered only from those sources, with references back to the passages used. Integrating these into a workflow means deciding which step the AI helper does, what data it may read, and where a person checks the result before it is used.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a team wants an AI helper to answer questions about its internal policy documents. Should the helper be allowed to see every document in the company, or only the ones the asking employee could already open? Why?
lessons.teach:
An AI agent is a program that takes a goal, breaks it into steps, and calls tools or data sources to finish those steps. A grounded answer is one built from specific source material you supply, rather than from the model's general memory. NotebookLM works this way: you choose a set of sources, and its answers point back to passages in them. Gemini Enterprise applies the same idea across a company, where an assistant can search work content and where what it can see follows the signed-in user's permissions.

Why does this work? The model is good at reading, summarising and drafting, but it does not know your current facts unless you supply them when it answers. Grounding supplies those facts, and permissions decide which facts are allowed in. A safe design keeps three things separate: what the AI is allowed to read, what it is allowed to do, and who approves its output.

Worked example. A support lead wants a weekly summary of customer escalations. Step 1: a person selects the escalation notes folder as the source set. Step 2: the assistant reads only the documents the lead can already open. Step 3: it drafts a summary with a reference to each note it used. Step 4: the lead checks the references and edits the summary before sending it. If the draft cites a note the lead cannot open, the permission setup is wrong and must be fixed before anyone relies on it.

Common mistake: treating AI output as verified because it sounds confident. A grounded answer is only as good as its sources, and an agent that acts without a review step can repeat a wrong action very quickly.

Consequence: an agent with broad write access to a shared system can change many records in minutes, so any action that cannot be undone needs a human approval step before it runs.

questions.prompt: A regional freight firm uses an agent to check supplier invoices against delivery records. The finance analyst follows this sequence. Step 1: the analyst selects the June invoice folder as the source set. Step 2: the agent reads only the invoices the analyst's account can open. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: a finance controller reviews the cited lines and approves the batch before anything is posted to the ledger. Which completes step 3?
choices: The agent drafts each proposed correction and attaches a reference to the invoice line it relied on.
The agent approves its own corrections, since it has already checked the sources it was given.
The agent reads every invoice in the company's archive so its check is complete, whatever the analyst can open.
The agent posts each proposed payment correction directly to the ledger so the batch closes faster.
questions.why: Step 3 is the drafting step, and in this design every draft must point back to the source it used, so the controller in step 4 has something to check.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does it mean for an AI answer to be grounded?
choices: The answer is produced from the model's general memory and then checked against the company handbook.
The answer is built from specific source material you supply, so it can be traced back to those sources.
The answer is stored permanently in the system so that it cannot be changed by later users.
The answer is written in a formal tone that signals it has been approved by a manager.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a grounded answer as one built from supplied source material rather than from the model's general memory, and the traceability to sources is what makes it checkable.

questions.prompt: A small online shop sets up an agent with write access to its shared stock system. Overnight the agent misreads a supplier file and sets 600 product counts to zero, and the change cannot be reversed from the system's log. Which design choice would have best limited this harm?
choices: Requiring a person to approve any change the agent makes that cannot be undone before it runs.
Giving the agent a larger source folder so it reads more supplier files before deciding.
Letting the agent run on a faster schedule so that mistakes are caught earlier in the day.
Asking the agent to write a confident summary of each change so the team trusts the output.
questions.why: An agent with broad write access can change many records in minutes, so irreversible actions need a human approval step before they run, which is what would have stopped the bad counts.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm lets its staff ask the company's Gemini Enterprise assistant questions about internal work documents. A warehouse supervisor asks about a pricing review that is restricted to the sales team. Which outcome is correct under the design described in the teaching text?
choices: The assistant's answer excludes the restricted content, because what it can see follows the signed-in user's permissions.
The assistant answers from its general memory of pricing practices, since it cannot read the restricted review at all.
The assistant answers fully, because the supervisor is a signed-in employee of the same company.
The assistant answers with the restricted content, but marks it as unverified so the supervisor knows to ignore it.
questions.why: The teaching text states that what the assistant can see follows the signed-in user's permissions, so content the supervisor cannot open must stay out of the answer.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how you would bring an AI agent or NotebookLM into a document-heavy team workflow. Name one limit or tradeoff you would guard against.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by picking one repeatable step, such as turning meeting notes into an action list, rather than automating the whole process. For a NotebookLM-style tool, I would load only the approved sources for that step and make clear to the team that answers are only as good as those sources. For an agent that can act, I would give it the narrowest access it needs and require a person to approve anything that changes a record or sends a message. The main tradeoff is speed against trust: the assistant saves time on reading and drafting, but someone still has to check the references and the output, and that review time belongs in the plan. I would also confirm that the assistant respects the same permissions people have, so it cannot reveal documents to someone who could not open them.
rubricPoints: Names a concrete workflow step to automate instead of the whole process.
Explains that outputs are grounded in chosen sources and are only as reliable as those sources.
Limits agent access to the narrowest permissions needed and requires human approval for changes.
Names a tradeoff such as speed versus review effort, or data exposure.
Notes that the assistant's access should follow the user's existing permissions.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an access-and-approval scenario adds more than reading alone, and no listed mission or planned engine covers AI assistants.

lessons.plain: A foundation model is a large pretrained AI program that can read text, look at images, or write answers. Model Garden is a catalogue on Google Cloud where you can browse many such models, from Google's own to open-source and partner models, and choose one for a job. Integrating one means connecting it to your application so the app can send it a request, such as a question or a product photo, and use the answer. Think of it like hiring a specialist through an agency: you pick the specialist, agree how work is handed over, and make sure only your own staff can call them.
lessons.guessPrompt: A retail app wants to generate a short product description from a product's name and features. Before any teaching, what are the main decisions you would need to make before the app can call an AI model in production, and which would you make first?
lessons.teach:
Model Garden is the part of Google Cloud's AI platform that lists available models, including Google's own Gemini family, open models you can run yourself, and partner models. Each entry tells you what the model is good at, where it can run, and how you are charged. Choosing a model is the first integration decision.

There are two broad ways to use a model. A managed model is hosted by the provider; your application sends a request to its endpoint, which is a network address that accepts requests and returns results, and you pay per request or per unit of text. A self-deployed model runs on compute capacity you create and configure, so you control the machine type and region, but you pay for that capacity while it runs, whether or not anyone calls it.

Integration has three parts: the call path, the identity, and the limits. The call path is the request your service sends and how it handles the reply. The identity is the service account, a non-human identity your application runs as, which should be granted only permission to invoke the model. The limits are quotas, the caps on requests per minute, and the fact that models can be slow or occasionally fail.

Worked example. A retailer's product page service needs descriptions. Step 1: pick a text model in the catalogue that fits the task and the region where the data may be processed. Step 2: create a service account for the product service and grant it only the invoke permission. Step 3: the service calls the managed endpoint with the product name and features. Step 4: it caches each result so every product is generated once, and retries with a short wait on rate-limit errors. Step 5: if the model fails, it serves the stored description and logs the failure.

Common mistake: putting a long-lived API key in source code, or calling the model on every page view with no cache. Consequence: a traffic peak exhausts the quota, requests return errors, and without a fallback the product pages stop rendering.

A model is a dependency like any other, so plan for its latency, its cost, and its outages.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency wants a short plain-language summary of each service alert shown on its rider app. Its team has already done three things. Step 1: they picked a managed text model from the catalogue that fits summarising short notices and that is hosted in a region approved for rider data. Step 2: they created a service account for the alerts service and granted it only the invoke permission. Step 3: the service sends each alert's text to the model's endpoint and receives the summary. Step 4: the service stores each summary keyed by alert ID so repeat page views reuse it, and it retries rate-limit errors after a short wait. Step 5 is missing. What should the service do when the model call still fails after the retries?
choices: It switches to a self-deployed model automatically, because managed endpoints cannot fail.
It shows the most recent stored summary for that alert, or the original alert text if none exists, and logs the failure.
It retries the model call every second until it succeeds, holding the rider's page open while it waits.
It returns an error page to riders and turns off logging so the alerts feed stays quiet.
questions.why: A model is a dependency that can fail, so the service should fall back to data it already holds and record the failure, which keeps the page working and leaves a trace for the team.

questions.prompt: In Model Garden terms, how is a managed model billed compared with a self-deployed model?
choices: Both are billed only when a request arrives, so the difference is in the region chosen.
A managed model is billed per request or per unit of text, while a self-deployed model is billed for its compute capacity whether or not anyone calls it.
Both are billed a flat monthly fee regardless of how many requests are sent.
A managed model is billed for the machine it runs on, and a self-deployed model is billed per request.
questions.why: The teaching text says managed models charge per request or per unit of text, while self-deployed models charge for the capacity you create, even when idle.

questions.prompt: A small internal HR tool calls a text model only about twenty times a day, and nobody uses it outside office hours. Which deployment choice is more sensible on cost, and why?
choices: A self-deployed model, because a dedicated machine always gives the lowest price per call.
Either option, because the choice of managed or self-deployed has no effect on what you pay.
A self-deployed model in the cheapest region, because the region sets the request price.
A managed model, because you pay per request and not for a machine sitting idle overnight.
questions.why: With very low and irregular traffic, paying per request avoids paying for compute capacity that sits idle, which is the cost trap of self-deployment described in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: A developer wants the product service to call a Model Garden model. Which identity setup fits the integration guidance?
choices: Create a dedicated service account for the service and grant it only permission to invoke the model.
Paste a long-lived API key into the service's source code so it works after every redeploy.
Run the service as the project owner account so it never hits a permission error.
Share one human engineer's login credentials between all services that call the model.
questions.why: The teaching text says the identity should be a non-human service account with only invoke permission, and it names a long-lived key in source code as a common mistake.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never used AI models, in your own words, how you would integrate a Model Garden model into an application, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by choosing a model from the catalogue that matches the task, and checking where the data is processed, since that decides whether it is acceptable for our customer data. For a first version I would use a managed model, because the provider runs the hosting and we pay per request. The application would call the model's endpoint from a backend service running under its own service account, which has only permission to invoke the model, so no shared key sits in the code. The main tradeoff is cost and dependency: every request is billed, and calls can hit quotas or slow down under load, so I would cache results and build a fallback. A self-deployed model would give more control over the machine and region, but it adds capacity we must pay for and operate even when idle.
rubricPoints: Explains the difference between a managed model called through an endpoint and a self-deployed model on compute you run
Names the service account and least-privilege permission as the way the application authenticates to the model
Identifies quotas, latency, or cost as a real limit, and mentions caching or a fallback to handle it
Mentions checking the model's data handling and region before sending business or customer data

suggested.rationale: Choosing between a managed and a self-deployed model for a given business case is an exam-style reasoning task, and no listed mission or planned engine covers AI model integration directly.

lessons.plain: Designing IAM for a solution means deciding which people and programs may perform which actions on which cloud resources, and writing those decisions down so no grant is broader than the job needs. IAM stands for identity and access management. Think of a building with keycards: you decide which badge opens which doors, and you give each person only the doors their work requires. In Google Cloud the badge is a role, the person or program is a principal, and the doors are resources such as projects, storage buckets or databases. Good design means granting the smallest useful set of roles at the smallest useful level, then checking that those grants still match what the system really does.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web app needs to read files from one storage bucket and nothing else in its project. Should you grant its service account the Owner role on the whole project, or a narrow read role on that one bucket? Why?
lessons.teach:
A principal is any identity that can be granted access: a person's account, a group of people, a service account (an identity used by a program or virtual machine rather than a human), or a workload identity. A role is a named bundle of permissions, where a permission is one allowed action, such as reading objects from a bucket. A policy is the set of bindings attached to a resource, and each binding says this principal holds this role on this resource. Google Cloud resources sit in a hierarchy of organization, folders, projects and individual resources, and a policy set higher up is inherited by everything below it. That is why design matters: a role granted at the project level silently applies to every resource in that project.

Why it works: access is additive. Permissions accumulate across every binding that applies, and nothing lower in the hierarchy can take a permission away. So the safe habit is to grant at the lowest level that still works, and to prefer predefined roles scoped to one job over broad basic roles such as Owner, Editor or Viewer, which bundle far more than most workloads need. When no predefined role fits, a custom role can list the exact permissions required.

Worked example: a nightly report job runs as a service account. Step 1: identify the action, which is reading objects from the bucket reports-raw. Step 2: choose a role that contains only that read permission for storage objects. Step 3: bind the service account to that role on the one bucket, not on the project. Step 4: the job can read reports-raw, and a compromised job cannot delete the project or read other buckets.

Common mistake: granting Editor to a service account to stop an error, which hides the real missing permission and gives the program power far beyond its need.

Consequence: if the key for an over-privileged service account leaks, an attacker inherits everything that account can do, so narrow grants directly limit the damage. Access is therefore a design decision you record and review, not an accident you fix when something breaks.

questions.prompt: Pinecrest Dental runs a nightly script that uploads scan files to a Cloud Storage bucket named pinecrest-xrays-backup. The script runs as a service account, which is an identity used by a program rather than a person. The job needs to create new files in that one bucket and nothing else. Step 1: identify the action, which is creating objects in pinecrest-xrays-backup. Step 2: choose a predefined role that contains only the permissions needed to create storage objects, not a basic role such as Editor. Step 3 is missing: decide where to attach the binding that gives the service account that role. Which completion of Step 3 is correct?
choices: Make the bucket publicly writable so the script needs no binding at all
Bind the service account to the role on the whole project so new buckets are covered automatically
Grant Owner on the project because it is the only role that lets the script write files
Bind the service account to the role on that one bucket only
questions.why: A binding should sit at the lowest level that still works, which here is the single bucket, so the script gains no power over other resources in the project.

questions.prompt: In Google Cloud access control, what is a binding?
choices: A saved password that a service account uses to sign in to a virtual machine
A limit that stops a permission from being inherited by lower levels of the hierarchy
A named list of every resource that a folder contains, used for billing reports
The statement that one principal holds one role on one resource, which is part of a resource's policy
questions.why: A binding ties a principal to a role on a specific resource, and the set of bindings on a resource forms its policy.

questions.prompt: A contractor group, contractors@larkspur-freight.example, needs to read the 40 shipment manifests stored in the bucket manifests-2024 and nothing else in the project. Which grant follows the least-access habit described in the text?
choices: Grant Viewer on the entire organization so the group can see every bucket later if needed
Bind the group to a predefined storage object viewer role on the manifests-2024 bucket only
Add the group to a custom role that includes every permission on every bucket in the project
Grant Editor on the whole project so the group never hits a missing-permission error
questions.why: A predefined role scoped to reading objects, bound on the single bucket, gives exactly the access the group needs and no more.

questions.prompt: An administrator grants the Viewer basic role on a folder named Finance-2024 that contains 12 projects, just to fix one team's read access in one project. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Every project under that folder inherits the view access, and no lower-level setting can take it away
The grant is ignored until someone binds it to each project individually
Only the one project that the team needed gets view access, because folders do not pass grants down
Viewer on a folder automatically upgrades to Editor on every project it contains
questions.why: Policies set higher in the hierarchy are inherited downward and access is additive, so the broad grant reaches all 12 projects and cannot be reduced by lower bindings.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes giving every developer on the team the Editor role on the production project so nobody is blocked. Explain to them, in your own words, how IAM roles and inheritance work here, and name one limit or tradeoff of your recommended alternative.
lessons.modelAnswer: Roles are bundles of permissions bound to a principal on a resource, and a binding made on a parent such as a project flows down to everything inside it. So Editor on production lets each developer change almost every resource there, including ones unrelated to their work, and because access is additive, nothing lower can take it back. My alternative is narrower predefined roles, for example a role to view logs and another to deploy to one service, granted at the level where the work happens. The tradeoff is upfront effort: someone has to work out which permissions each job needs, and developers will occasionally hit a denial and need a quick, audited way to request access. I would also grant through groups, so access follows team membership and is easy to review, and schedule a periodic review to remove grants nobody uses.
rubricPoints: Explains that a role is a bundle of permissions granted to a principal on a resource.
States that policies are inherited downward, so a grant on a project covers everything inside it.
Notes that access is additive and a lower-level binding cannot remove a permission.
Names a tradeoff, such as more upfront effort or occasional denials, with a mitigation such as narrower roles or group grants.

suggested.rationale: The planned authorization policy evaluator would let the learner test who gets which access across a hierarchy, which is the core skill this objective needs.

lessons.plain: When a company runs many cloud projects, someone has to decide how they are grouped, who can change what, and which rules apply everywhere. Google Cloud's resource hierarchy is that grouping: an organization sits at the top as the root for your company, folders are optional groups inside it, and projects are the containers where resources such as servers, storage and databases actually live. Permissions and rules set high in the tree flow down to everything below, much like a permission set on a parent folder reaches every file inside it. Getting this layout right early makes access control, cost tracking and safety rules much easier to manage later.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has a payments team, a marketing team and a shared logging service, all running on the cloud. If you set one security rule at the very top of the company's cloud structure, which of these groups would it reach, and which would you want kept separate from the others?
lessons.teach:
The organization is the root node of the hierarchy, tied to your company's domain name. A folder is an optional grouping layer under the organization, used to mirror teams, environments or business units. A project is the container where resources are created and where billing and enabled services attach. Access grants and organization policies (rules that restrict what can be configured anywhere below them) are inherited: a grant or rule set on a node applies to every node beneath it. Inheritance is additive for access. A child cannot remove a permission its parent granted, so a broad grant high in the tree is hard to undo lower down.

Worked example: Cymbal Retail creates an organization, a Production folder and a Development folder. It places the project shop-payments-prod inside Production. Step 1: the security team grants an auditor role on the Production folder. Step 2: shop-payments-prod inherits that grant automatically. Step 3: a project created later under Production inherits it too. Step 4: a project under Development does not, because it sits in a different branch.

Common mistake: granting a broad editor role at the organization node to solve one team's access problem. That grants the role over every project in the company, including payments. The fix is to grant at the lowest node that covers the need.

Consequence: an over-broad grant at the top means one compromised account can change production resources it never needed to touch.

Good hierarchy design places each boundary where you want permissions and rules to stop, so the tree itself enforces separation.

questions.prompt: Lumen Freight has an organization, a Logistics folder and an Analytics folder. The project fleet-tracker-dev sits inside Logistics. Step 1: an administrator grants a contractor group a viewer role on the Logistics folder. Step 2: fleet-tracker-dev inherits that grant automatically, since access grants flow down to every node beneath the one where they were set. Step 3: a team member opens fleet-tracker-dev and tries to remove the contractor grant from that project alone. Step 4 is the missing one: what happens to the contractor's access to fleet-tracker-dev, and where must the grant be removed to stop it?
choices: The grant stays, since a child cannot remove a parent's grant; it must be revoked at the Logistics folder.
The grant is removed from every project in the company at once, since the folder is the top of the tree.
The removal succeeds, because a project's own access page can override a grant made on its parent folder.
The grant is cancelled automatically once the project's billing account is linked to a new billing account.
questions.why: Access grants are additive, so a child node cannot take away a permission its parent granted, and only the node where the grant was made can revoke it.

questions.prompt: A small company called Brightwater Labs asks what a folder is for in its new Google Cloud hierarchy. Which answer is correct?
choices: An optional grouping layer under the organization, used to mirror teams or environments
A rule that restricts which configurations are allowed anywhere below it
The container where resources are created and where billing attaches
The root node of the tree, tied to the company's domain name
questions.why: A folder is an optional grouping layer under the organization, used to mirror teams, environments or business units, which is why it is the second choice.

questions.prompt: Halden Pharmacy Group has a Pharmacy-Ops folder containing the project rx-refill-prod, and an Analytics folder containing the project rx-reports-staging. Only the Analytics team needs read access to rx-reports-staging, and nobody else needs it. At which node should the grant be placed?
choices: At the organization node, so every future project is covered
At the rx-reports-staging project, the lowest node that covers the need
At the Analytics folder, so the whole branch is covered including future projects
At the Pharmacy-Ops folder, since rx-refill-prod sits there
questions.why: The guidance is to grant at the lowest node that covers the need, and here that is the single project, because the requirement names only that project.

questions.prompt: Vantage Freight's administrator grants the editor role on the organization node so one developer can fix a billing dashboard. What is the most accurate description of the risk this creates?
choices: The grant lapses once the dashboard project is closed
The editor role applies to every project in the company, including production
Only the billing dashboard project is affected, because grants apply only to the project where they were first typed in
Nothing changes until a new folder is created under the organization
questions.why: A grant set on the organization node is inherited by every node beneath it, so the editor role reaches all projects, including production, which is the over-broad risk the teaching describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: A new teammate asks why we do not put every project directly under the organization and manage access per project. In your own words, explain when folders help, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on inheritance from higher levels.
lessons.modelAnswer: Folders give us a way to group projects by environment, team or business unit, so one rule or grant applies to a whole branch instead of being repeated per project. Production and development can sit in separate folders, and an auditor role on the Production folder covers every production project automatically, including ones created later. The tradeoff is that inheritance is additive: a child cannot take away a permission its parent granted. So a broad grant placed too high is easy to create and hard to narrow down later. For that reason, we grant at the lowest node that meets the need, and we review the tree periodically to see what each folder is inheriting.
rubricPoints: Folders group projects so one grant or rule covers a whole branch
Inheritance flows downward from organization to folder to project
Access grants are additive and a child cannot remove a parent's grant
Grant at the lowest node that meets the need to avoid over-broad access

suggested.rationale: An exam-style situation where the learner must decide where to place a grant or rule in a company's tree adds the most, and no listed mission covers cloud hierarchy.

lessons.plain: When a company stores data, that data should be scrambled so that someone who steals a disk or copy cannot read it without a separate secret. Encryption is the scrambling, and a key is the secret that unlocks it. Designing data security means deciding who holds those keys, how often they are replaced, and where the passwords and tokens that applications need are kept. Good designs keep keys apart from the data they protect, never write passwords into code or config files, and keep a clear record of who can use each key. The real question is not just whether data is encrypted, but who can decrypt it and what happens if a key is lost or leaked.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company stores customer records in a cloud database. If an attacker copies the raw storage disks, what single thing would stop them reading the records, and who should be the only party able to hold it?
lessons.teach:
Encryption at rest means data stored on disk is turned into unreadable bytes using an algorithm and a key. Decryption reverses this with the right key. A key management service is a managed system that creates, stores, rotates (replaces on a schedule), and audits keys, so that raw key material does not sit inside your application.

Envelope encryption is the pattern that makes this practical. Large data is encrypted with a data encryption key (DEK). That DEK is then encrypted with a key encryption key (KEK), which lives in the key service and never leaves it. Encrypting a key with another key is called wrapping. Only the small wrapped DEK is stored beside the data. To read, the system asks the key service to unwrap the DEK, then uses it on the data. This means the top-level key can be rotated or revoked without re-encrypting every byte.

On Google Cloud, data at rest is encrypted by default with Google-managed keys. Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) let you hold the top-level key in your own key service so you control rotation and can cut off access. Secrets such as database passwords or API tokens belong in a dedicated secret store, not in source code, images, or environment files, where they get copied into logs and backups. Applications fetch a secret at runtime using an identity that is allowed to read it.

Worked example: an order service must store a payment token. Step 1, the service generates a DEK and encrypts the token with it. Step 2, the key service wraps the DEK with the KEK. Step 3, the wrapped DEK and the ciphertext are stored together. Step 4, to read, the service asks the key service to unwrap the DEK, receives it, and decrypts the token.

Common mistake: keeping the database password in a config file committed to git, then calling the system secure because the disk is encrypted. Anyone with repository access reads the password in plain text.

Consequence: if the KEK is disabled, every DEK it wrapped becomes unusable, so the data is unreadable until access is restored. A sound design must make that recovery possible and tested.

questions.prompt: A parcel-tracking company archives 40 GB of scan logs each night. Its backup job works like this. Step 1: it asks the key service for a new 256-bit data encryption key (DEK, the key that encrypts the bulk data). Step 2: it encrypts the 40 GB archive with that DEK. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: it clears the plain DEK from memory and stores the archive. On restore, the job asks the key service to unwrap the stored DEK, then decrypts the archive. Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Encrypt the 40 GB archive a second time directly with the key encryption key (KEK, the top-level key that stays in the key service).
Write the DEK into the backup job's configuration file so it survives restarts.
Wrap the DEK with the KEK inside the key service, then store the wrapped DEK beside the encrypted archive.
Store the plain DEK beside the archive so restores do not need the key service.
questions.why: Envelope encryption requires wrapping the DEK with the KEK and storing only the wrapped DEK with the ciphertext, so the restore step can unwrap it.

questions.prompt: A hospital's developers copy the raw bytes of their key encryption key (KEK) into an environment variable so the app can wrap data keys locally without calling the key service. What is the main problem with this?
choices: The app will run slower because it cannot cache the key in memory.
Key rotation becomes impossible because the key service no longer schedules replacements.
The data keys can no longer be encrypted, so the database will reject writes.
Raw key material leaves the managed key service and can be copied into logs, images, or config, undermining the reason the KEK lives there.
questions.why: A key management service exists so raw key material does not sit inside the application, and copying the KEK into an environment variable defeats that protection.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm disables its KEK during a cleanup of unused keys. Weeks later it finds that its archived shipment records cannot be opened. What explains this?
choices: Each DEK wrapped by that KEK is unusable while the KEK is disabled, so the records stay unreadable until access is restored.
The records were stored unencrypted, so disabling the key had no effect on them.
The encrypted records were deleted automatically when the key was disabled.
The DEKs were re-encrypted with a new KEK, which the archive cannot read.
questions.why: Disabling a KEK makes every DEK it wrapped unusable, so the data it protects cannot be decrypted until the KEK is re-enabled.

questions.prompt: A payments startup's Cloud Run service needs an API token at runtime to call a partner. Which design best meets the requirement of keeping the token out of code, images, and logs?
choices: Keep the token in a .env file in the repository, and add that file to .gitignore.
Print the token to the startup log once so the team can verify it, then remove the log later.
Store the token in a dedicated secret store, and grant only the service's identity permission to read that one secret at runtime.
Bake the token into the container image so it is present from the moment the service starts.
questions.why: Secrets belong in a dedicated secret store and are fetched at runtime by an identity allowed to read them, not placed in code, images, or logs.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says our data is encrypted, so the database password in the repository is safe. In your own words, explain why that reasoning is wrong, and name one limit or tradeoff of the design you would propose instead, such as the operational risk of managing your own keys.
lessons.modelAnswer: Disk encryption protects the storage layer: whoever gets the raw disk cannot read it without the key. But anyone who can read the repository has the password in plain text, so disk encryption protects nothing on that path. Secrets should live in a dedicated secret store and be read at runtime by an identity allowed to read that one secret, never committed or baked into images. For the data itself, envelope encryption lets us rotate the top-level key without rewriting everything. The tradeoff is that customer-managed keys give us control but make us responsible for disabling or losing them by mistake. We would need rotation schedules, access auditing, and a tested recovery plan, and we accept more operational work than the default Google-managed keys require.
rubricPoints: Disk encryption does not protect a secret stored in plain text where many people can read it.
Secrets belong in a dedicated secret store and are fetched at runtime by an allowed identity.
Envelope encryption lets the top-level key be rotated or revoked without re-encrypting all data.
Customer-managed keys give control but add the risk of disabling or losing a key, so recovery must be planned.

suggested.rationale: Envelope encryption and key wrapping are easiest to grasp by building a small lab that wraps and unwraps data keys.

lessons.plain: Separation of duties means that no single person can carry out a risky task from start to finish alone. The work is split so one person requests or writes a change and a different person approves or runs it, so a mistake or bad intent by one individual cannot slip through unchecked. Think of a bank where the person who can move money cannot also approve their own transfers. In a cloud setting, this idea shapes who may hold which permissions, which projects hold which systems, and which activity gets recorded for later review. The goal is not distrust of people. It is making sure errors and misuse are caught by a second check.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer who can deploy new code to the live payment service also has permission to read the production database contents. Without any other control, what could go wrong, and what single change would reduce that risk without slowing the team too much?
lessons.teach:
Separation of duties is a control design in which a sensitive task is divided into steps owned by different people, so that no one identity can complete it alone. Two terms first. A principal is any identity that can act in the system: a person, a group, or a service account, which is an identity used by an application or automated job. A role is a named bundle of permissions, such as the ability to view data or change a setting. You grant roles to principals on a particular resource, which is any thing you can control in the cloud, such as a project, a storage bucket or an encryption key.

Why it works: a single actor can make a mistake or abuse access, but if the steps need two different actors, the second one acts as a check, and an error or attack now has to involve two identities. The design has three levers. First, split roles so that the deploy role cannot also read secrets or manage encryption keys. Second, keep environments apart, usually with separate projects for development and production, so a test identity has no path into live data. Third, rely on audit logs, which are records of who did what, so reviewers can spot misuse afterwards.

Worked example, Cymbal Retail's payment service. Step 1: the developer holds a role that deploys new versions of the service. Step 2: a separate security administrator holds the role that manages the encryption key protecting card data. Step 3: the service account that runs the live service receives read access only to the one secret it needs. Step 4: any change to key permissions appears in the audit log, and a reviewer checks it. No single person can both deploy code that quietly sends card data elsewhere and decrypt that data.

Common mistake: granting broad basic roles such as owner or editor to a whole team because it is convenient. Those roles bundle many powers, so one person ends up holding every step. Consequence in a running system: a compromised developer laptop with owner access could change IAM settings, disable logging and read data in one session, and the audit trail may no longer show clearly what happened.

questions.prompt: Lantern Logistics runs a nightly job that exports invoice totals to a reporting bucket. The design has three steps. Step 1: a data engineer holds the role that deploys the export job. Step 2: a finance controller holds a read-only role on the invoice dataset. Step 3: the export job's service account receives write access only to the one reporting bucket it fills. Step 4 is missing. Which identity should own step 4, which is approving any later grant of write access to that bucket?
choices: The export job's service account, so the job can manage its own access when it needs to change.
Any member of the finance team with read-only access, because they are closest to the reporting output.
The data engineer who deployed the export job, so the person who knows the job best can approve changes quickly.
A separate administrator who did not deploy the job and does not hold the export's write role.
questions.why: Separation of duties needs the approver to be a different identity from the one that deploys the job and from the one that would gain the access, so no single actor can grant themselves or the job new power.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does separation of duties aim to guarantee for a sensitive task?
choices: Each service account is given owner rights so recovery is faster after an outage.
Every employee holds the same role, so no one is treated differently.
Audit logs are switched off for that task so routine activity creates less noise.
No single identity can complete the sensitive task alone, because a second identity must be involved.
questions.why: The definition of separation of duties is that a sensitive task is split into steps owned by different identities, so one identity cannot finish it by itself.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Clinic's developer needs to test a new appointment-reminder feature. Which setup best keeps that developer away from live patient records?
choices: Give the developer a role on a separate test project, and grant no roles on the production project that holds live records.
Grant the developer read-only access on production, since reading cannot change anything.
Grant the developer the editor role on the production project so the feature can be tested against real data.
Put the test and production environments in one shared project so the developer's activity is easier to watch.
questions.why: Keeping environments in separate projects and granting no production roles means a test identity has no path into live data, whereas any read or edit role on production still lets the developer reach patient records.

questions.prompt: A small team gives every member the basic owner role on a project, saying it saves time. What is the core risk this creates for separation of duties?
choices: Owner cannot be granted to a group, so the team must add each person one by one.
It lets one identity carry out steps that should need two different identities.
Owner makes audit logs unavailable, so nobody can later see what happened.
Owner is slower to apply than narrow roles, which delays each deployment.
questions.why: Broad basic roles bundle many powers, so a single compromised or careless identity can perform every step of a sensitive task without any second identity acting as a check.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how separation of duties applies to deploying a service that handles customer payments. Name one specific Google Cloud control you would use to split the duties, and state one limit or tradeoff of that control.
lessons.modelAnswer: Separation of duties means a risky task is split across people or identities so no single one can complete it alone. For a payment service, I would keep deploying code and handling the encryption key in different hands. The deploy identity gets a role that can release new versions but cannot read the key or the card data, and a separate security role manages the key. I would also put development and production in separate projects so test access cannot reach live data, and I would review Cloud Audit Logs to confirm changes came from the expected identity. The tradeoff is friction: every split adds a handoff, so releases can slow down. A small team may also end up with one person holding both roles, which is why the design needs review rather than assumption. Permissions drift as people change jobs, so the split needs ongoing upkeep.
rubricPoints: Defines separation of duties as splitting a sensitive task so no single identity completes it alone
Names a specific control such as splitting IAM roles, separating projects, or reviewing audit logs
Explains that an owner or editor style broad role undermines the split
States a real tradeoff such as slower releases, team size limits, or permission drift

suggested.rationale: Evaluating which identity may perform each step of a split task against authorization rules builds the reasoning this objective tests.

lessons.plain: Security controls on Google Cloud are the fences and switches that decide who can reach your data, what settings people may change, and what gets recorded when something happens. This objective covers five of them: audit logs that record who did what, service perimeters that stop data being copied out of a protected group of projects, access levels that check things like device and location before letting a request in, organization policies that block risky settings across a whole company, and hierarchical firewall policies that set traffic rules once at the top of the tree instead of in every project. Think of them as layers. Each answers a different question, and a good design picks the one that matches the requirement in front of you.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank says its customer data must never be copied out of its storage project to a personal account, even by an administrator who holds valid credentials. Which kind of control would you reach for first, and why would an ordinary permission grant not be enough?
lessons.teach:
Each control answers one kind of question. Audit logs record who did what and when. Cloud Audit Logs are the built-in records Google Cloud writes for administrative changes and, in some cases, data access, and you read them to prove what happened. An organization policy is a rule set at the top of the resource tree (the organization, a folder, or a project) that forbids certain settings everywhere beneath it, such as restricting which regions resources may be created in. A hierarchical firewall policy is a set of network traffic rules attached to an organization or folder, so it applies to every project below and is evaluated before the rules inside a single VPC network. VPC Service Controls (a feature that builds a service perimeter around projects and managed services such as storage or analytics) blocks API calls that try to move data across the perimeter, even when the caller has valid credentials. Context-aware access uses access levels, built with Access Context Manager, that admit a request only when conditions such as device state, source IP range, or user location are met.

Why it works: identity and permission grants answer who may act, but not from where or on which data boundary. A perimeter adds a boundary around the data itself, so a stolen or misused credential still cannot copy the data out.

Worked example: a retailer keeps sales exports in a storage bucket inside project P. Step 1: place project P and its storage service inside a service perimeter. Step 2: an analyst with valid rights tries to copy an object into a project outside the perimeter. Step 3: the request crosses the boundary and is denied. Step 4: the denial appears in the audit logs, so the security team can see the attempt.

Common mistake: treating these controls as interchangeable. An organization policy does not stop data leaving through an API call, and a firewall rule cannot check whether a user's laptop is managed. Choose the control that matches the question being asked.

Consequence: a perimeter set too tightly can break legitimate pipelines that cross projects, so changes should be tested in a dry-run mode before they are enforced.

questions.prompt: Harbor Lane Dental keeps patient intake forms in a storage bucket inside project H. The security team wants staff to open the forms only from company-managed laptops. Step 1: an access level is created in Access Context Manager that requires a managed device. Step 2: that access level is attached to the application that reads the bucket. Step 3: a dental assistant signs in with correct credentials from a personal, unmanaged laptop. The missing step 4 is what the access level decides for this request.
choices: The request is denied, because the access level's device condition is not met.
The request is denied by a hierarchical firewall policy, which checks each device's management status before traffic reaches a VPC network.
The request is admitted, since valid credentials were supplied.
The request is admitted, and only an organization policy can block it later.
questions.why: A context-aware access level admits a request only when its conditions, such as device state, are met, so a valid password on an unmanaged laptop is refused.

questions.prompt: A team lead needs the built-in record that shows who changed a project's settings and when, so the change can be proven later. Which control provides that record?
choices: An organization policy
A VPC Service Controls perimeter
A context-aware access level
Cloud Audit Logs
questions.why: Cloud Audit Logs are the records Google Cloud writes for administrative changes and some data access, and they are what you read to prove what happened.

questions.prompt: A media company's folder contains many projects, and engineers must never create resources outside Europe, whatever their own permissions. Which control should be used?
choices: An access level requiring a managed device
An organization policy that restricts resource locations
A VPC Service Controls perimeter around the storage service
A hierarchical firewall policy attached to the folder
questions.why: An organization policy is a rule set at the resource tree that forbids certain settings, such as creation regions, everywhere beneath the node it is attached to.

questions.prompt: A stolen service account key is used from an unknown location to copy objects out of a project. The project's organization policy already restricts regions. Why does that policy not stop the copy?
choices: Organization policies only apply to projects created after the policy was set, so older projects are not covered by it.
The copy is a network packet, so only a hierarchical firewall policy can see it.
It limits which settings and regions are allowed, but does not block API calls that move data out.
The key has valid credentials, so no control on the resource tree can refuse it.
questions.why: An organization policy forbids certain settings but does not stop an allowed API call from moving data across a boundary, which is the job of a VPC Service Controls perimeter.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between an organization policy, a VPC Service Controls perimeter, and a context-aware access level for a new requirement, and name one limit or tradeoff of the control you would pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking what the requirement actually restricts. If it limits which settings people can configure, such as allowed regions or banning public IP addresses, I use an organization policy, set at the folder or organization so it covers every project below. If it limits data leaving a protected set of projects, even by someone with valid credentials, I use a VPC Service Controls perimeter, because it checks the boundary of the API call rather than the identity. If it limits who can connect and from which device or network, I use an access level from Access Context Manager, which is evaluated when the request arrives. The tradeoff I would name for a perimeter is that it can break legitimate cross-project workflows, so I would run it in dry-run mode, read the violation logs, and only then enforce it.
rubricPoints: Matches the control to the question: settings limits point to organization policy, data boundary to a perimeter, and device or location conditions to access levels.
Explains that a perimeter blocks data movement regardless of valid credentials, which permissions alone do not do.
Names a real limit or tradeoff, such as breaking legitimate cross-project pipelines when a perimeter is enforced too early.
Mentions checking audit or violation logs to verify what a control is doing.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine teaches choosing among these named Google Cloud controls, so reasoning through exam-style requirements is the best practice available.

lessons.plain: Encryption scrambles data so that only someone holding the right key can read it. When a cloud provider encrypts your data by default, it manages those keys for you. Customer-managed encryption keys mean you choose and control the keys yourself, using a key service called Cloud KMS, which stores them and records who uses them. You decide who may use a key, how often it is replaced, and in which geographic location it lives. The tradeoff is responsibility: if you disable or destroy a key, the data it protects becomes unreadable, even to you. This matters whenever a rule says your organization must hold the keys.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a cloud service encrypts your stored files with a key that you control, and you then disable that key, what happens to the files, and why might a company still want this control?
lessons.teach:
A key is a secret value that an encryption algorithm uses to lock or unlock data. Cloud KMS, the Google Cloud key management service, creates and stores keys and lets other services ask it to encrypt or decrypt small pieces of data. A key ring is a named grouping of keys in one location, and each key sits inside a ring. Each key has versions. The primary version encrypts new data, and older versions are kept so existing data can still be opened. Rotation means creating a new version and making it primary, which limits how long any one version protects data.

Why it works: most services use envelope encryption. The service encrypts your data with a random data encryption key, then encrypts that small data key with your Cloud KMS key. The wrapped data key is stored alongside the data. To read the data, the service asks KMS to unwrap the data key, which requires permission on your key. Your key never leaves KMS, so you can revoke access by changing permissions or disabling the key.

Worked example: a company stores vehicle records in a storage bucket linked to a customer-managed key named records-key in europe-west1. Step 1: the bucket is created and linked to records-key. Step 2: an object is written; the service generates a data key, encrypts the object with it, then asks KMS to wrap the data key using records-key version 1. Step 3: a rotation creates version 2 as primary; new objects use version 2, while older objects still open with version 1. Step 4: an administrator disables the key, and reads of its data fail until it is re-enabled.

Common mistake: assuming the key's location does not matter, or that rotation instantly re-encrypts everything. The key must be in a compatible location with the resource it protects, and rotation changes which version is used for new writes.

Consequence: in a running system, disabling or destroying a key stops every service that depends on it, so key changes need the same change control as a production deploy.

questions.prompt: Harbor Freight Logistics stores shipment manifests in a Cloud Storage bucket. The bucket uses a customer-managed encryption key, meaning a key the customer creates and controls in Cloud KMS (Google Cloud's key management service), named manifest-key, in the key ring freight-ring, located in us-west1. The key's primary version is version 3. Step 1: a manifest is written, and the storage service generates a random data encryption key, a short-lived key that encrypts the file itself. Step 2: the service encrypts the manifest with that data key and asks KMS to wrap the data key using manifest-key version 3, storing the wrapped copy beside the manifest. Step 3: a dispatcher later reads the manifest. The service sends the wrapped data key to KMS. Step 4: [missing step]. Step 5: the service uses the recovered data key to decrypt the manifest and returns it to the dispatcher.
choices: The service generates a fresh data key and uses it to read the manifest
KMS unwraps the wrapped data key using manifest-key, which requires permission on that key
The service re-encrypts the manifest with manifest-key version 3 before returning it
The service copies manifest-key out of KMS so it can decrypt the file locally
questions.why: To read envelope-encrypted data, KMS must unwrap the stored data key with the customer key, which is why permission on that key controls reads, and the key itself never leaves KMS.

questions.prompt: A logistics company rotated its Cloud KMS key ops-key from version 4 to version 5 and made version 5 the primary version. Which statement is correct?
choices: Version 4 is deleted, so any data it protected has to be rewritten by hand before it can be read
Version 5 can only decrypt data written after the rotation, so older data becomes unreadable
New writes use version 5, and data written under version 4 still opens because older versions are kept
Rotation instantly re-encrypts every existing object under version 5 across all buckets that use the key
questions.why: Rotation makes a new version primary for new encryption, and older versions are retained so existing data can still be opened; it does not rewrite old data.

questions.prompt: A payroll service stores pay files encrypted with a customer-managed key named payroll-key. On Friday evening an administrator disables payroll-key in Cloud KMS. What happens next?
choices: Only new uploads fail, because existing files stay readable from data already decrypted in memory
Reads of pay files whose data keys were wrapped by payroll-key fail until the key is re-enabled, because KMS will not unwrap them
The key's material is copied into the payroll service so that reads continue without a call to KMS
The payroll service keeps working from a cached copy of the key for about 24 hours before failing
questions.why: A disabled key cannot be used to unwrap data keys, so every dependent read fails until the key is re-enabled, and the stored files themselves are unchanged.

questions.prompt: A design review asks why a storage service sends only a small wrapped data key to Cloud KMS instead of sending the whole file to KMS for encryption. Which answer is best?
choices: KMS charges by the byte for each operation, so sending small keys is cheaper than sending full files
KMS has a fixed size limit for each request, and whole files would always exceed it in practice
Only the small data key needs a KMS call, so the bulk data stays with the service and the customer key never leaves KMS
Wrapping the whole file would make it readable by anyone who holds bucket read access, so the file is kept unwrapped
questions.why: Envelope encryption keeps bulk data with the service while KMS handles only the small wrapped key, so the customer key never leaves KMS.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what customer-managed encryption keys with Cloud KMS give you compared with the default encryption, and name one limit or tradeoff you would warn them about.
lessons.modelAnswer: By default, the cloud provider generates and manages the keys that protect our stored data, so we do not control them. With customer-managed keys in Cloud KMS, we create the key, choose its location, control which identities may use it, and can rotate or disable it. That gives us a way to meet requirements that say we must hold the keys. The main tradeoff is that the key becomes a dependency for our data. If someone disables or destroys the key, or removes the permission a service needs, reads and writes fail, and the outage can look like a storage problem. So we treat key changes like production changes, keep the key in a location that matches the data, and monitor key usage.
rubricPoints: Customer-managed keys let the organization choose, control, rotate, and disable the key, unlike default provider-managed keys.
Cloud KMS stores the key, and services use it through envelope encryption, wrapping a data key rather than the data itself.
The key must be in a compatible location and access is governed by permissions on the key.
Disabling or destroying the key makes the protected data unreadable, so key changes need careful change control.

suggested.rationale: The planned envelope encryption lab would let the learner wrap and unwrap data keys hands-on, which is the core mechanism behind customer-managed keys.

lessons.plain: Remote access is how people and programs reach systems they are not sitting next to, such as an internal web tool or a private database. The secure design questions are who is asking, whether they should be let in, and whether a caller can act as another identity without holding a long-lived password or key file. Google Cloud offers several separate tools for these jobs: one checks who may reach a web app, one lets a trusted identity borrow another identity's permissions for a short time, one manages the browsers on company devices, and one lets outside systems such as a build pipeline prove who they are without a stored key. Knowing which job each tool does is the skill being tested.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a script on your laptop needs access to a cloud project. Would you rather copy a long-lived key file onto the laptop, or let the script borrow short-lived access when it runs? What goes wrong with each choice if the laptop is stolen next month?
lessons.teach: Remote access should check identity on every request and grant short-lived access, not hand out long-lived secrets. Four tools cover different parts of that rule. Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) is a gateway placed in front of a web application or virtual machine. Before a request reaches the app, the proxy checks that the caller has signed in with a known identity and holds an allowed role. The app itself does not change, which is why the pattern suits internal tools. A service account is an identity for a program rather than a person. Impersonation lets a permitted user or program obtain short-lived credentials for a service account, so they can act as it without ever holding its key file. Workload Identity Federation does the same job for outside systems: it accepts a token from an external provider, such as a build pipeline's identity token, and exchanges it for short-lived Google Cloud credentials, so no key is stored in the pipeline. Chrome Enterprise Premium is the browser-side layer. It manages browsers on company devices and can enforce context-aware rules, such as blocking copying of sensitive data or denying access from unmanaged devices. Worked example: an internal dashboard runs on a virtual machine. First, place it behind IAP so every browser request is checked against identity and role. Second, a deploy pipeline needs to push code. Workload Identity Federation trusts the pipeline's token and issues credentials valid for about an hour, so no key file exists. Third, a developer debugging a nightly job impersonates that job's service account for one session, which leaves an audit record. Common mistake: creating a service account key file just to get something working. That file is a long-lived secret; if it leaks from a laptop or repository, it keeps working until someone notices and revokes it. Short-lived tokens limit the damage of a leak to a short window. Designing remote access means choosing the gateway, the identity, and the credential lifetime together.

questions.prompt: Bramble Logistics runs a route-planning web tool on one virtual machine. Its staff must reach it from a browser, and its nightly export job runs on an outside continuous integration service that needs to write reports to storage. Step one: put the virtual machine behind Identity-Aware Proxy (a gateway that checks each browser request for a known sign-in and an allowed role before it reaches the app), so the app itself needs no changes. Step two: configure Workload Identity Federation (a way to trade a token from an outside system for short-lived Google Cloud credentials) to trust the continuous integration service's identity token, so the export job gets credentials that last about an hour and no key file is created. Step three is missing: an on-call engineer must inspect what the export job's service account is doing during one session, without ever holding that account's key file. What should the engineer do?
choices: Impersonate the export job's service account for that one session, which gives short-lived credentials and leaves an audit record.
Add the engineer's personal account as an owner of the whole project so it can act on any resource.
Put the service account's email address in the team wiki so the engineer can sign in as it through the browser.
Download a new key file for the service account and keep it on the laptop until the session ends.
questions.why: Impersonation lets a permitted person obtain short-lived credentials for a service account without holding its key, and the session is recorded, which matches the step the scenario leaves open.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does an identity-aware gateway in front of a web application do that a normal network firewall rule does not?
choices: It encrypts the application's database files on disk so that a stolen copy is unreadable.
It copies every request into a log so the application can be restored after a crash.
It checks who the caller is and whether they hold an allowed role on every request before the request reaches the app.
It assigns the application a permanent key file that the developers use to sign in.
questions.why: Identity-Aware Proxy checks the caller's signed-in identity and role on each request before forwarding it, which is an identity check rather than a network-address or encryption control.

questions.prompt: A build server in an outside company needs to deploy to Google Cloud. A junior engineer proposes creating a service account key file and storing it as a secret in the build server's settings, arguing it is simpler. Which risk best describes why this design is weak?
choices: The key file gives the build server read access only, so it cannot push any code.
The key file is short-lived, so it expires before the next deployment and the build fails.
The key file cannot be used from outside Google Cloud, so the build server cannot authenticate at all.
The key file is a long-lived secret, so if it leaks it keeps working until someone notices and revokes it.
questions.why: A service account key file is a long-lived credential; a leak keeps it usable until revocation, whereas federated short-lived credentials limit the exposure window.

questions.prompt: A company wants to stop employees from copying customer records out of a web application while they use company laptops, and to block access from personal phones. Which Google Cloud tool is designed for this browser-side, device-context control?
choices: Workload Identity Federation, because it accepts tokens from outside providers and exchanges them for credentials.
Identity-Aware Proxy alone, because it places a gateway in front of the application and so covers both copying and device checks.
Chrome Enterprise Premium, because it manages browsers on company devices and enforces context-aware rules such as blocking copying or denying unmanaged devices.
Service account impersonation, because it lets a user act as a program identity for one session.
questions.why: Chrome Enterprise Premium is the browser-side layer that enforces device and context rules like blocking copying from sensitive data and denying unmanaged devices, which the other tools do not do.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would give an outside contractor access to an internal admin web tool without giving them a key file, and name one limit of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would put the admin tool behind Identity-Aware Proxy and grant the contractor's Google identity the specific role that lets them pass the proxy, so every browser request is checked against who they are and what they may reach. They never receive a key file, so there is no long-lived secret to leak, and removing the role cuts their access quickly. The limit is that IAP only controls the front door. Once the contractor is inside, the app's own permission checks still decide what they can do, so the app needs its own authorization. Also, the contractor must sign in with an identity the organization manages, so a personal account will not work unless policy allows it. For automated jobs I would not use this pattern at all; I would use service account impersonation or Workload Identity Federation instead.
rubricPoints: Identity-Aware Proxy checks identity and role on each request before it reaches the app.
Avoiding key files removes a long-lived secret that can leak and stay usable.
A real limit is named, such as IAP not replacing the app's own authorization or requiring a managed identity.
Impersonation or federation is the right choice for programs, not user-facing access.

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right control for a remote-access scenario is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this objective directly.

lessons.plain: Software supply chain security means making sure the code you run in production is the code you meant to build, built from sources you trust, with its parts checked along the way. Think of a factory making car parts: you want to know where each part came from, that nobody swapped one on the line, and that each part is inspected before it goes into a vehicle. For cloud software, that means controlling where build outputs are stored, checking them for known weaknesses, recording who built what and how, and refusing to run anything that lacks the required approval.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a container image was built last night from a clean repository, and later someone pushed a different image under the same tag name in your registry. What could go wrong when a server pulls that tag, and what single property would let you detect the swap?
lessons.teach:
An artifact is any build output a system runs or ships, such as a container image. A registry is a store for artifacts; on Google Cloud the managed one is Artifact Registry. A tag is a human-friendly label such as latest or v2, and it can be moved to point at different bytes at any time. A digest is a fingerprint computed from the exact contents of an artifact, so two different images can never share one. Provenance is a record of how an artifact was made: its source, its build system, and its inputs. An attestation is a signed statement about an artifact, such as 'this was built by our approved pipeline' or 'this passed a vulnerability scan'. Vulnerability scanning compares an artifact's packages against databases of known flaws. Binary Authorization is the deploy-time gate: it admits an image only if the required attestations exist and were signed by trusted keys.

It works because each check binds a claim to exact bytes. Worked example: the pipeline builds an image and gets digest sha256 starting with a3f. The build step records provenance and signs an attestation for that digest. The scanner finds no critical flaws and signs a second attestation. The deploy requests the image by digest, not tag. Binary Authorization looks up both attestations for that digest, verifies the signatures, and admits it. Someone who later pushes a tampered image gets a new digest with no attestations, so the deploy is refused.

The common mistake is deploying by a mutable tag such as latest, which lets the bytes change without anyone noticing, or running scans in report-only mode where nothing blocks a bad image. In a running system, an enforcement gate that fails closed will also block an urgent hotfix, so a break-glass path with logged approval is part of the design. Trust in production comes from the deploy gate checking signed evidence about exact bytes, not from the tag name or from anyone's memory of what was built.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Freight runs a route-planner service built by a pipeline. Step 1: the build produces an image with digest sha256:9c1e04, and the build step records provenance and signs a build attestation for that digest. Step 2: the vulnerability scanner finds zero critical flaws and signs a scan attestation for the same digest 9c1e04. Step 3: the deploy manifest is changed from route-planner:stable to route-planner@sha256:9c1e04, so the deploy asks for exact bytes rather than a tag. Step 4 is missing. What does Binary Authorization do at deploy time?
choices: It admits the image without checking anything, because the manifest no longer uses a tag.
It rebuilds the image from source to confirm the digest matches before admitting it.
It admits the image because the scanner found no critical flaws, so the signed attestations are not needed.
It looks up the attestations for digest 9c1e04, verifies their signatures against trusted keys, and admits the image only if they check out.
questions.why: Binary Authorization admits an image only when the required attestations exist for that exact digest and were signed by trusted keys, so a clean scan result alone is not enough.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly separates a tag from a digest?
choices: A digest and a tag are both fingerprints, and two different images can share the same one if they have the same name.
A digest is a fingerprint computed from exact contents so two images cannot share one, while a tag is a movable human label.
A tag is a fingerprint of the image contents, while a digest is a label that the registry operator can move to other bytes.
A digest is a human-friendly label such as v2, while a tag is computed from the exact bytes of the artifact.
questions.why: A digest is computed from the exact contents, so different images never share one, whereas a tag is a friendly label that can be pointed at different bytes at any time.

questions.prompt: Northgate Insurance runs a nightly vulnerability scan on every image in its registry. The scan results are emailed to the security team, and deploys are never checked against them. A critical flaw in a deployed image goes unnoticed for three weeks. What is the control gap?
choices: The scan runs in report-only mode, and no signed scan attestation is required at deploy, so nothing blocks the flawed image.
The nightly schedule is too infrequent, so the team should scan on every commit instead of every night.
The registry stores images in only one region, so the scan cannot reach all copies quickly.
The team deploys by digest rather than by tag, which prevents the scan from reading the package list.
questions.why: A scan that only reports does not stop a bad image; the deploy gate needs a signed scan attestation for the exact digest before it admits the image.

questions.prompt: Harbor Lane's claims-api is deployed by digest 4b7a, which was admitted earlier. A later rebuild gets new digest 5e0c and is pushed to the registry, which moves the tag v2.4 from 4b7a to 5e0c. The rebuild has no attestations. An engineer now deploys using the tag v2.4. What happens?
choices: Binary Authorization admits it, because the tag v2.4 was unchanged in name and so still refers to an approved release.
