Why it works: you cannot improve what you have not measured, and intuition about slow code is often wrong. Profiling points at the real cost. Benchmarking gives a baseline, so a change is judged by numbers rather than by feeling. Repeatability is what makes the comparison fair: same data, same load, same environment.

Worked example: the positions API has a p95 latency of 900 ms under a steady load of 200 requests per second. Step one, profile a sample of request traces. About 700 ms is spent in one database query and 50 ms in JSON encoding. Step two, add an index on the vehicle-id column so the query stops scanning the whole table. Step three, rerun the identical benchmark. The p95 falls to 150 ms, throughput stays at 200 requests per second, and errors stay at zero. Only the database step changed, which is why profiling came first.

Common mistake: benchmarking against a small test database or a single run, then trusting the result. Production data volume and traffic mix differ, and a change that wins on toy data can lose under real load.

Consequence: a system tuned on an unrealistic benchmark can fail at its first real peak, when queues build up and timeouts cascade.

Profiling and benchmarking together tell you what is slow and how much a fix really helps.

questions.prompt: A bike-share company runs a checkout service. Under a steady load of 80 requests per second, its p95 latency is 1.2 seconds. Step 1: the team profiles sampled request traces and finds about 850 ms is spent waiting on a call to a fraud-scoring service, 300 ms on a cache lookup, and 30 ms on rendering the receipt page. Step 2: the team names the fraud-scoring call as the bottleneck. Step 3: [missing; the team makes one change to that call and reruns its tests]. Afterward, p95 falls to 410 ms, throughput stays at 80 requests per second, and errors stay at zero.
choices: Move the 30 ms receipt rendering onto a faster template engine, because it is the simplest code to change.
Batch the fraud-scoring calls so each checkout makes one call instead of several, then rerun the identical benchmark.
Add more checkout servers without profiling, since throughput is the number that matters most.
Rerun the benchmark at 10 requests per second so the fix can be measured quickly.
questions.why: Profiling named the fraud-scoring call as the largest cost, so the fix belongs there, and reusing the identical benchmark keeps the before-and-after comparison fair.

questions.prompt: A dashboard reports p95 latency of 300 ms for a parcel-tracking API. What does this mean?
choices: 5 percent of requests finish within 300 ms, so most take longer.
The API can handle 95 requests per second while each takes 300 ms.
95 percent of requests finish within 300 ms, so 5 percent take longer.
The average request takes 300 ms to finish.
questions.why: The p95 is the time within which 95 percent of requests finish, so the slowest 5 percent are not captured by it and are outside the bound.

questions.prompt: A team benchmarks a new search index using one run on a staging copy that holds 2 percent of production rows. The new index beats the current system by 40 percent, and the team wants to ship it. What is the main risk?
choices: Staging is always slower than production, so the 40 percent win is a conservative estimate.
One run on a small copy is too short to measure the average response time at all.
Two percent of the rows and a single run may not reflect production volume and traffic mix, so the win may disappear at real peak load.
Throughput is the wrong metric to report on a search index, so the result is meaningless.
questions.why: A benchmark that uses unrealistic data volume or a single run can produce a win that fails under real load, which is the central risk of benchmarking on toy data.

questions.prompt: A shipping quote service has a p95 of 800 ms. Profiling sampled requests shows 600 ms in a call to a third-party rate API, 150 ms in a database query, and 50 ms in logging. Which step should the team change first, and why?
choices: The logging, because it is the easiest part of the request to switch off without side effects.
The server CPU, because the request is slow overall and more CPU should speed up every step.
The database query, because database calls are the most common cause of slowness in web services.
The third-party rate API call, because it takes the most time in the request, so a fix there moves p95 the most.
questions.why: Profiling shows where the time goes, and the rate API call accounts for most of the 800 ms, so that is the bottleneck that limits the whole request.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between profiling and benchmarking, and name one limit or tradeoff of using benchmark results to decide a release is safe.
lessons.modelAnswer: Profiling answers where time goes inside a running system. It breaks a request or a process into steps or functions and shows which one costs the most. Benchmarking answers how well the system performs under a defined, repeatable load, usually as throughput and latency percentiles, and lets us compare versions. I use profiling first to find the bottleneck, then a benchmark to show that a change helped under the same conditions. The main limit is that a benchmark is only as good as its workload. If the test data volume, request mix, or environment differs from production, the numbers can look great and still mislead. So before calling a release safe, I would check the benchmark against realistic traffic and watch the production p95 after the rollout, not just trust the test result.
rubricPoints: Profiling finds where time or resources are spent inside a running system.
Benchmarking runs a fixed, repeatable workload to produce comparable numbers.
Percentile latency such as p95 reveals slow requests that averages hide.
A benchmark is only valid if its data, load mix, and environment resemble production.

suggested.rationale: That mission has you diagnose a slow API after a deploy, which means finding the real bottleneck before changing anything, the core of profiling.

lessons.plain: An alert is a message that wakes a person or opens a ticket when something measurable goes wrong. Designing an alerting strategy means deciding what to watch, how bad it must get before someone is told, and how to avoid telling people about things that do not matter. A good strategy focuses on what customers actually feel, such as failed orders, rather than every internal number that moves. Think of a smoke alarm that chirps for burnt toast every minute: people stop listening. The job is to make each alert worth interrupting someone for.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your server's CPU hits 95 percent for two minutes at 3 a.m., but no customer requests are failing. Should that page a person, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
An alert is an automatic notification that fires when a measured value, called a metric, crosses a rule you set, such as an error rate staying above a limit for a period of time. An alerting strategy is the set of decisions behind those rules: what to measure, how far a value must move before it matters, who gets woken, and how often this happens.

The core idea is to alert on symptoms that users feel, not on every internal cause. A busy CPU is a cause that may or may not hurt anyone; the share of checkout requests that fail is a symptom. A common way to set the bar is an SLO, a service level objective: a target for the fraction of good events, such as 99.9 percent of requests succeeding over 30 days. The gap between 100 percent and the target is the error budget, here 0.1 percent of requests. Burn rate is how many times faster than allowed you are spending that budget.

Worked example. Suppose the error rate over the last hour is 1.44 percent. Step one: the burn rate is the error rate divided by the allowed rate, so 1.44 divided by 0.1 gives 14.4. Step two: at that pace the whole month's budget is gone in 30 divided by 14.4, about two days. Step three: page when burn rate exceeds 14.4 over both a one-hour window and a five-minute window, so a brief spike that has already ended does not page anyone.

Common mistake: alerting on CPU or on any single error. Those produce noise, and people learn to ignore the pager.

Consequence: if the pager fires for a CPU blip at 3 a.m. while checkout failures go unseen, the alerts are working exactly as configured, but the strategy is wrong. A sound strategy pages on user-visible budget burn and sends cause-level signals to dashboards or tickets.

questions.prompt: A file-upload service at Brightpath Storage has an SLO (service level objective, a target for the share of good events) of 99.5 percent of uploads succeeding over 28 days. Its error budget (the allowed share of failures, here 100 percent minus the target) is therefore 0.5 percent. Over the last hour, 4.0 percent of uploads failed. Step one: the allowed error rate is 0.5 percent, as above. Step two: [missing]. Step three: at that pace the 28-day budget is gone in 28 divided by the burn rate, which works out to 3.5 days. What belongs in step two?
choices: Divide the observed 4.0 percent error rate by the 0.5 percent allowed rate to get a burn rate of 8.0
Multiply the observed 4.0 percent error rate by the 0.5 percent allowed rate to get a burn rate of 2.0
Divide the 28-day window by the 4.0 percent error rate to get a burn rate of 7.0
Subtract the 0.5 percent allowed rate from the 4.0 percent error rate to get 3.5 times the allowed pace
questions.why: Burn rate is the observed error rate divided by the allowed rate, so 4.0 divided by 0.5 gives 8.0, which is also the figure that makes the 3.5-day result in step three consistent.

questions.prompt: Harbor Lending sets an SLO that 99.95 percent of login requests succeed over a 90-day period. What is its error budget?
choices: 0.05 percent of login requests
0.005 percent of login requests
99.95 percent of login requests
0.5 percent of login requests
questions.why: The error budget is the gap between 100 percent and the SLO target, and 100 minus 99.95 is 0.05 percent.

questions.prompt: Lumen Streams runs a video service. Its transcoder (the component that converts video into playable formats) CPU sits at 95 percent for a few minutes each evening, while 2.5 percent of playback starts fail over the same hour, and the playback-start success rate is the measure users feel. Which alerting design best follows the principle of alerting on user-visible symptoms?
choices: Send the transcoder CPU signal to a dashboard or ticket, and page on the burn rate of playback-start failures against the SLO
Page on both signals equally, so that no failure is ever missed
Disable paging entirely and review the CPU graph each morning
Page the on-call engineer whenever transcoder CPU exceeds 90 percent, so the cause is caught early
questions.why: Playback-start failure is the symptom users feel and should drive paging through budget burn, while CPU is a cause-level signal that belongs on a dashboard or in a ticket.

questions.prompt: A team pages when burn rate is above a set threshold over both a long window and a short window. A brief error spike happened 20 minutes ago and has since stopped. Why does requiring both windows keep this spike from paging anyone?
choices: The long window alone always shows the spike as zero, so the rule can never be met
The alert system ignores any spike that is older than the long window, regardless of the short window
The short window has returned to normal, so the combined condition no longer holds and nobody is paged
The threshold automatically doubles whenever a spike ends, which blocks the page
questions.why: Because the short window reflects only the most recent few minutes, a spike that has already ended drops below the threshold there, so the requirement that both windows exceed it fails and no page is sent.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why an alert should usually be based on a user-facing symptom, such as failed requests, rather than a cause, such as high CPU. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Paging on a user symptom, like the share of failed requests burning the error budget, tells us customers are hurt right now, so a human response is justified. High CPU is a cause. It might be harmless, like a batch job finishing, or it might come before a failure, but on its own it does not show that anything is broken. If we page on every cause, the pager becomes noisy and people start ignoring it. The tradeoff is that a symptom alert reacts after users are already affected, and it may not tell you which component is at fault. So I keep symptom alerts as the pages, send cause signals like CPU and queue depth to dashboards for diagnosis, and use paired windows so brief spikes do not page. The limit is that a symptom alert is only as good as its measurement of success; if that measurement is wrong, the alert stays silent when it should fire.
rubricPoints: Explains that a symptom alert reflects what users actually experience, while a cause alert may or may not matter
Describes the tradeoff of alert noise and fatigue when pages are based on causes
Notes that symptom alerts react after users are affected and may need cause signals to diagnose
Mentions that the measurement behind a symptom alert must be accurate

suggested.rationale: The planned metric alarm builder engine would let the learner set thresholds and windows and see how noisy or silent each rule becomes.

lessons.plain: Managing deployment and release means deciding how a new version of a service reaches production without harming the people who use it. A deployment is putting the new code onto the machines or platform that run it. A release is the decision to send real user traffic to that code. Good teams do not switch everyone over at once. They send a small share of traffic to the new version first, watch how it behaves, and widen the share only when the numbers look healthy. If something goes wrong, they send traffic back to the old version quickly. The architect's job is to pick the approach that matches how much risk the business can accept.
lessons.guessPrompt: You shipped a new version of a checkout service to every user at once, and the error rate jumps five minutes later. What is the fastest safe way you could have limited the damage, and what would you need running beforehand to do it?
lessons.teach: A deployment puts a new build of a service onto the machines or platform that run it. A release is the decision to send real user traffic to that build. Keeping the two apart helps, because you can deploy a version and send it no traffic yet, then release it later. The main strategies differ in how much traffic the new version sees first. A rolling update replaces instances a few at a time, so old and new versions run side by side and a bad batch stops the process. A canary sends a small share of requests, such as five percent, to the new version while the rest stay on the old one, then raises that share if error rates and latency match the baseline. Blue-green keeps two full environments and switches all traffic at once, so rollback is a single switch back. Rollback means returning traffic to the last version you know works, and it is only fast if the old version is still running and can still read the data. Worked example: a ride-dispatch API with ten instances on version 2.4 is moving to 2.5. Step one, deploy 2.5 and send it five percent of traffic. Step two, after fifteen minutes the 2.5 error rate is 0.3 percent against 0.1 percent for 2.4, so the rollout halts and the new version receives zero traffic. Step three, the team fixes the bug and tries again. Common mistake: treating a canary as safe when the new version changes a database column the old version cannot read. Once the new version writes that data, rolling back the code does not undo the damage. In a running system, every release should stay backward compatible with the version it replaces, so old and new code can coexist throughout the rollout. Rollback is a plan you rehearse before the release, not a button you hunt for during an incident.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm called Lumen Parcel runs its parcel-tracking service using blue-green deployment. Blue is the environment serving live users on version 7. Version 8 is deployed to the idle green environment, and green receives no user traffic while it is checked against blue's error rate and response time. The team's plan reads: Step one, deploy version 8 to green. Step two, check green against blue while green has no users. Step four, switch all user traffic from blue to green at once. The plan is missing the step that belongs between step two and step four, which must make a bad switch quick to undo. Which step fills that gap?
choices: Delete the blue environment once green is deployed, to free up capacity.
Send five percent of users to green before the full switch, so the team learns about problems early.
Rebuild version 8 from source code so the team knows the build is clean.
Confirm that blue is still running and can still read the current database, so that switching back is a single action.
questions.why: Blue-green rollback is only fast if the old environment is still running and can still read the data, so confirming that is the step that makes the switch reversible.

questions.prompt: A Cymbal Retail team uploads a new build of its pricing service to its servers on Friday, but leaves the new build without any customer traffic until the following Monday. Which term best describes the Friday action?
choices: A rollback, because the team is preparing to return to an earlier build.
A canary, because the team is sending the new build a small test group.
A release, because the team has decided the new build will eventually serve customers.
A deployment, because the new build has been placed onto the machines that run the service but has not yet been sent traffic.
questions.why: A deployment puts a build onto the running machines, while a release is the separate decision to send real user traffic to it, so the Friday step is a deployment.

questions.prompt: Altostrat Media runs a video-thumbnail service on forty instances. The team wants to replace the old build a few instances at a time, so that old and new versions run side by side and a bad batch stops the process before it reaches everyone. Which release strategy matches this plan?
choices: A blue-green cutover, because it keeps two full environments and switches all traffic at once.
A canary that sends five percent of requests to the new build first.
A single full redeploy that stops every instance and starts the new build everywhere together.
A rolling update, because it replaces instances in small batches and can halt if a batch looks bad.
questions.why: A rolling update replaces instances a few at a time with old and new versions coexisting, which is exactly the behaviour described, whereas the other options switch traffic in different ways.

questions.prompt: Harbor Stay, a hotel booking company, released a new version of its reservations service using blue-green. The new version renamed a database column that the old version reads. After the switch, errors appeared, and the team switched traffic back to the old environment. The errors continued. What is the most accurate explanation?
choices: The old version cannot read the data the new version has already written, so returning traffic to it does not undo the damage.
The team should have used a canary, because blue-green always stores data in a format that the old version cannot read.
Blue-green switches cannot be reversed once any traffic has reached the new environment.
The old environment was too small to handle the load, so the switch back could not help.
questions.why: Rolling back code does not undo data the new version has already written, and an old version that cannot read that data cannot recover the service, which is why releases must stay backward compatible.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is about to release a change to a payments service why you would choose a canary over a blue-green switch, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would pick a canary when the risk is in real traffic behaviour that tests miss and I want to limit how many users see a bad version. A canary sends a small share, say five percent, to the new version while the rest stay on the old one. I compare error rate and latency between the two groups and widen the share only if the new one looks healthy. Blue-green is better when I need a clean, instant switch and the old environment can take all traffic, but it doubles capacity during the change and sends everyone to the new version at once when I flip. The tradeoff with a canary is that it takes longer to reach full traffic and needs good metrics per version, because a tiny slice shows nothing useful without them. It also means old and new versions run together, so the new version must work with the existing data and interfaces during that period.
rubricPoints: Names the canary approach: a small share of traffic goes to the new version first.
Compares it with blue-green: an instant switch that affects all users at once and needs double capacity.
States a real tradeoff: a canary is slower and needs per-version metrics to judge health.
Notes that old and new versions must coexist, so changes must stay backward compatible.

suggested.rationale: The planned deploy-shift engine would let the learner compare rolling, canary and blue-green releases by watching how each one behaves under failure.

lessons.plain: Supporting a deployed solution means keeping a system that is already live working after launch. An architect does not usually fix every fault by hand. Instead, they help the team find out what is wrong, collect the facts that matter, decide how urgent it is, and get the right people or the vendor's support team working on it quickly. Think of it like a doctor referring a patient to a specialist: the referral only helps if the notes are complete. This lesson covers the habits and information that make that handoff work, using a service that suddenly starts returning errors.
lessons.guessPrompt: A checkout API starts failing right after a deploy. Before anyone opens a vendor ticket, what three facts would you write down first, and why would each one matter to the people who try to help?
lessons.teach:
Supporting a deployed solution means helping a live system stay healthy after it launches. Several terms matter here. Triage is the first sorting step: deciding what is broken, how many users are affected, and whether the problem is getting worse. A support case is a ticket you open with a cloud vendor's support team; it records the problem, its impact, and the evidence. Severity is the urgency level you assign to that case, and it should reflect business impact, not how alarming an error message looks.

Why this works: support engineers can act faster when the report is specific. A good case names the project and resources affected, gives the exact time the symptom began, includes the error text, notes what changed just before (a deploy, a config edit, a traffic spike), and lists what you already tried. Your own logs and dashboards provide that evidence.

Worked example: at 14:05 a checkout API starts returning 503 errors for 30 percent of requests. Step 1: check your change history; a deploy finished at 14:00. Step 2: check whether the errors come from the new version in the logs. Step 3: roll back the deploy and confirm the error rate falls. Step 4: if the problem persists or cannot be explained from your side, open a support case with severity set by impact on paying customers, attaching timestamps, log excerpts, and the rollback result.

Common mistake: opening a case that says only 'it is broken', with no timeline, which forces the vendor to spend time on basic questions. Another mistake is marking everything as top severity, which hides the real emergencies.

In a running system, every minute of a checkout outage costs revenue, so the evidence collected in the first hour largely determines how fast the problem gets solved.

questions.prompt: A shipment-tracking API starts timing out for 18 percent of requests at 07:45. Work through the steps. Step 1: Check the change history. A database maintenance job dropped an index on the shipments table at 07:40. Step 2: [MISSING; choose what belongs here]. Step 3: Recreate the index and confirm the timeout rate falls back to under 1 percent. Step 4: Because the cause was an internal change that is now reversed, no vendor case is needed.
choices: Scale the API to more instances and watch whether the timeout rate drops, since extra capacity often fixes slow responses.
Ask the support team to tell you whether the database maintenance caused the problem before you check anything yourself.
Check the logs to see whether the timeouts come only from queries that use the dropped index.
Open a vendor support case now with the highest severity, because the shipment API is customer-facing, and let the vendor work out which change caused the timeouts.
questions.why: Step 2 is the step that connects the symptom to the change by confirming in your own logs that the failing requests use the index that was dropped, which is the evidence the teaching text says you should gather before deciding on any vendor case.

questions.prompt: A reporting service's error rate jumped at 11:30, and the on-call engineer has a few minutes before the next status update. Which action is triage in the sense used here?
choices: Writing the final incident report so the team can close the ticket.
Deciding what is broken, how many users are affected, and whether the problem is getting worse.
Sending the vendor a case with the full log export attached.
Choosing the highest severity so that no urgent problem is missed.
questions.why: Triage is the first sorting step that establishes what is broken, the number of affected users, and whether the problem is worsening, which is exactly what option three describes.

questions.prompt: A nightly export for an internal finance team fails with an alarming error message. No customer-facing service is affected, and the export can be rerun the next morning. What severity should the support case carry?
choices: Highest, because any failed job is an emergency and top severity guarantees the vendor responds first.
Low or moderate, because the impact is internal and the error text does not set severity.
Medium by default, because every case gets medium severity until a manager reviews it.
Highest, because the error message uses the word failed and that word signals a critical case.
questions.why: Severity should follow business impact, and an internal export that can be rerun without harming customers has low or moderate impact no matter how alarming the message looks.

questions.prompt: A team opens a vendor case that says only 'our object storage has been slow since Tuesday'. Which problem is most likely to slow the vendor's response?
choices: The case does not state a cause, which the vendor must be given before it can start work on the problem.
The case lacks an exact start time, error text, and a list of recent changes, so the vendor must ask basic questions first.
The case does not name a severity level.
The case was filed on a Tuesday rather than a Monday.
questions.why: A case without a timeline, error text, or recent changes forces the vendor to spend time on basic questions, which is the common mistake the teaching text describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would hand a live production problem to a vendor's support team. Name one limit or tradeoff of that handoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first confirm the problem is real and measure its impact: which users, which region, since when. Then I would check our own changes, such as recent deploys or config edits, and try the safest fix, usually a rollback, while keeping the evidence. If we still cannot explain it, I would open a support case with a clear timeline, the affected project and resources, error samples, what changed, and what we already tried. I would set severity by customer impact, not by how scary the error looks. The main limit is that the vendor only sees what we send them and cannot see our internal context, so a vague report slows everything down. Also, support response depends on our support plan, so we should not assume a fast answer during a critical outage.
rubricPoints: Confirm the problem and measure its impact before escalating
Check your own recent changes and attempt a safe mitigation first
Include timeline, affected resources, error evidence and steps already tried in the case
Set severity by business impact and recognise that vendor response depends on the support plan

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a live incident triage and escalation scenario adds the most value here, and no listed mission covers vendor escalation directly.

lessons.plain: Quality control measures are the checks a team puts in place to find out whether a system really works, before and after it changes. Think of a bakery that tastes every batch, weighs the flour, and keeps a record of past burnt loaves. Each check produces evidence, and the evidence tells you whether the bread you designed is the bread you actually sell. For a cloud architect, this means asking not only whether a system was designed to be reliable, but what proof exists today that it is. The objective here is judging which checks give real evidence and which only give comfort.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team says their service is reliable because its architecture diagram has redundant servers in two zones and its test suite passes. What single piece of evidence would you ask for before you believed them, and why?
lessons.teach:
A quality control measure is any check that produces evidence about how a system behaves, as opposed to a plan describing how it should behave. Examples include automated tests that run on every change, a review by a second engineer before code ships, a load test that pushes the system to expected peak traffic, a restore test that actually rebuilds data from a backup, and a service level objective (SLO), which is a measurable target such as 99.9 percent of requests succeeding over a month. The error budget is the allowed shortfall that follows from that target. When it is used up, the team slows changes and fixes reliability first.

Why this works: a design describes intent, while a measure observes behavior. A check is only useful if it could fail. A test suite that never touches the failover path cannot tell you whether failover works.

Worked example: a backup is listed in the design. Step 1, ask when a restore was last rehearsed. Step 2, find the answer is never. Step 3, the backup exists but the restore procedure has never been run, so recovery time is unknown. Step 4, the missing measure is a scheduled restore drill with a recorded duration.

Common mistake: treating a green pipeline as proof of production reliability. Passing tests show that known cases still work, not that real traffic will be handled.

Consequence: a system with a passing suite but no load test before a product launch can fail at its first real peak, and the team learns the limit from customers.

Quality controls are evidence-producing checks, and their value depends on whether they could actually detect a failure.

questions.prompt: A parcel-tracking company, Lumen Parcel, has a checkout service that its design document says can handle 3,000 requests per second at the holiday peak. Step 1: ask what evidence supports that claim. Step 2: the only load test on record ran in staging last March at 1,000 requests per second, so it never reached the forecast peak. Step 3: the gap is that the design says 3,000 but nothing has observed the service at 3,000. Step 4: the missing measure is ____
choices: Ask a second engineer to re-read the design document and confirm the number
Run a load test at the forecast 3,000 requests per second in an environment that matches production, and record latency and error rate
Add more unit tests to the checkout module so each function is covered
Wait for the holiday period and watch the live dashboards as traffic arrives
questions.why: Only a load test at the real target, in a production-like setup, produces observed behavior at that peak, while the other options either check code or repeat the design intent.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of a quality control measure as the teaching text defines it?
choices: A written policy that says all releases must be reviewed by two people
A scheduled restore of a database backup into a scratch project, with the elapsed time recorded
A list of target response times agreed with the product team at kickoff
A architecture diagram that shows the planned connections between services
questions.why: A check that produces evidence about actual behavior, such as a timed restore, is a quality control measure, whereas diagrams, policies, and agreed targets describe intent.

questions.prompt: A ride-booking team's test suite passes on every commit, yet customers report that payments fail during peak hours. The suite only calls a health endpoint that returns success and never submits a payment. What is the most accurate explanation?
choices: The team should have a larger suite with more endpoints tested in parallel
Payments fail only at peak, so a passing suite at off-peak times is expected to be wrong
The suite is green because it cannot fail on the payment path, so it gives no evidence about payments
The health endpoint is probably returning success because the database is slow
questions.why: A check is only useful if it could fail, and a suite that never exercises the payment path cannot reveal payment failures, so its green result says nothing about them.

questions.prompt: A ride-booking API has a 99.5 percent monthly success SLO over a 30-day month. Its error budget is the allowed shortfall. Roughly how much budget is available across the month, expressed as time that could be spent failing if failures were spread evenly?
choices: 3.6 hours
0.5 hours
7.2 hours
36 hours
questions.why: 0.5 percent of 30 days (720 hours) is 3.6 hours, which is the shortfall the target allows; when that is spent, the team slows changes and works on reliability.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether a team's quality controls actually prove a system is reliable, and name one limit of the checks you would rely on.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by separating checks that produce evidence from checks that only describe intent. A design diagram or a passing unit test suite tells me what was planned or that known cases work. I want to see measures that run against the real system: a recent load test at expected peak, a restore drill with a recorded time, SLO dashboards showing whether the error budget is being spent, and post-incident reviews that led to changed checks. Then I would ask when each was last run, because a test from last year on an old version proves little. The limit I would name is that every check only covers what someone thought to check. A load test at twice expected traffic still will not reveal a failure mode nobody modelled, so I would treat quality controls as a way to lower uncertainty rather than remove it.
rubricPoints: Separates evidence from intent: a design or a passing suite is not proof of production behavior.
Names concrete measures such as load tests, restore drills, and SLO tracking against an error budget.
Checks how recent the evidence is and whether it covers the real system.
States a limit: checks only cover failure modes someone anticipated.

suggested.rationale: Judging whether a team's quality claims hold up is an exam-style reasoning task that benefits from working through a realistic situation.

lessons.plain: Designing a system to be reliable is not the same as proving it is. Reliability checks test a running system on purpose. Load testing sends a controlled, growing amount of traffic to see where the system slows down or breaks, before real customers find out. Chaos engineering breaks a small, planned part of the system, such as a server or a network link, to see whether it recovers the way the design promised. Penetration testing means an authorised tester attacks the system the way a real intruder might, to find security holes. Each one answers a different question: can it handle the load, does it survive failure, and can an attacker get in?
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose your team designed a web service with two servers behind a load balancer, and the design document says the service survives one server failing. What is the most convincing way to find out whether that is true, and why would reading the design document alone not be enough?
lessons.teach:
Three verification practices test whether a production system behaves as its design claims. Each one applies a deliberate stress and then measures the result.

Load testing applies a controlled, measured amount of demand, usually increasing it step by step, and records latency (how long a request takes), error rate, and throughput (requests completed per second). Its purpose is to find the point where the system stops meeting its targets, and which part fails first, such as a database connection pool.

Chaos engineering injects a planned failure into a system that is serving realistic traffic: stopping an instance, adding network delay, or blocking access to a dependency. You state a hypothesis first, for example: when one zone is removed, the service keeps answering within its latency target. Then you run the experiment with a small blast radius (the amount of users or systems it can affect) and a way to stop it immediately.

Penetration testing is an authorised attempt to break into a system using techniques a real attacker would try, under written scope and rules of engagement. It finds exploitable weaknesses. It does not prove that none exist.

Worked example: a team claims its service handles 1,000 requests per second. A load test ramps from 200 to 1,400 requests per second. At about 1,050, the error rate climbs past 2 percent. The cause is a connection pool capped at 50. The test shows the real limit is lower than the design claim. The team raises the cap, reruns the test, and confirms the new limit.

Common mistake: treating a passed test in a staging environment as proof for production, when the data, traffic mix and scale differ.

Consequence: a system can look healthy in a design review and still fail at the first real traffic peak or the first zone outage, because nobody measured it under those conditions.

Verification is the evidence that turns a design claim into a known operating limit.

questions.prompt: Lumen Parcel's package-tracking API handles about 4,000 requests per second across three availability zones. The team writes this hypothesis before testing: if one zone is removed, the p95 latency stays under 300 ms and the error rate stays under 0.5 percent. They send 2 percent of live traffic through a test path, remove one zone from that path only, and keep a switch that restores routing in one command. They run the experiment for 20 minutes. Steps 1 to 4 are done as described. Step 5 is missing: before the team can call the hypothesis confirmed or rejected, they must ___. Which completion fills the gap?
choices: Skip restoring routing, since the experiment window has already ended
Expand the removal to 100 percent of traffic so the result covers every user
Rewrite the hypothesis after the run so it matches the numbers that were observed
Compare the measured p95 latency and error rate against the stated targets, then restore routing
questions.why: A chaos experiment is judged by checking the observed measurements against the hypothesis's targets, and the blast radius is kept small with routing restored afterward, so the comparison is the step that completes the test.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Lending wants to find the request rate at which its loan-quote API begins to time out. It plans to increase traffic in steps and record latency, error rate and requests completed per second at each step. Which verification practice fits this goal?
choices: Penetration testing, because it measures how fast the API responds to traffic
Code review, because it checks each function for correctness before release
Chaos engineering, because it stops servers at random to see when quotes time out
Load testing, because it applies controlled, increasing demand to locate the point where targets fail
questions.why: Load testing applies measured, step-by-step demand to find where a system stops meeting its targets, which is exactly what Brightwater wants to learn.

questions.prompt: A vendor says its penetration test of a file-sharing service passed, so the service is now secure. Which statement best describes what that result actually supports?
choices: Penetration testing replaces load testing, because both measure how the system holds up under pressure
A pen test finds exploitable weaknesses within its agreed scope and cannot prove that none exist
The developers who built the service should run the penetration test themselves, without written rules
A passed penetration test proves no vulnerabilities exist when the scope was broad enough
questions.why: Penetration testing is an authorised attack within written scope that finds exploitable weaknesses, but it does not prove the absence of weaknesses.

questions.prompt: Corvid Ticketing's design document claims its checkout service handles 800 requests per second. A load test ramps from 100 to 1,000 requests per second. At about 620 requests per second, the p99 latency jumps and 503 errors begin rising. The logs show the worker thread pool, capped at 32, is fully busy, while database CPU is only around 40 percent. What does the test show?
choices: The service meets its 800 requests per second claim because the errors only began after 620 requests per second
The 800 requests per second design claim is not supported, the real limit is near 620, and the worker thread pool is the first part to fail
The database is the first part to fail, so the database must be scaled before the 800 claim can be checked again
The test is invalid because a ramp test cannot reveal where a system's limit lies
questions.why: The test found the real operating limit below the claim and identified the thread pool, not the database, as the first component to saturate.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only deployed code how load testing, chaos engineering and penetration testing differ in the question each one answers. Then name one limit of running chaos experiments in production.
lessons.modelAnswer: Load testing answers how much demand the system can take before it misses its targets. We ramp traffic up in steps and watch latency and errors, so we find the real ceiling and which component hits it first. Chaos engineering answers whether the system keeps working when a part of it fails. We state a hypothesis, such as a zone outage leaving latency within target, then inject a small, controlled failure and check the result. Penetration testing answers whether an attacker can get in. An authorised tester tries real attack paths within agreed scope. One limit of chaos experiments in production is blast radius. Even with a small scope and an automatic stop, an experiment can hurt real customers if the stop mechanism fails, so we only run it when we can halt it quickly and have agreed the risk.
rubricPoints: Load testing measures behaviour under increasing demand to find the real capacity limit.
Chaos engineering tests recovery from a planned failure against a stated hypothesis.
Penetration testing is an authorised attack that finds exploitable weaknesses within agreed scope.
A named limit: chaos experiments can affect real users, so blast radius and a stop mechanism are required.

suggested.rationale: Choosing which verification method fits a described production scenario is an exam-style reasoning skill, and no listed mission or planned engine teaches it directly.

scenarios.title: Harbor Lantern Ticketing: First Cloud Move for the Booking Platform
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Lantern Ticketing is a fictional company that sells tickets for regional concerts and sports matches. Its booking website and mobile app currently run on two physical servers in a rented server room. The chief executive expects ticket sales to spike many times over in the hour after a popular artist announces a show, and wants the platform moved to Google Cloud before the next major sale. You have been asked to draft the first architecture proposal. The product team has written three requests: customers must be able to reserve seats without waiting in a queue of more than a few seconds; the system must keep taking bookings even if one data centre zone (an isolated building or site within a cloud region) fails; and the finance director wants monthly running costs to stay flat in quiet months. Ticket PDFs and venue seat-map images also need a home, and the team is unsure whether to store them alongside the booking records.

Work through the following.

1. Sort the three product requests into functional and non-functional requirements (a functional requirement describes what the system must do; a non-functional requirement describes how well it must do it, such as speed, uptime, or cost). For each non-functional requirement, name the Well-Architected Framework pillar it serves (the six areas Google uses to judge a cloud design: operational excellence, security, reliability, cost optimization, performance optimization, and sustainability).

2. Choose a storage type for the ticket PDFs and seat-map images, and a database type for the booking records. Use the three storage categories: object storage (whole files stored under a name and fetched as a unit, suited to images and documents), file storage (shared folders mounted like a disk), and databases (structured records you can query and update safely). Name the real trade-off of your database choice.

3. Propose a compute platform for the booking service. Name one cost option you would consider and one you would reject for the checkout step, and state the trade-off for each.
subParts: Sort requests into functional and non-functional, and map non-functional ones to Well-Architected pillars
Choose storage type for files and database type for bookings, and name the trade-off
Propose compute platform for bookings and justify one accepted and one rejected cost option
modelAnswer: The seat reservation and the confirmation step are functional requirements, because they describe actions the system performs. The queue wait of a few seconds is non-functional and serves the performance optimization pillar, because it is about speed under load. Staying available when one zone fails is non-functional and serves the reliability pillar, because it is about the system continuing to work through a failure. The flat monthly cost in quiet months is non-functional and serves the cost optimization pillar. A strong answer also notes the tension: a flat cost floor conflicts with automatic scaling up for a sale, so the design should aim for a low baseline that grows only during spikes, and the proposal should say so openly rather than promising both perfectly.

Ticket PDFs and seat-map images fit object storage, which keeps whole files under a name and serves them cheaply and durably, and it suits content that is written once and read many times. Booking records fit a managed relational database, which stores structured rows and supports transactions, so a seat is either fully booked or not booked at all, and two customers cannot both take the last seat. The real trade-off of the relational database is that strong consistency and transactions make seat locking reliable, but scaling writes across many regions or very large volumes is harder and more expensive than with simpler stores. A common mistake is storing the PDFs as large fields inside the booking database; this bloats the database, slows backups and restores, and can slow the booking path that customers are waiting on.

Cloud Run, a managed service that runs packaged containers and scales instances up and down with request volume, fits a booking API that must absorb a spike and then shrink, and it is billed by use rather than by idle servers. Google Kubernetes Engine (a managed Kubernetes cluster) is an alternative that offers more control over the environment but adds operational work the team would have to staff. For the cost option, a committed use discount (a reduced rate in exchange for agreeing to pay for a fixed amount of compute over a set term) can be considered for the steady baseline of the database and always-on services; its trade-off is that you pay for the commitment even if demand falls. Spot VMs (discounted virtual machines that Google may reclaim at short notice) should be rejected for checkout, because a reclaimed machine mid-payment could leave a seat held with no confirmation, which harms customers and the reliability requirement.

scenarios.title: Harbourline Freight: Hybrid Link, Archive, and Batch Compute
scenarios.scenario: Harbourline Freight is a fictional regional shipping company. Its shipment-tracking system still runs in an on-premises data center, meaning servers the company owns and operates in its own building rather than in a cloud provider's facility. The team is moving reporting and archive workloads to Google Cloud in three stages, and you are the junior architect supporting the first stage. Harbourline needs its data center to reach a Google Cloud Virtual Private Cloud (VPC, a private, isolated network you define inside Google Cloud) over a private path, not the open internet. The expected traffic is about 200 Mbps on average, with bursts during month-end reporting. Second, the company stores about 40 TB of scanned delivery-proof images. Images are needed often for 30 days, rarely after that, and must be kept for 7 years by law. Third, a nightly job reprocesses route data. It can tolerate interruption because each run saves progress every 10 minutes. A separate live dashboard for dispatchers must never pause. Write your recommendations for the three items below. 1. Choose a private connection from the data center to the VPC, name the Google Cloud product you would use, and explain why it fits the bandwidth and why the public internet is not the right path. 2. Design the storage for the scanned images, including the storage class for the first 30 days, the rule that moves older objects to a cheaper class, and how you would enforce the 7-year retention period. 3. Decide which compute option runs the nightly reprocessing job and which runs the dispatcher dashboard, and explain the trade-off that makes this split sensible.
subParts: Private hybrid connection choice and justification
Storage tiering and retention design for scanned images
Compute volatility split between batch job and live dashboard
modelAnswer: Recommend Cloud VPN (HA VPN, a high-availability encrypted tunnel between the data center and the VPC) for the first stage, because at about 200 Mbps average with bursts it provides a private, encrypted path over the existing internet connection, can be provisioned quickly, and costs less than a dedicated line. Note that traffic still crosses the public internet inside the encrypted tunnel, so the path is private but not a dedicated physical link. Cloud Interconnect (a dedicated or partner physical link into Google's network) is the upgrade path if sustained throughput or latency needs grow. The public internet alone is wrong because traffic is unencrypted and unmanaged between the two sites, and it is exposed to congestion without any routing control. Name the VPC, use Cloud Router for dynamic routes, and mention that bandwidth should be checked against measured peak traffic.

Store the scanned images in a Cloud Storage bucket (a named container for stored objects, which are files plus metadata). Use the Standard storage class for the first 30 days, since those objects are read often and Standard has the lowest access cost. Add an Object Lifecycle Management rule (an automatic policy that changes or deletes objects based on age) that moves objects older than 30 days to Archive storage, the cheapest class for rarely read data, with a higher retrieval cost. Enforce the 7-year requirement with a retention policy on the bucket set to 7 years, which blocks deletion or overwrite of objects until they age past that period. Optionally lock the retention policy so it cannot be shortened later, which satisfies auditors. Mistake to avoid: a lifecycle delete rule set shorter than the legal period would destroy records the law requires you to keep.

Run the nightly route reprocessing on Spot VMs (Compute Engine virtual machines offered at a steep discount, which Google can reclaim with only a short warning). This is acceptable because the job checkpoints progress every 10 minutes, so a reclaimed run resumes from the last checkpoint rather than restarting from zero, and the job is not time-critical to the minute. Run the live dispatcher dashboard on standard on-demand VMs, which Google does not reclaim for capacity reasons, so the dashboard does not pause. The trade-off is lower cost for the interruptible batch work versus guaranteed availability for the user-facing service. Mistake to avoid: placing the dashboard on Spot VMs, which could drop dispatchers mid-shift.

scenarios.title: Verdant Pet Pharmacy: card data, keys and the audit trail
scenarios.scenario:
Verdant Pet Pharmacy is a fictional online company that sells prescription medication for pets. It takes card payments, stores pet owners' contact details and veterinary prescription records, and plans to open to customers in the European Union next quarter. Its engineering team is moving everything to Google Cloud, and you have just joined as the cloud engineer. The security lead, Priya, has asked you for a short design note covering three areas. Organization is the top node in Google Cloud's resource hierarchy, which belongs to the company's domain. Folders group projects, and projects are the containers that hold resources such as storage buckets and databases. Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the system that decides who can do what to which resource. Answer each numbered sub-task in plain language, naming the specific Google Cloud control you would use.

1. Design the resource hierarchy and IAM so that production, staging and development are kept apart, and so that the people who deploy changes to production cannot also approve those changes or read the audit logs.

2. The payment-processor API key and the card data need protection. Explain which key management service you would use to control the encryption keys, where the payment-processor API key should live instead of in application code, and how you would find and mask card numbers that have leaked into logs or storage. Explain how you would also stop data from being copied out of the project to an outside account. Card data falls under the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), a set of rules for handling card numbers that the company must meet.

3. Auditors will ask for a record of who accessed pet owner data and changed settings, kept for at least one year and unable to be deleted early. Explain which logs you would turn on, where you would send them for long-term keeping, and how you would make sure all new resources stay in EU locations.
subParts: Resource hierarchy and IAM design for separation of duties
Key management, secret storage, card data discovery and data exfiltration controls
Audit logging, long-term retention and data location control
modelAnswer: Create one organization with three folders, one each for production, staging and development, and place separate projects inside each folder. Policies and IAM grants set on a folder pass down to its projects, so a grant on staging never reaches production. Grant roles to groups, not to individual people, and at the narrowest level that works, following least privilege (giving only the access needed for the job). For separation of duties, use distinct groups for deployers, change approvers and auditors so that no single group can both push a change to production and sign it off or read the logs that record it. Example: a developer receives the Viewer role on the staging folder only, and gets nothing on production. Common mistake: granting Owner at the organization level so it applies everywhere. The consequence is that one compromised account can reach every project and can change or erase evidence.

Use Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) to create a customer-managed encryption key (CMEK), which is an encryption key the company controls and can rotate, disable or destroy, and set the storage buckets and BigQuery datasets to encrypt with it. Store the payment-processor API key in Secret Manager, a service that holds secrets encrypted and gives access by IAM role, and have the application read it at run time rather than keeping it in code or config files. Run Sensitive Data Protection, a scanning service that detects patterns such as card numbers, over logs and storage, and use its masking or redaction to hide what it finds. Put the storage and BigQuery projects inside a VPC Service Controls perimeter, which is a boundary around Google Cloud services that blocks data from being copied to projects outside it even by someone with valid credentials. Common mistake: writing full card numbers to application logs. The consequence is that copies of those logs spread to many systems, which widens the PCI DSS scope and turns every one of those systems into something the company must audit and protect.

Turn on Cloud Audit Logs for the sensitive projects, including Data Access logs, because some services do not record data reads unless you enable them. Create a log sink, which is a rule that copies selected log entries to a destination, and send these logs to a Cloud Storage bucket with a retention policy of at least one year and a bucket lock so the policy cannot be shortened or the objects deleted before that period ends. Use an organization policy, a rule set at the organization or folder level that every project inherits, with the resource locations constraint to allow only EU regions, so new resources cannot be created elsewhere. Common mistake: relying on the default retention of Cloud Logging, which is shorter than the one-year period auditors require. The consequence is that the evidence an auditor asks for may already be gone, and the company cannot show what happened to pet owner data.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Parcels: Fixing Risky Releases and Planning for Outages
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Parcels is a fictional regional parcel-delivery company with about 300 staff. Its small software team ships changes to the package-tracking website by hand: a developer copies files onto the production server on Friday afternoons. Over the last quarter, three releases broke the customer tracking page, and each rollback (returning the site to its previous working version) took most of a day. Dana Okafor, the chief financial officer, wants a written recommendation before the next budget meeting. You are the cloud architect advising on process, not on server sizing. Answer the following:
1. Describe how you would find the root cause of the broken releases, meaning the underlying process gap rather than the single bad change. Then name one step in an automated delivery pipeline (CI/CD, meaning continuous integration and continuous delivery: a chain that automatically builds, tests, and then ships each code change) that would catch this kind of failure before customers see it.
2. Dana asks whether moving the tracking platform to a pay-as-you-go cloud service is a capital expense (CapEx, a one-time purchase of long-lived equipment) or an operating expense (OpEx, an ongoing cost paid as you use a service). Explain the difference in plain terms, say what the shift means for the budget, and describe how you would present the trade-off honestly.
3. Brightwater has no written plan for a regional data-centre outage and has never agreed how long it can be down or how much recent data it can afford to lose. Explain how disaster recovery (the technical steps to bring systems back) differs from business continuity (keeping the business functioning during and after a disruption), propose a recovery time objective (RTO, the maximum acceptable downtime) and recovery point objective (RPO, the maximum acceptable data loss) approach for leadership to decide on, and explain how you would get that decision made.
subParts: Root cause and a pipeline testing gate
CapEx versus OpEx and the budget trade-off
Disaster recovery versus business continuity, and RTO and RPO decisions
modelAnswer: Root cause: I would review the last three failed releases with the team in a blameless way, asking why each problem reached production, not who made the change. Repeated questioning (for example, why did the tracking page break, why was it not tested, why was there no staging check, why do releases happen by hand on Fridays) usually shows that nothing automatic checks changes before they go live. The fix is a pipeline step such as an automated test suite plus a staging deployment, run on every change, that blocks promotion to production if the tracking page checks fail. Good answers name the process gap (manual, unchecked, risky timing) and a concrete gate that would have caught the failure.

CapEx versus OpEx: CapEx is money spent up front on assets the company owns, such as servers, which are depreciated (spread over several years on the books). OpEx is money spent on services as they are used, such as a pay-as-you-go cloud bill, which is usually expensed in the period it is incurred. Moving to cloud generally shifts spending from CapEx toward OpEx, which can lower the upfront cash need but makes monthly costs variable and depends on usage. A strong answer presents both sides: total cost over three to five years, the effect on the budget and cash flow, and the risk of surprise bills if usage grows without monitoring. I would recommend budget alerts and cost reviews so the trade-off is visible, not hidden.

Disaster recovery is the set of technical actions to restore systems after a failure, such as restoring backups in another region. Business continuity is broader: it covers how staff, customers, suppliers, and decisions keep working during and after an outage. Recovery targets are business decisions, so I would propose a short options table (for example, a tracking page back within 4 hours with at most 1 hour of data lost, versus 24 hours and 24 hours at lower cost) with the cost of each. I would run a facilitated workshop with operations, finance, and customer service, record the chosen RTO and RPO, and get a named executive to sign off. Without that sign-off, the technical design has no agreed target to build against.

scenarios.title: Harbor Lantern Logistics: advising a half-finished deployment
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Lantern Logistics is a fictional freight company that is moving its shipment-tracking service onto Google Cloud. A small dev/ops team has already started building it and asks you, the Professional Cloud Architect, for advice before they release it to customers next month. You advise and review; the team does the building. Three things are in progress. First, the team has written the cloud resources (networks, a database, a messaging topic, and the service that runs the tracking code) as Infrastructure as Code, meaning the resources are described in version-controlled text files rather than clicked together in a console. They plan to use Terraform, an open-source tool that reads those files, shows a preview of what would change (the plan), and then creates or changes resources to match (the apply). Second, the tracking service listens for delivery events on Pub/Sub, a managed messaging service where publishers send messages to a topic and subscribers pull them, and the team has no reliable way to test that code on a laptop without touching the real cloud project. They also want a load test before launch. Third, partner companies will call the tracking API, and the team wants to know how partners should authenticate, how the team should avoid putting secret keys into code, and whether Apigee, Google's API management product (a gateway placed in front of APIs that handles keys, quotas, and traffic policies), should sit in front of the service. Answer the team's questions as an advisor.

1. Advise the team on how to use the Terraform plan step before any change reaches the production project, and what a reviewer should check in that plan.
2. Advise the team on which testing types to use for this service (unit, integration, load), what each one proves, and how a Pub/Sub emulator, a local stand-in for the real messaging service, fits into the testing before the real project is involved.
3. Advise the team on how partners and the tracking service should authenticate to Google APIs without embedding long-lived secret keys in code, and whether Apigee should sit in front of the API and why.
subParts: Choosing unit, integration, and load tests with a Pub/Sub emulator
Authentication for partners and services, and whether to use Apigee
modelAnswer: Advise the team to run terraform plan and save its output, then have a second person review it before anyone runs terraform apply. The plan lists each resource that will be created, changed, or destroyed, without making any change. The reviewer should look for deletions or replacements of the database or topic, which can cause data loss or downtime, check that the right project and region are named, and confirm the state file (the record Terraform keeps of what it has built) is stored remotely with locking so two people cannot apply at once. Common mistake: applying straight from a laptop with no saved plan, so what is reviewed is not what runs. Consequence: an unreviewed replacement of the production database can delete customer tracking history.

Advise unit tests for small functions such as parsing a delivery event, which are fast and run on every change. Advise integration tests to check the service talks correctly to Pub/Sub and the database, which prove the pieces work together. Advise load tests to measure how the service behaves under expected and peak traffic, which prove capacity and latency, not correctness. The Pub/Sub emulator is a local fake that behaves like the real messaging service, so developers can publish and receive test messages on a laptop or in a build pipeline without using the live project, cost, or real customer data. It is good for integration checks but does not prove real-world performance, so load tests must still run against a non-production environment that mirrors production. Common mistake: relying only on the emulator and assuming load behaviour is proven. Consequence: the service may pass every local test and still fail at launch traffic.

Advise that services and partners should use Google Cloud service accounts, which are identities for software rather than people, and that the service should receive short-lived credentials through its attached identity, not a downloaded key file stored in code or a repository. Partners should be given individual credentials that can be revoked, and the team should grant each identity only the roles it needs (least privilege, meaning the minimum access). Advise placing Apigee in front of the API: it handles API keys and OAuth-style tokens for partners, enforces quotas and rate limits, and gives one place to monitor and change traffic policy without changing the tracking code. Common mistake: committing a service account key file to the repository, which anyone with repository access can copy and use indefinitely. Consequence: a leaked key lets an outsider act as the tracking service until someone notices and rotates it.

scenarios.title: Ticket Checkout Launch at Brightwell Tickets
scenarios.scenario: Brightwell Tickets is a fictional online seller of concert tickets, based in a mid-sized city. Its checkout service runs on Google Cloud and handles payment requests from a web app and a mobile app. Next month, a famous band releases tickets at 10:00 a.m., and the company expects roughly twenty times its normal peak traffic in the first five minutes. The platform team has been asked by the operations manager, Priya, to show that the system is reliable before launch, not just that it was designed to be. The team already has dashboards, but they are mostly CPU and memory graphs that nobody checks at night. Priya wants a plan that shows how the team will know quickly when customers are failing, how they will prove the system can take the load, and how they will ship the new version of the checkout code without risking a bad launch. Think of the system as a managed service that the team operates, where every failed payment is a lost sale and an angry customer. Answer the three tasks below in plain language, explaining your reasoning as you go. 1. Brightwell wants an alert that wakes the on-call engineer only when customers are truly affected. Explain what a service level objective (an agreed target for how well the service should behave, such as the share of checkouts that succeed) is, and describe the alert you would set up, including the signal you would watch and why CPU alone is a poor choice for paging someone. 2. Before the sale, the team must run a load test (a controlled experiment that sends artificial traffic to the system to see how it behaves under pressure). Describe what you would measure, what result would count as a pass, and how you would make the test realistic enough to trust. 3. The new checkout version will be released during a quiet week. Explain how you would roll it out so that only a small share of users see it first, what you would watch during that rollout, and the exact steps you would take to return to the old version if the new one misbehaves.
subParts: Alerting based on a service level objective, with the signal chosen and why CPU alone is a poor paging signal
Load test design: what to measure, what counts as a pass, and how to keep the test realistic
Gradual release (canary) with monitored signals and a tested rollback plan
modelAnswer: A service level objective is an agreed, measurable target for how well a service should behave from the customer's point of view, for example, 99.5 percent of checkout requests succeed within two seconds over a rolling 30-day window. Because it is measured from the customer's side, it tells you whether people are being harmed. The alert should watch a user-facing signal such as the ratio of failed checkout requests (HTTP 5xx errors or payment declines caused by the system, not by the customer) to total checkout requests, and the latency of successful checkouts. Good practice is to page on a burn rate: an alert fires when the team is using up its error budget (the allowed amount of failure implied by the objective) much faster than planned, for example if a large fraction of a month's budget would be spent within one hour. This avoids paging for brief blips while still catching a real outage quickly. CPU alone is a poor paging signal because a server can run at high CPU while serving customers perfectly well, and it can sit at low CPU while every request fails because of a broken database connection. Use CPU and memory as diagnostic dashboards that help the on-call engineer find the cause after the customer-facing alert fires. Common mistake: paging on every single error, which produces alert fatigue, so engineers begin ignoring the pager.

Measure throughput (requests per second the system completes), error rate, and latency, reported as percentiles such as the 95th percentile (the response time that 95 percent of requests beat) rather than averages, because averages hide slow outliers that frustrate customers. Also measure resource saturation, such as database connections in use, to find the bottleneck. Define the pass criteria before the test runs: for example, at 20 times normal peak traffic, the 95th percentile latency stays under two seconds, the error rate stays under 0.5 percent, and autoscaling adds capacity within the time the team has promised. Make the test realistic by copying the real request mix (browsing, adding to cart, paying), using realistic user think times between clicks, running against a production-like environment with the same database size and settings, and including the third-party payment provider or a faithful stand-in with realistic delays. Ramp traffic up gradually so you can see where the system starts to degrade rather than just whether it survives one spike. Common mistake: testing only the front page, which is cached and cheap, and declaring the system ready while the expensive payment path has never been exercised at scale. Consequence for a running system: if the test is unrealistic, the launch day becomes the real test, and the first sign of a bottleneck is lost sales.

Use a canary release, meaning the new version is deployed alongside the old one and receives a small share of traffic first, for example 5 percent, chosen at random or by a traffic-splitting rule the platform supports. Keep both versions running and compare them on the same signals used for the alert: checkout success rate, latency percentiles, and error counts, with the old version as the baseline. Increase the share in steps (for example 5, 25, 50, then 100 percent) only when each step stays within agreed limits for a fixed observation period. Rollback must be rehearsed in advance: the team keeps the previous version available, records the exact command or console action that shifts all traffic back to it, and confirms that a database migration in the release is backward compatible so the old version still works after the change. The decision to roll back should be triggered by a rule written beforehand, such as the new version's error rate exceeding the old version's by a set margin for five minutes. Common mistake: releasing a schema change that the old version cannot read, which makes rollback impossible in practice. Consequence: a rollback that takes thirty minutes instead of two leaves customers failing during a window the business could not afford.
